title: OpenCode 2.0
body_text: OpenCode 2.0 Anomaly â All posts OpenCode 2.0 OpenCode 2.0 Carry the disk Nothing waiting on the desk OpenCode 2.0 is a major over haul. It draws on mil lions of daily users' expe ri ence to deliver a system that can flex to every thing an agent needs to be. There are quite a lot of new fea tures, per for mance improve ments, and bug fixes but here are some of the more impact ful user-facing changes. The Service From the begin ning OpenCode adopted a client/server model. However, this was not some thing it took advan tage of by default and was mostly used by power users. In 2.0 this server now auto mat i cally runs as a single back ground process on your machine. When you open up a TUI, the web inter face or the desktop app they're all talking to the same central process. Terminal Fix flaky test Web Fix flaky test Desktop Add dark mode review.ts Review changes opencode pid 48213 Stopped Starting Running Sessions Fix flaky test Add dark mode Review changes If you're using the pro gram matic client @opencode/client to make your own scripts, they will autodis cover the local service and just work. This is par tic u larly useful for sched uled tasks. You can also call it via CLI by using opencode api com mands. You can expose it to other hosts and run /pair or opencode pair to connect it to other appli ca tions. We have native apps in the works that take advan tage of this flow. The API The old API grew hap haz ardly as we and the world col lec tively learned what agents are and should be. It was bad. We started from scratch and exam ined all the weird use cases across the mil lions of users who use OpenCode every day. It now sup ports nearly any thing you need to be able to do. OpenCode is also aware of its own API and will call it to do useful things like moving the current session into a git work tree when start ing new work. Session New session YOU Start rate limiting uploads in a new worktree. execute { code } âº opencode. worktree_create [name=rate-limit] âº opencode. session_rename [title=Rate limit uploads] âº opencode. session_move [directory=~/worktrees/rate-limit] YOU The flaky test session is stuck. Stop it, have it quarantine the test, and close my finished tabs. execute { code } âº opencode. session_list âº opencode. session_context [sessionID=ses_7c41e09a] â "Retrying uploads.test.ts againâ¦" execute { code } âº opencode. session_interrupt [sessionID=ses_7c41e09a] âº opencode. session_prompt [sessionID=ses_7c41e09a, text=Quarantine uploads.test.ts] âº opencode. tab_close [sessionID=ses_2f9d61b4] Stopped it, told it to quarantine the test, closed the config tab. OpenCode ~/app Fix flaky upload test interrupted Migrate config loader tab closed New session this session ~/worktrees/rate-limit We've also shipped a new client package @opencode/client that con tains clients for vanilla JavaScript as well as Effect. review.ts import { OpenCode } from "@opencode/client" import { Service } from "@opencode/client/service" const endpoint = await Service. ensure () const client = OpenCode. make ({ baseUrl: endpoint.url, headers: Service. headers (endpoint), }) const session = await client.session. create ({ location: { directory: process. cwd () }, }) await client.session. prompt ({ sessionID: session.id, text: "Review the current changes" , }) Code Mode The models love to write code and OpenCode 2.0 takes advan tage of that more than any other coding agent. We've built a minimal JavaScript inter preter in the @opencode/codemode package. Session YOU File GitHub bugs in Linear. execute { code } tools.github.list_issues tools.linear.save_issue execute { code } ["OC-412", "OC-413", "OC-414"] Code Mode return [ search ({ query: "list github issues" }), search ({ query: "create linear issue" })] const { issues } = await tools.github. list_issues ({ owner: "anomalyco" , repo: "opencode" , labels: [ "bug" ], state: "OPEN" , }) const filed = await Promise . all (issues. map (({ title }) => tools.linear. save_issue ({ team: "OC" , title }))) return filed. map ( issue => issue.identifier) MCP servers github linear sentry This package ingests MCP servers or OpenAPI end points, con vert ing them into func tions that the agent can call in a script. It can run these scripts natively without the com plex ity of Node.js VMs or embed ding com pli cated solu tions like QuickJS. This lets your agent write scripts that can do things like call a tool, map over the results and call another tool. Single round trip instead of calling them one at a time. All MCP servers in 2.0 are opted into code mode by default. This means you can add a thou sand of them with minimal context bloat and your agent will dis cover and compose them to get things done. Background Tasks The latest batch of models are incred i bly good at orches tra tion and it is impor tant for har nesses to let them express the full extent of that capa bil ity. Session YOU Spawn a background fable subagent to review this code. subagent review this code fable background 2 comments $ shell bun test background 148 passed edit src/retry.ts +12 $ $ shell bun run build background done Press ctrl b to move running work to the background YOU Update the changelog too. edit CHANGELOG.md +3 All done. The review left 2 comments, 148 tests passed, the build succeeded and the changelog is updated. Background review this code fable $ bun test $ bun run build ctrl b First, we've added back ground sub agents. This allows the primary agent to kick off some work to another one while it con tin ues. This happens auto mat i cally but you can also trigger it man u ally - even with a dif fer ent model. It lets you do things like âspawn a back ground fable sub agent to review this codeâ while you keep prompt ing. Second, we've added back ground shell com mands. The shell tool can be invoked asyn chronously so long-running work does not have to block the primary agent. It'll be noti fied when things are com plete. If any fore ground shell command or sub agent takes longer than you expect, you can hit a hotkey to move them to the back ground so you can keep prompt ing. Plugins Although OpenCode 1.0 had a plugin system, it never got the atten tion it needed. To correct that, we forced our selves to imple ment nearly every OpenCode 2.0 feature as an inter nal plugin and there are now 80+ of them. This guar an tees that the Plugin API stays well main tained. We've also pro moted TUI plugins from exper i men tal to stable. Since it is all powered by OpenTUI, you can build nearly any thing. Here is an example of some thing useless. We also spent quite a lot of time ensuring everything in OpenCode 2.0 can be hot-reloaded. So it can write a plugin for itself mid-session and use it right away - we covered the design of this in a previous blogpost . You can ask OpenCode to build whatever plugin you want and it knows how to. But if you do want to read the docs, they are available here . The SDK OpenCode can also now be used as a library with the @opencode/sdk package. This is the exact same code that powers our CLI. This means you can strip it down and make your own flavor of OpenCode that runs on a server or in spe cial ized envi ron ments like Durable Objects. And then you can connect to it from any OpenCode client since it speaks the stan dard OpenCode server pro to col. It also has an optional Effect-based API. This one is still in development as things are shifting but you can already use it . Upgrading To upgrade the CLI, make sure you're on the latest 1.x release, then run opencode upgrade --major . To upgrade your desktop app, download the latest here . There are some break ing changes. 1.0 plugins will not work in 2.0 Server API is completely different tui.json config is moved to json There are a lot of other changes but they are backwards compatible. It is worth pointing OpenCode at this doc so it can migrate things for you.

title: Things to know when you get cancer – 2026 Edition
body_text: of the document before the main stylesheets are loaded. --> Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition) · JJ Maxwell index Back to top Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition) 2026.10.14 I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far. You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation. AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note. You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups. You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines . You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case. If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is. Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion. I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time. Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation . Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors. Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings . The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). The rest of the HN comments are worth reading too.

Passkeys are not a trap
body_text: Passkeys Are Not a Trap Home Speaking Training Media Contact Sponsor 🌙 Subscribe Sponsored by:   Report URI - Passkeys protect login, not the session. Monitor what happens after authentication. Passkeys Passkeys Are Not a Trap Scott Helme Security researcher, entrepreneur and international speaker who specialises in web technologies. More posts by Scott Helme. Scott Helme 14 Oct 2026 • 4 min read A post called Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. has been doing the rounds over the last few days, making it pretty high on Hacker News, and I've had it sent to me many times with an 'is this true?' kind of vibe. It's written for "non-technical citizens of the web", and the headline advice is to stop using passkeys and go back to TOTP codes and passwords. The Argument The post makes what appears to be one central claim: Passkeys support something called attestation, which lets a website ask for cryptographic proof of what made the passkey. The author calls this a "hidden dial" and argues that sites will slowly turn it up, until you're only allowed to log in with approved software on an approved operating system, with no modifications, no LineageOS and no sharing your Netflix password. Throw in uBlock Origin, the FIDO Alliance membership list and the UK's image-scanning proposals, and the conclusion is that passkeys are "not designed to prioritize your interests". <that-escalated-quickly.gif> It's a compelling story. It just doesn't match how any of this actually works... Your Passkeys Don't Attest The passkeys most people use are synced passkeys, stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden or whatever other software of your choosing. These passkeys don't give websites an attestation statement at all, and though a site can ask, what comes back is none . I know this because I wrote an opensource passkeys library and made it available to everyone. If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that? Besides, the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for years now. Attestation Isn't What You Think It Is The post describes attestation as proving "that an approved passkey manager, operating system, and firmware are in use" which is simply not true. When it is present, WebAuthn attestation tells the site the make and model of the authenticator, identified by its AAGUID , with a certificate chain from the vendor to back it up. It says nothing about your OS, your browser, your extensions, whether your phone is rooted or jailbroken, your firmware version, or even what colour it is. The YubiKey Recommendation This is the part that surprised me the most. For people who want stronger security, the post recommends a hardware security key like a YubiKey, because it "avoids OS-wide attestation". YubiKeys are the authenticators that do attestation. Every one of them ships with a Yubico-issued attestation certificate, and enterprise attestation exists specifically so organisations can require approved hardware keys. I'd still recommend a YubiKey to anyone who wants one, they're excellent and I use them, but if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it! TOTP Is a Step Backwards The post holds up TOTP as "already" a great solution. TOTP is better than a password alone, absolutely, but it has one big weakness: you can type the code into the wrong website, just ask my good friend Troy Hunt . Phishing kits like Evilginx sit in the middle, relay your password and code to the real site in real time, and walk away with your session. This isn't theoretical, it's how a huge number of account takeovers happen today and we have the evidence to prove it. This is the problem that passkeys solve. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created for, so your browser simply won't use your example.com passkey on examp1e.com . There's no code to read out and nothing for the user to get wrong. The author even concedes this in the addendum, saying that passkeys are domain-bound and resist man-in-the-middle attacks, but still tells readers to avoid them. Swapping a phishing-resistant credential for a phishable one is a really bad trade... What You Should Do Keep using passkeys! Wherever a site offers one, take it, and store it in a password/passkey manager you trust. If you want to be able to move your credentials around, pick a provider that supports that. If you're worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that's worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn't happened, the biggest providers don't support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won't protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing. Sources I have some experience in this area: I created WhyNoPasskeys.com to track the availability of passkeys on the Web. I built and deployed passkeys support on my own SaaS company. We built our own passkeys library and had it security reviewed. I wrote about Security considerations when using Passkeys on your website . I wrote Passkeys 101: An Introduction to Passkeys and How They Work . I made our passkeys library opensource for everyone to use. I've done extensive security testing of passkeys implementations. I've openly acknowledged the limitations of not using attestation on passkeys. I think most of all that it's important to say I use passkeys everywhere I can because they're currently the best thing we have available to protect our accounts. And they're not a trap. title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
body_text: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics. | CSO Online Topics Latest Newsletters Resources Buyer’s Guides Events Editions Search Menu Topics Close Analytics Application Security Artificial Intelligence Business Continuity Business Operations Careers Cloud Security Compliance Contributor Content Critical Infrastructure Cybercrime Enterprise Buyer’s Guides Generative AI Identity and Access Management Industry IT Leadership IT Management Network Security Physical Security Privacy Risk Management Security Security Infrastructure Software Development Vulnerabilities Back Close Search US - EN Topics Latest Newsletters Resources Buyer’s Guides Events More Awards Blogs BrandPosts Events Podcasts Videos Buyer’s Guides & Enterprise Spotlights Topics Topics Analytics Application Security Artificial Intelligence Business Continuity Business Operations Careers Cloud Security Compliance Contributor Content Critical Infrastructure Cybercrime Enterprise Buyer’s Guides Generative AI Identity and Access Management Industry IT Leadership IT Management Network Security Physical Security Privacy Risk Management Security Security Infrastructure Software Development Vulnerabilities Americas United States Asia ASEAN India Europe United Kingdom Oceania Australia Home Artificial Intelligence by Cynthia Brumfield Contributing Writer AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics. News Analysis Oct 14, 2026 9 mins Cyber experts say AI labs’ containment and monitoring failures — not agents with minds of their own — are to blame for recent alarming hacking reports. CISOs should vet their AI vendors and tighten security basics as safeguards. Credit: PeopleImages / Shutterstock Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.” The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend. Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.” Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades. [ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ] Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise. “They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.” Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment. Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments. “These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’” “You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.” Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.” Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity. “I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off. And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.” On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.” Divorcing safety from security One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices. “I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.” SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.” Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.” But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.” Bad cybersecurity could increase liability If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions. Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers. However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok. Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures. BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.” He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.” SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’” What security leaders should do now Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved , CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires. First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.” For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.” But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’” “We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.” See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? Artificial Intelligence Technology Industry Access Control Identity and Access Management Security Intrusion Detection Software Security Monitoring Software Security Software Threat and Vulnerability Management by Cynthia Brumfield Contributing Writer Cynthia Brumfield is a veteran communications and technology analyst who is currently focused on cybersecurity. She runs a cybersecurity news destination site, Metacurity.com , consults with companies through her firm DCT-Associates, and is the author of the book published by Wiley, Cybersecurity Risk Management: Mastering the Fundamentals Using the NIST Cybersecurity Framework . Cynthia holds a Master of Planning Degree from the University of Virginia and a Bachelor’s degree from The George Washington University. She has won multiple AZBEE awards for her work on CSO, including two in 2025. title: Fire at Starlink site in Bulgaria after suspected sabotage in Poland
body_text: Fire at Starlink site in Bulgaria after suspected sabotage in Poland | dpa international Politics Economics Culture & Science Sports General News Trends & Features war medtop:20000062 conflict dpasubject:114 internet dpasubject:377 fire medtop:20000150 Bulgaria dpacountry:31 Russia dpacountry:139 Ukraine dpacountry:181 Poland dpacountry:135 updateme dpauserneed:updateme Fire at Starlink site in Bulgaria after suspected sabotage in Poland 14.10.2026, 20:51 Uhr By Elena Lalowa, dpa Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed on Wednesday that there had been a fire at a facility of the Starlink satellite internet service near the capital Sofia last week. Two young men holding German passports have been taken into custody in connection with the suspected attack, Bulgarian media later reported, citing investigators. The satellite network is a strategically important part of Ukraine's defence in the war against Russia's invasion. The fire had previously been made public by the pro-Western opposition alliance Democratic Bulgaria (DB). Radev said he would not provide any further details in light of the ongoing investigations. According to DB, 11 of 17 antennas at a Starlink facility near Sofia were deliberately set on fire on October 9. The antennas were used in the war in Ukraine, DB said. Pro-Western opposition parties said they suspected Russia was linked to the attack. Two German passport holders in custody Two men aged 20 and 21, both holding German passports, were detained in Bulgaria on Monday in connection with the suspected attack, several Bulgarian media outlets reported on Wednesday evening, citing investigators. According to the news outlet Faktor.bg, the two suspects have migrant backgrounds and had legally entered Bulgaria from Greece through the Kulata border crossing. The website reported that investigators were examining whether the suspects belonged to a larger sabotage network potentially linked to two men arrested in Germany earlier this week over a recent attack on a Starlink facility in Poland. Sabotage suspected Bulgarian officials stressed that the Starlink facility near Sofia was privately owned. Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told parliament that additional security measures had been introduced at similar facilities, even though responsibility for their protection rested with their owners. Plamen Tonchev, head of Bulgaria's State Agency for National Security (DANS), said he believed the fire at the Starlink facility was an act of sabotage. "Such acts of sabotage cannot be ruled out in the future either," he warned lawmakers. A fire also broke out at a Starlink ground terminal south of Warsaw on September 23. Two suspected saboteurs accused of carrying out that attack in Poland were arrested on Tuesday in NÃ¼rtingen, near Stuttgart in south-western Germany. The government in Warsaw suspects Russian intelligence services were behind the attack. (c) 2026 dpa Deutsche Presse Agentur GmbH powered by dpa-newslab | Legal Notice | About Us / Contact | Privacy

title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke
body_text: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke · sunshowers sunshowers about work about work Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke 2026-10-14 · 2 min read vcs shorts Discuss on Hacker News or Lobsters . Here is Anthropic describing ( archive link ) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient: How Anthropic describes Scion’s derived data. Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient: How I described Mononoke’s derived data. I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights 1 . The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.) I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.) But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle ) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke. Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse. For an example of a system with similar insights but many key design differences, see Vicent Marti’s blog post for Cursor .  ↩︎ Read other posts iddqd, or the hardest kind of unsafe Rust → sunshowers Created with love in Oakland, CA. © Rain 2020-present. title: Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote
body_text: Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote - Startup Fortune Search S F Oct 15, 2026 · 1:02 AM – Users Online Online US | INTERNATIONAL | ASIA | Discussions Community 💬 S F Startup Fortune Search ⌕ Home News AI Entrepreneur Interviews Guides Tech Opinion Latest Community Metropolix Most Read Banks are now trying to offload… Seedance 3.0 Brings Feature-Length Control to… Cisco turns Webex into an AI… An AI agent that reverse engineers… Banks are now trying to offload… Seedance 3.0 Brings Feature-Length Control to… Cisco turns Webex into an AI… An AI agent that reverse engineers… Home › Ai Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote JPMorgan and MUFG are part of the group that has spent more than six months trying to distribute $38 billion in construction debt tied to a Texas and Wisconsin data center project leased to Oracle. Janet Harrison Oct 11, 2026 · 12:25 AM · 5 min read · 65.8K reads this.classList.remove('sf-copied'),1500)" aria-label="Copy link"> JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG are quietly shopping pieces of the AI debt pile they helped build, a sign the lenders closest to the money have started hedging their own bet. Six months ago, banks were racing each other to underwrite data center loans tied to Oracle, Meta and the rest of the AI buildout. Now some of the same banks are trying to get that debt off their books. JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG have been exploring significant risk transfers, according to a report from the Financial Times. These are deals that let a bank keep a loan on paper while shifting its riskiest slice to outside investors. The banks are doing this because they are bumping up against internal limits on how much AI-linked exposure any one lender can hold. One case shows how stuck this has gotten. A group of banks including JPMorgan and MUFG has spent more than six months trying to distribute $38 billion in construction debt tied to a Texas and Wisconsin data center project leased to Oracle, Bloomberg has reported. Some lenders are now willing to sell pieces of it to non-bank buyers at a discount, just to move it. Six months is a long time to sit on debt nobody underwrote to hold forever. Matthew Moniot, co-head of credit risk sharing at Man Group, told the Financial Times the deal sizes involved are "out of scale to anything we've thought about, ever." That is not a hedge-fund manager talking down a trade he wants no part of. It is someone whose job is pricing exactly this kind of risk, saying the numbers no longer fit any model he has used before. Oracle is the clearest tell. Its five-year credit default swaps, the cost of insuring against the company defaulting, climbed to around 151 basis points in early October, levels last seen in 2009, according to market data cited by Bloomberg. S&P had already cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, a single notch above junk, back in July. The company is reportedly targeting more than $40 billion in additional debt and equity this fiscal year. That is on top of the $18 billion in bonds it sold in a single day last September, and the money is needed to keep funding its Texas, Wisconsin and New Mexico sites. Oracle Sues Wisconsin Over A $7 Billion Data Center Collateral Bill Oracle sued Wisconsin's Public Service Commission over a rule that could force it to post more than $7 billion in collateral for its Port Washington data center campus. The fight helped push S&P to cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, one notch above junk, as the company's AI spending outpaces its cash flow. - Oracle Wisconsin data center collateral dispute - utilities regulator $7 billion lawsuit Demand for that paper has thinned out, too. Bonds from Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle now trade at a premium to similarly rated non-AI corporate debt. Order books for their offerings have shrunk from roughly five times the amount on sale back in February to under two times by July, Bloomberg has reported. That is the difference between a bond that sells itself and one a bank has to work to place. None of this is happening in isolation. The 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.304% this month, its highest since 2002, after a $39 billion auction cleared at 5.30%, the highest auction yield since 2000. The Federal Reserve's own September meeting minutes named AI-related corporate borrowing as a contributor to that move. Capital Economics argues the bigger driver is plain old inflation and government deficits, not tech company bond sales. Whoever is right about the cause, the effect is the same for anyone trying to finance a data center right now: the risk-free rate they are borrowing against just got a lot more expensive. Frankly, the mechanics here matter more than the headline number. Banks do not sell down debt they are confident in. They sell down debt when they are worried about concentration, which is exactly what "approaching internal limits" means in plain English: too much of this bank's balance sheet is now one bet on one sector holding up. Spreading $120 billion of AI infrastructure spending across special purpose vehicles was supposed to make that risk easier to swallow. That is the structure Oracle, Meta, xAI and CoreWeave have all used to keep debt off their own balance sheets. Instead the risk is turning up at the banks that financed the SPVs in the first place. The investors who still want in have gotten pickier about where. Capital is rotating toward data centers leased to investment-grade hyperscalers like Microsoft and Google, and away from weaker credits, Bloomberg has reported. That is exactly why CoreWeave-leased paper prices at 7.00% to 9.875%, against the 5.70% to 7.875% that hyperscaler-leased bonds command, per bond market data compiled by CCIR. A smaller, less capitalized AI infrastructure company trying to raise debt next quarter is now competing for the same nervous pool of lenders as Oracle. Except without Oracle's balance sheet or its existing customer base to point to. That's the part of this story that does not show up in a single day's stock move. The AI boom still runs on the assumption that credit stays open indefinitely at reasonable terms. Six months of a bank struggling to sell $38 billion in loans is the clearest evidence yet that assumption is being tested in real time, not in some theoretical downturn still years away. Ben Butcher Data Editor Updated 13 October 2026 5:22pm BST Published 13 October 2026 5:05pm BST Suicide rates among middle-aged men are higher than ever, new figures have revealed. Men in their early 50s were more likely to die by suicide than anyone else last year, according to data from the Office for National Statistics . There were also increases in suicides among pensioners, with the biggest rise among those aged 75 and older, while the rates among men under 45 fell slightly. Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink Mental Illness, said the rate of deaths by suicide remained “stubbornly high”. He said: “Every suicide is a devastating tragedy, and these figures are a stark reminder that many people are reaching crisis point without getting the help they need.” The reasons behind suicide were “complex”, he said, but added that many people were “facing significant pressures in their lives, including financial issues, job insecurity, rising housing costs, loneliness and poor mental health ”. Suicide rate highest on record Mr Winstanley added: “While these factors affect everyone differently, they can contribute to distress and overwhelm, and leave people at risk of suicide.” The data, which cover England and Wales, showed that 6,162 suicide deaths had been registered in 2025. This was down from 6,190 last year, but the overall rate remained broadly the same at 11.3 deaths per 100,000 people. The stats watchdog uses deaths per 100,000 people to calculate changing rates while accounting for changes in the size of the population. Almost a third of the deaths were among men aged 45 to 64, which was up by 49 compared with 2024. The rate increased to 23.8 per 100,000, up from 23.2 the year before and the highest on record since data collection began in 1981. For men aged 50 to 54 specifically, the rate increased to 28, suggesting this group was at the highest risk. Men continued to be more than three times as likely to take their own lives as women overall. Among middle-aged women, there were 553 deaths – a rate of seven per 100,000, which was the same as 2024. Sonya Trivedy, the executive director of external engagement at Samaritans, said the figures “show that suicide rates are among the highest recorded rates this century”. She said: “The evidence is clear that successive governments have failed to deliver on their promise to reduce suicide rates and make suicide prevention a priority. Today must act as a wake up call. The current approach is not working; we need meaningful action and proper funding if lives are to be saved.” The data show a growing gap in suicide rates between middle-aged men and those aged 25 to 44. Recommended Simon Reeve: 'I was a whisker away from taking my own life' Read more There were 19.5 deaths per 100,000 men aged 25 to 44 last year, which is the widest gap since 2009, when middle-aged male suicide rates overtook those of younger adults. The rate increased from 14 to 14.4 per 100,000 for those aged 65 to 74 and from 13.2 to 15.4 among those aged 75 or older. Marjorie Wallace, the chief executive of mental health charity Sane, said she was “not surprised” by the data. She said: “Analysis of the contact we receive reflects this – almost 60 per cent of our callers now talk about suicide or self-harm, a very different picture than 10 years ago. “While middle-aged men in their forties and fifties still remain at greatest risk, our other concern is the number of young people, particularly girls and women aged 16 to 24, who report anxiety and depression on a scale not experienced before.” Join the conversation Show comments The Telegraph values your comments but kindly requests all posts are on topic, constructive and respectful. How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
body_text: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet Subscribe! Not-Ship Charting the age of uncertainty. Subscribe! October 14, 2026 How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet Amanda Shendruk Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition. But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because... 💙 Amanda Support Not-Ship! Last week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over : the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop. In a nutshell, here's what's happening: This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon. Let's get into it. Amazon charges sellers a lot of fees Amazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales . But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half! Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top. Where an Amazon sale goes Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising. There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article. Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice. Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options: In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising. So, sellers have to raise prices Here's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices. Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too. And they can't charge less elsewhere Now here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller , if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales. The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon. It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit , California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target. Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go. There's no easy way out For sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales . For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option. At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon, arguing that it illegally maintains its monopoly power by, among other things, punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere, effectively forcing them to use its warehouses and charging ever-higher fees. Amazon denies any wrongdoing, and the case is set to go to trial next year. In Europe, Germany ordered Amazon to stop controlling its sellers' prices earlier this year, though the decision isn't yet final. After last week's piece , a Not-Ship reader wrote to say none of this is new: plenty of online stores push ads and fake discounts. That is true. But what's different about Amazon is its reach. When prices increase on Amazon, they tend to increase elsewhere too. You can, of course, choose not to shop on Amazon. But if the FTC is right, you may be paying Amazon's prices anyway. Calling out capitalism — with data. Not-Ship's data dispatch. In your inbox, weekly. Subscribe Email sent! Check your inbox to complete your signup. No spam. Just lots of charts. Unsubscribe anytime. FULL DISCLOSURE I spent two years working at the Washington Post, which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos owns. During that time, he was busy  dismantling the publication , so he wasn't well loved in the newsroom. CLASSIC ENSHITTIFICATION In August, I saw Cory Doctorow speak at the Edinburgh International Book Festival. His enshittification concept — the process by which online platforms shift from serving their users to squeezing them — inspired this two-part series on Amazon. If you want to understand it all a lot better, I highly recommend his book Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It. Somehow it makes antitrust issues both accessible and entertaining! FROM ELSEWHERE Here's what I found interesting, important or delightful this week: Life after death? Alvin Chang's latest masterpiece has dropped! It’s about what people around the world believe happens after we die, drawn from surveys of nearly 130,000 people in 23 countries. (Proud to count Alvin as a Not-Ship subscriber 💙.) Stunning embroidery. If you haven't seen the work of Irene Saputra, get yourself over to Instagram . Endlessly inspirational. Instant knowledge. The Ars Notoria was a medieval magic book that promised scholars university learning through prayers, rituals and diagrams. No studying required! Style Aile Etoile Weight 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 Slope Italic Oblique AMONG the many valuable contributions of William Dwight Whitney to linguistic science is one especially important and fundamental principle. It may be stated in these words. In explaining the prehistoric phenomena of language we must assume no other factors than those which we are able to observe and estimate in the historical period of language development. The factors that produced changes in human speech five thousand or ten thousand years ago cannot have been essentially different from those which are now operating to transform living languages. On the basis of this principle we look to-day at a much-discussed problem of Indo-European philology with views very different from the views held by the founders of Comparative Philology and their immediate successors. I refer to the problem, how the Indo-European people came to assign gender to nouns, to distinguish between masculine, feminine, and neuter. This question is of interest to others besides philologists. What man of culture who has learned languages such as the Greek, Latin, or French has not at times wondered that objects which have no possible connection with the natural gender of animals appear constantly in the language as male or female? In German, for example, it is der fuss, but die hand; der geist, but die seele; in Latin, hīc hortus, hīc animus, hīc amor, but haec planta, haec anima, haec felicitas; in Greek, ὁ πλοῦτος, ὁ οἶκος, but ἡ πενία, ἡ οἰκία. This gender distinction pervades all the older Indo-European languages, and must therefore be regarded as having its origin in the time of the pro-ethnic Indo-European community. Not only is the subject itself full of interest, but also the treatment it has received from the philological research of our century. The various efforts made to solve the problem may very aptly illustrate an essential difference which exists between the theories of language development held in the beginning and middle of this century and those which prevail to-day, — a difference of method existing not in comparative linguistics alone, but also in other fields of philological and historical research that border on it. 248 Explore the latest Slide 1 of 4 Solving frontier problems with experts Researchers, engineers, and security specialists are pairing with Argon to push the boundaries of science, math, robotics and cyber defense. Unlocking new scientific breakthroughs Argon is helping researchers at Google and the scientific community accelerate their path to discovery and real-world impact. Accelerating robotics Argon autonomously turns raw video to a physics-accurate simulation, estimating depth and physical boundaries, and writing the exact simulation code required to replicate those real-world environments. Scaling cybersecurity defense responsibly Argon ties for #1 on CWE-Bench (68%) for vulnerability remediation, is our most resilient model against indirect prompt injections, and is expanding to hundreds of additional Fairwind Program partners today. Hands-on Performance Safety Try Gemini 4 Argon Solving complex engineering tasks Across Google and our early access partners, Argon is quickly becoming the preferred model for engineers tackling long-horizon software engineering. Your browser does not support the video tag. Untangling browser feature code in Chrome Quantum chemistry open-source package optimization Optimizing a production Python codebase in hours Making our open Gemma models nearly three times as fast Migrating legacy code Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromiumâs 40 million-line codebase. Piping multiple clean code changes at a time, Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome's billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes. xTB (Semiempirical Extended Tight-Binding) is one of the most-cited open-source quantum chemistry packages for molecules. Scientists use it to predict molecules' 3D shapes and to screen large numbers of drug and materials candidates. Using Argon in Antigravity, our researchers made xTB up to 2.3x faster at predicting molecular structures and 1.8x faster at conformer search. The changes have been contributed to the official xTB repository on GitHub. Argon in Antigravity is helping the team behind Google's open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK), a framework powering enterprise agents, push their performance engineering further. The team gave Argon their .agents/skills rulebook and a one-paragraph goal to eliminate framework overhead without breaking existing apps. Working autonomously overnight, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and sped up cold imports by 21%. Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the upstream pull requests (optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes. Argon in Antigravity migrated a backlog of 700+ Google Skills training labs off of hardcoded system images and runtimes spread across five code repositories, catching 16+ hidden timeout and race-condition bugs on the way. The work saved 955 engineering hours and reduced recurring cleanup sweeps from roughly 540 hours a year to a single 3-hour update. Delivering complex 3D visualizations Argon brings major improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision, and visual coding compared to previous Gemini models. Starting from a single Nano Banana image in Antigravity, Argon drives Blender MCP in an autonomous loop, aligning camera grids, sculpting Gothic architecture, and staging audio-reactive lighting, to create a finished 3D scene. Transforming critical business and professional workflows Argon combines frontier reasoning, deep visual perception, expanded domain knowledge, and stronger writing capabilities across legal, finance, science, and coding to handle high-stakes professional workflows. Your browser does not support the video tag. At Isomorphic Labs, the team is using Argon as a partner to accelerate their drug discovery and design research workflows. Argon is able to quickly synthesize complex PDFs and patents to extract pertinent information, reducing a process that typically takes weeks into hours. Ambience Healthcare Amplitude Axiom Bio Box Cartwheel Deloitte Kepler LexisNexis MinutalA Quadrillion Quora Roboflow âOn over 200 complex synthetic longitudinal charts, Gemini 4 achieved the highest recall and ICD-10 code specificity among the models we evaluated, producing concise problem lists without external lookups. That combination of medical knowledge and long-context understanding shows promise for clinician-reviewed chart workflows. We're now validating it on real patient records and excited to try it out more broadly.â Brendan Fortuner SVP Technology, Ambience Healthcare âArgon is doing a great job at understanding what people actually mean. Customers collect endless signals that they don't know what to do with. Argon consistently scored amongst the top in our evals for building charts that help visualize the solutions for customers. It's also meaningfully persistent about finding those kinds of needle in a haystack answers that are valuable to customers.â Curtis Liu CTO, Amplitude âGemini 4 represents a step change in what AI can accomplish in real-world science. We've seen it reason through complex experimental data, from cellular imaging to mass spectrometry, and make subtle findings that traditionally require expert scientists to identify. On our Scientific Agent Benchmark, Gemini 4 was at the frontier across most tasks, including our hardest: ranking the clinical risk between two drugs.â Alex Cabrera Founding Engineer, Axiom Bio âGemini 4 Argon is at the frontier of enterprise knowledge work, achieving a 14% improvement in accuracy compared to Gemini 3.1 Pro. In Boxâs evaluation, Argon connected evidence across the full set of documents, including details embedded in figures, and carried multi-step analyses through to complete answers. This is especially valuable in data analysis and in technical fields like healthcare and life sciences, where teams need to find and interpret information across many kinds of source material.â Yashodha Bhavnani VP of AI Products at Box âBy integrating Gemini 4 into our 3D spatial reconstruction engine, we turn everyday video into articulated, physics-ready 3D scenes in seconds instead of hours. Across our benchmarks, Gemini outperformed every model we tested â cutting runtime nearly 100Ã and token usage by 90%, unlocking physics ready and watertight 3D asset creation for our customers.â Andrew Carr Co-founder and Chief Scientist, Cartwheel âEarly impressions from Gemini 4 are very strong: for long-running tasks across these workflows, it completed successfully 100% of the time in our evals, maintaining context and running through multiple tools across impressive spans. Its depth of reasoning delivers significantly higher, clearer output. Performing in-depth reasoning for domain-specific tasks without detailed prior logic or instructions is something weâve never seen with any model in its class before.â Gopal Srinivasan Global AI and Data Lead, Deloitte âOn our core financial analysis benchmarks, which span building multi-year financial statements straight from SEC filings to valuing companies with complex capital structures and announced acquisitions, Gemini 4 matched our analyst-built reference models on more than 99% of figures. title: Grace Hopper Celebration Cancelled
body_text: Press-Release About Events & Programs Support Our Cause Research Resources News & Stories Become a Member Donate Press Release An Important Update About Grace Hopper Celebration It is with deep regret that we are announcing the cancellation of this year’s Grace Hopper Celebration in Anaheim, CA. This is not a decision we made lightly; we understand it leaves many of our community disappointed. It is a function of not having the funds required to move forward with the Celebration, unlike in years past. Unlike past events, this year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below our expectations and, ultimately, below the level needed to cover critical operating expenses. We know this decision affects far more than an event. Many of you have made travel arrangements, booked hotels, received visas, secured time away from work, organized teams, and planned important moments around being together. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this creates. If you have plans to attend GHC, please take the following steps now: Cancel or modify your airline, train, or other travel reservations directly with your travel provider. Cancel hotel reservations made independently directly with the hotel or booking provider, and any other reservations or commitments connected to your trip. Information regarding GHC registration, sponsorships, exhibitor commitments, and other financial matters will be communicated directly to the individuals and organizations affected. AnitaB.org will contact registrants about registration fees by October 26. We recognize that each person’s circumstances may be different. For questions or assistance specifically related to the cancellation, please contact [ GHC@AnitaB.org ]. We ask that you use this address so we can centralize inquiries and respond as effectively as possible. To our attendees, sponsors, speakers, volunteers, partners, and everyone who has invested in making Grace Hopper Celebration possible: we are profoundly grateful, and profoundly sorry. GHC has always been about more than a place or a moment on the calendar. It is about a community that has spent decades opening doors, expanding opportunity, and making sure women technologists have a voice in shaping the future of technology. GHC has been central to our mission, and the circumstances leading to its cancellation have adversely affected our finances. We are evaluating strategic alternatives and the type of programming we can offer in the future. I anticipate further announcements will be made in the coming weeks as we gain greater clarity on key variables. Brenda Darden Wilkerson President & CEO AnitaB.org Frequently Asked Questions Why was this year’s Grace Hopper Celebration cancelled? AnitaB.org has determined that it will not have the funds required to pay the costs of producing the Celebration. This year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below prior years and, ultimately, below the level required to cover basic operating expenses. What happens to my in-person or virtual registration fee? Information regarding GHC registration and other financial matters will be communicated to you promptly once we obtain a clearer understanding of AnitaB.org ’s financial condition. Do I need to do anything right now? We encourage you to review cancellation and refund eligibility with your travel and accommodation provider. Many providers offer more flexibility the earlier a change is requested. My visa was approved for this trip. What does cancellation mean for me? AnitaB.org is unable to advise on immigration matters. Please consult a qualified immigration attorney or your sponsoring institution. I had interviews scheduled through the career fair. What now? Employers who had scheduled interviews are being notified, and we are asking them to continue those conversations directly where possible. We are a sponsor or exhibitor. Who should we contact? Your A nitaB.org contact is reaching out directly. Information regarding sponsorships, exhibitor commitments, and related financial matters will be communicated to the organizations affected. For anything urgent, please use GHC@AnitaB.org . How will I hear about updates, and when is the next one? Updates will be posted on the GHC website, the most recent updates will appear at the top of the Press Release page. Who do I contact? Please use GHC@AnitaB.org , for anything related to the cancellation. Using one address allows us to centralize inquiries and respond as effectively as possible. Is Grace Hopper Celebration India still taking place? Yes, Grace Hopper Celebration India (GHCI) is still taking place in Bangalore, India, January 20-22, 2027. Learn more here: GHCI 27 - AnitaB.org India . We also encourage corporate sponsors to consider GHCI sponsorship inclusive of bulk registration opportunities to send your teams. Email corporate@anitabindia.org to learn more. I uploaded my resume through the GHC 26 platform. Will participating companies still have access to it? Yes. If you uploaded your resume through the GHC 26 Resume Hub, participating companies will continue to have access to your submitted resume. title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
body_text: AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. - yyhh.org Toggle navigation yyhh.org About Experience Notebook Opinion AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. Date Mon 12 October 2026 By Huahai Tags AI LLM Tools Clojure In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does. Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs. One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful: it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its answers matter. An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse. Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not? The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful. Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does. What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any. I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment. The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool. Welcome Guide Home News Security Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts By Bill Toulas October 12, 2026 12:27 PM 1 Ledger has confirmed that some of its devices distributed through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with a hardware implant that drained users' cryptocurrency wallets. The company has been investigating reports of users losing funds from wallets purchased through CryptoBilis, a major Malaysia-based hardware wallet retailer operating across Southeast Asia. Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware. Ledger wallets are physical devices designed to securely store the private keys that control cryptocurrency assets and authorize transactions. On October 9, Ledger said it had launched an investigation into user reports of cryptocurrency losses and asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices. The next day, the company confirmed hardware tampering on at least one device, though it’s still unclear exactly how or when the devices were tampered with. "Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger is reaching out to impacted users as part of the ongoing investigation," Ledger said. The crypto wallet maker also noted that it was working with authorities to identify the perpetrator and bring them to justice. “[...]Ledger recommends users who purchased a Ledger device from this reseller to not initiate set up if they have not yet done so. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with a new seed),” warned Ledger . Yesterday, Ledger provided another update , confirming that all user reports of unexpected fund drains were linked to devices sold through CryptoBilis and describing the affected volume as “limited.” While the company did not disclose the type of devices compromised in this supply-chain attack, reports online talk about a spy implant in Ledger X devices that blends with the legitimate hardware. Mark Karpelès, currently leading Karpeles Lab Inc. and CTO at Shells.com, showed a picture of the new implant in Ledger X, saying that it was "quite an evolution" from previous versions featuring manually soldered wires. Hardware implant inside Ledger X device source:  Mark Karpelès The former CEO of Mt. Gox said the implant was concealed behind the screen, but its antenna cable would have indicated that something was wrong. According to Karpelès, the malicious hardware captured the device's display output and button presses to identify the seed phrase, then transmitted it to the attacker over an LTE connection using an eSIM. "Ledger Nano X are used to store crypto. The spy implants are used to steal whatever crypto you store in those Ledger Nano X," Karpelès explained . Although the CEO did not name CryptoBilis as the vendor of the compromised LedgerX, he said the device was not purchased via Ledger's recommended channels but from "a well known platform via a Chinese seller (product shipped from Malaysia)." Tibane Labs, a cryptocurrency research and development studio, confirmed Karpelès' finding, adding that there were two implant versions for Ledger X. The researchers obtained two variants, one in a Ledger device bought on Amazon Japan from " China-based seller · shipped from Malaysia," the other purchased on Yahoo! Auctions, Japan. In a report over the weekend, Tibane Labs notes that the threat actor made room for the malicious circuitry by replacing the original battery with a smaller one, which powers both the implant and the Ledger X. "Under the battery and antenna sits an ST STM32G431KBU6 (Arm Cortex‑M4, 128 KB flash, UFQFPN‑32)," the researchers found inside one of the devices. For connectivity, the actor used "a tiny eSIM, an 8‑pad package just 2×2 mm, next to the MCU, and a shielded LTE module that sends the words out." In the second hardware wallet analyzed, Tibane researchers found that markings on both the MCU (Microcontroller Unit) and the eSIM had been scraped off to hide the part numbers. The second variant, which appears to be the same one that Karpelès described, is more advanced. It ran on the original battery and fit into the space normally occupied by the foam padding under the OLED display. In both cases, the tell tale was the antenna wire, which ran along the top edge in the case of the second implant. In the first implant, the antenna is taped across the top of the battery and the shielded LTE module. Hardware implant inside Ledger X source: Tibane Labs The researchers warned that the specimen above used "a designed, panelised flex PCB, the kind ordered from a board house, not a hand-built one-off." Ledger is advising users to avoid purchasing from unauthorized resellers as they run an increased risk of getting counterfeit or modified devices. The company is also reminding its authorized resellers and distributors to get the products only through authorized channels and to avoid restocking returned products. Ledger provides a ‘Genuine Check’ mechanism to determine the authenticity of the device; however, it explicitly warns that it cannot detect added implants when the device’s original Secure Element remains intact. At this time, there’s no indication that any other Ledger resellers are shipping compromised wallets; however, the community’s trust in the resellers’ network has been compromised, with many now calling for its dismantling. Previous Article Next Article Comments tubrazysj - 1 day ago     A genuine-device verification check is not enough if a physical implant can bypass the user's security assumptions. Hardware wallet providers and distributors need robust anti-tampering controls, transparent incident reporting, and clear consumer remediation procedures. In crypto, security is not just a technical issue; it is also a matter of consumer protection and legal responsibility.
