Things I did From 2023 to 2025, I lead the Web Infrastructure and Desktop App teams at Notion. From 2021 until 2023, I lead a team called Payments Integration Experience working on the future of payments at Stripe. From 2016 to 2021, I worked as a Senior Staff Engineer and Engineering Manager at Slack, where I got to support a team of amazing C++ engineers building the cross-platform desktop framework Electron – as well as Slack's desktop apps for macOS, Windows, and Linux. I cared a lot about the Node.js and Electron ecosystems, so I wrote an O'Reilly guide called " Introducing Electron ". I still care today, I just write fewer books. Before joining the little fledgling Slack, I worked from 2014 to 2016 as an Open Source Engineer at Microsoft, spending my time coding or talking about Open Source. We tried to improve developer's lives by releasing quality code on GitHub — as well as touring the world and presenting the lessons we've learned. I built things like the windows-build-tools or npm-windows-upgrade . From 2011 to 2014, I worked with Microsoft Germany and Microsoft Silicon Valley specifically with younger companies as as Startup Developer Evangelist - first focusing on Berlin, then on the San Francisco Bay Area. I also once wrote an O'Reilly book on Windows App Development with JavaScript . It's in German, but even if you do read it, it's very solidly out of date now and contains nothing you should read. I once built a terrible but surprisingly successful game, being the single developer behind Awesome Zombie Sniper . The code was outrageous but it brought minor joy to more than a million players. The actual goal of the work was to help developers succeed on Windows, Windows Phone, and Xbox by exploring cross-platform issues with Unity and the game was a surprisingly lucky "Hello World" demo. From 2007 to 2011, I got my startup experience leading the German Apfeltalk.de magazine as Executive Editor where we served 10 million monthly users everything they needed to know about iOS and macOS. I'm proud that our team took the website from a small community to one of the biggest tech sites in Europe. Academically, I graduated from the MSc program at the University of Oxford's Internet Institute, researching at the intersection of sociology, law, economics, and computer science. Before that, I studied at the University of Duesseldorf where I also spent some time as visiting lecturer for app development and New Media Research Associate.

title: Show HN: Guitoro, a virtual guitar you strum with your keyboard
body_text: Virtual Guitar: Play Guitar Online Free | Guitoro in #stage, so the browser picks the same file. Browsers without AVIF skip this. --> Guitoro Online Virtual Guitar Loading guitar This guitar needs JavaScript to make sound. The most realistic virtual guitar online What is Guitoro? Guitoro is the most realistic and the most complete virtual guitar you can play online, free in your browser. Play it with your computer keyboard, your left hand on the chords and your right hand strumming, or swipe the strings with your finger on a phone or tablet. Choose a steel-string acoustic, a classic guitar, an electric guitar or a four-string bass. It's also a way to learn chords and songs that a chord chart or a video lesson can't show you. Each song plays its best-known part close to the original recording, stroke for stroke. Slow it down to 20% and watch it being played: each string lights up the moment it's hit, the pick swings down and up with the strum, and the neck shows which finger goes where. Then it's your turn. No guitar? Play the song on the keys or the screen, and it waits for you at every chord change. Have a guitar? Pick it up and play along at your own speed, with the strings, the strum and the fingering right in front of you. Every guitar and bass note is a recording of a real instrument. There's nothing to download and no account to create. If you played the Google guitar doodle, Guitoro takes the idea further: six real strings, 15 chords in every key, and 51 songs to play along with. Start playing How you learn with it 4 instruments 15 chords in every key 51 songs to play along with 20% slowest song speed 56 strum and picking patterns 15 drum styles Play Play guitar with your keyboard or your fingers No guitar needed. Guitoro is built to be played, not just clicked, on whatever you have in front of you. Computer keyboard Your left hand holds a chord on the letter keys and your right hand strums with H and J , the way you'd play a real guitar. 15 chords sit under your fingers, plus keys for arpeggios, single strings, chucks and palm mutes. Touch screen On a phone or tablet, tap a chord pad and swipe the strings with your finger. Up to five fingers at once, and you can tap the frets on the neck to play single notes. Mouse Drag across the strings. A fast swipe plays louder, a slow drag rolls the notes one by one, and a click plucks a single string. Melodies in Solo On a computer, switch to Solo and every keyboard row becomes a string and every column a fret, with bends and vibrato on the arrow keys. Learn by watching See every string and every stroke, as slowly as you need In a video lesson the hand moves fast and hides the strings, so you can't tell which ones were really hit. Guitar apps teach the basic chords and stop there. Guitoro plays the song's real part on the guitar in front of you, at the speed you choose, and shows exactly what the hands do. Then you play it, on the virtual guitar or on your own. Played like the record Each song plays its best-known part close to the original recording, stroke for stroke. Slow it anywhere from 20% to full speed and the chords, the strum and the band slow down together. See which strings are hit Each string lights up the moment it sounds, then vibrates as it rings. You can see whether a stroke hits all six strings, just the bass strings or only the top three. Watch the strumming hand Over a strummed part, the pick swings down and up like a real strumming hand, once per step of the pattern. Solid swings hit the strings and faint ones miss them, so you see the hand keep moving through the gaps. Fingers on the neck While a chord rings, the neck shows it: finger numbers from 1 to 4, barres, muted strings and the capo. Copy the shape onto your own guitar. No guitar? The song waits for you Play a song's chords on the keys or the screen and it follows you. The keys show its chords in order, the next one lights green, and the song holds until you play it. No score and no rush. Have a guitar? Play along Watch a part slowly, copy it on your guitar, then play along as you raise the speed. On a computer, choose My guitar: the on-screen keys step aside and the song box shows the strum or picking pattern, a chord strip you can click to jump around, and the speed. Realism Why it sounds and feels like a real guitar Most online guitars only let you click single strings or frets, or play a synthesized tone when you click a chord. On Guitoro you strum: swipe across the strings or use the keys, and every string sounds as you cross it, from recordings of real instruments. Recorded, not synthesized Every guitar and bass note is a recording of a real instrument: a steel-string acoustic, a classic guitar with nylon strings, a solid-body electric on its bridge pickup, and a four-string bass. Strums follow your hand Each string sounds as your finger or mouse crosses it. Swipe down or up, fast or slow, and you hear the difference, down to a slow roll across the strings. Real chord shapes Chords use the shapes guitarists play, with open strings, barres and muted strings, so a G sounds like a G on a guitar, not on a keyboard. Guitar techniques Chucks, palm mutes, hammer-ons, pull-offs, bends and vibrato, while the strings vibrate on screen as they ring. Use cases What people use it for Playing without a guitar Strum real chords and play whole songs with your computer keyboard or your fingers, with a backing band behind you. On a train, at the office or on the sofa, a laptop or a phone and headphones are enough. Learning real songs Songs like Wonderwall, Hallelujah and Let It Be come set up with the right key, capo, tempo and the strum from the record. Lead the chords from the keys, or pick up your own guitar and play along at any speed. Getting a strum right Slow a song's strum down, watch which way the pick moves on every beat, then strum it yourself over a drum beat until it feels steady. Learning their first chords See where each finger goes, hear how the chord should sound, then copy the shape on a real guitar. Every chord also has its own page in the guitar chord chart . Checking a chord chart Paste the chords of a song from a chord site and hear how it goes before you sit down to play it. Writing a song Type a chord progression under My songs, loop it with the backing band, and record the idea before it's gone. Teaching Show a class a chord shape or a strum on a big screen, slowed down, with every string and every pick stroke visible. Other musicians Singers, keyboard players and songwriters can hear how guitar chords are voiced and see how a progression lies on the fretboard, without learning to hold a guitar first. Features Everything in the app The most complete virtual guitar online: four instruments, every key, real chord shapes, songs, a backing band and recording, all free in one place. Four real instruments Steel-string acoustic, classic guitar, electric and four-string bass, each built from recorded samples. Pick a recording for the acoustic (Warm, Bright or Mellow) and the classic (Natural or Concert), and presets for the electric, from Clean to Crunch, Classic Rock, Metal, Lead and Ambient. 15 chords in every key Pick any of the 24 major and minor keys and the chord keys fill with the chords that fit it: the main chords, sevenths, and sus, add9 or sus2 colors. Edit puts any chord you type, like F#m7 or Dsus2, on a key. Chord shapes on the neck While a chord rings, the neck shows finger numbers, barres, muted strings and the capo. Standard is the shape most players learn first, Easy swaps a barre chord for a smaller shape, and Up plays the same chord higher up the neck. Songs at any speed 51 songs and classical pieces come set up to play, from Wonderwall and Hotel California to Canon in D. Slow them to 20%, lead their chords from the keys, or play along on your own guitar. 56 strum and picking patterns 14 everyday strums from Steady downs and the pop staple D DU U DU to shuffle and 6/8, 4 styles (reggae, funk and country), 26 more rhythms drawn from real songs, and 12 picking patterns like Travis and classical p-i-m-a. Choose one and you hear it straight away. A backing band Drums, bass and strings that follow your chords: 15 drum styles, including rock, funk, reggae, bossa nova and cajon, and 25 bass lines. The Band switch next to Play turns them on. Tempo goes from 10 to 220 BPM, with a metronome. Your own songs Paste a song from a chord site or as ChordPro text, pick a strum, and Guitoro plays it with the band. Write "x2" to repeat a line or a part. Lyrics are left out, and your songs stay in your browser. Solo mode Play single notes and melodies on the neck from the computer keyboard, with hammer-ons, pull-offs, bends and vibrato. Amp & FX Overdrive, distortion and fuzz on the electric, plus bass, mid and treble, room or hall reverb, and delay on every instrument. Tunings and capo 10 tunings, from Standard, Drop D and half step down to DADGAD and Open G, D and E, a capo up to fret 10, and a left-handed guitar. Record and export Record takes of up to 10 minutes with the band, replay them and save them as WAV or a small compressed file. Takes stay in your browser. Online tuner A free guitar tuner that listens through your microphone, with pages for drop D, open tunings, the bass and the ukulele . Getting started How to use Guitoro From silence to a song you lead yourself. The first two steps take a few seconds. Choose an instrument Pick Acoustic, Classic, Electric or Bass at the top of the page. On a phone, tap the guitar picture. You can switch at any time. Pick a chord Tap a chord pad, or press its letter on the keyboard. The default key is G major, so the middle row, A S D F G , holds G, C, D, Em and Am. Auto strum starts on, so the chord strums itself. Strum it yourself Turn Auto off, then swipe down across the strings for a downstroke and up for an upstroke. On a keyboard, H strums down and J strums up. Choose a pattern Open the Strum menu and pick a strum or picking pattern. You hear it once on your chord. With Auto and Loop on, it keeps playing while you hold a chord key. Play a song Open Songs & recordings and pick a song. Press Play to hear it, or press the chord key that lights green to lead it yourself. The tempo button next to Play slows it down. Add a band Turn on the Band switch next to Play. Its edit button opens Backing band, where you choose the drums, the bass line and the strings. Record a take Open Songs & recordings, choose Recordings, and press Record. Play, then use Stop next to the recording timer. Your takes stay in Recordings. Keyboard Play guitar with your computer keyboard Your left hand holds the chords and your right hand strums, just like on a guitar. Keys follow their physical position on a US QWERTY keyboard, and every key on screen shows its letter. Chords Three rows of five: A to G for the main chords, Q to T for sevenths, Z to B for more chords and colors like sus4 and add9 Strum H down, J up, K down when pressed and up when released, N hard down, M slow down Pick Y arpeggio, U bass note, I O P the top three strings Feel L chuck, ; palm mute, Shift hard strum, Alt slow strum Songs The chord keys show the song's chords in order and the next one lights green. With My guitar on, Space plays and pauses the song Solo mode Each row is a string and each column a fret. Left and Right arrows move up and down the neck, Up bends, Down adds vibrato Learn chords How to learn guitar chords with Guitoro Start with G, C, D and Em In the key of G these four chords sit on the middle row of keys, and together they play hundreds of pop and folk songs. Press each one and watch the neck: the numbers are your fingers, from 1 for the index to 4 for the little finger. An X marks a string you don't play, and a bar across the strings is a barre. Listen to the difference Play C, then Am. The chord name above the guitar tells you which is major and which is minor, and your ear learns the bright and the sad sound. Do the same with the sevenths on the top row. Copy the shape on a real guitar Put your fingers where the dots are, strum, and compare your sound with Guitoro's. A buzzing or dead string usually means a finger is too far from the fret or touching the next string. Many barre chords have an Easy version for while your hand gets stronger. Change chords in time Open Songs & recordings and pick a song, or paste one under My songs. Press each chord key as it lights green: the song waits for you at every change. Start slow, then raise the speed a little at a time. Try other keys, the capo and tunings Switch the key to hear the same chords higher or lower, or in a minor key. Put a capo on in Settings and the same shapes sound higher, which is how guitarists play in keys like A or B with easy open chords. Drop D and Open G show how a tuning changes the whole sound. 2 1 3 G 3 2 1 C 1 3 2 D 2 3 Em Low E string on the left. Numbers are fingers, O is an open string, X is a string you don't play. Learn strumming How to learn strumming patterns Strum patterns are written with D for a downstroke and U for an upstroke, and x for a muted chuck. The trick is to keep your hand moving down on every number and up on every "and", even when it misses the strings. In Guitoro you can watch the pick do exactly that. The pop staple D DU U DU Counted "1, 2 and, and, 4 and": the down on beat 3 is left out, but the hand still moves. 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & Down Up Miss the strings, keep moving Listen first Choose a pattern from the Strum menu and you hear it once on your chord. The menu shows each pattern as a grid of downs and ups. Watch it slowly Open a song with the strum you want and slow it to 50% or less. The pick swings down on the numbers and up on the "and"s: solid when it hits the strings, faint when it misses. The strings light up to show which ones each stroke hits. Play it yourself Turn Auto off, turn on the Band switch or the metronome, and strum along with H and J or by swiping the strings. Record and listen back Record a take and listen for uneven strokes. When it sounds steady, speed up. Build up in order Steady downs, then Down-up eighths, then the pop staple, then 6/8 ballad and Shuffle. After that, open songs like Wonderwall, Hallelujah and Knockin' on Heaven's Door and strum their own patterns. Songs Play along with a song Each song page has its chords with diagrams and its strum or picking pattern written out, and sets the guitar up for you: key, capo, tempo and chords. The easy guitar songs page groups them by how many chords they have. King) Tools Playing a real guitar along? The free online guitar tuner listens through your microphone, with pages for drop D, half step down and open tunings. There is a free ukulele tuner too. Guitar chords Every major, minor and seventh chord in all 12 keys, with finger charts and an easier version where there is one: the guitar chord chart . Search any chord there, hear it strummed, and open it on the guitar. FAQ Questions Is Guitoro free? Yes. It runs in your browser with no download and no sign-up. How is it different from a video lesson? A video shows a teacher's hand from one angle, at one speed, and the hand hides which strings it hits. Guitoro plays the song's part close to the original recording on a guitar you can see whole: each string lights up as it's hit, the pick shows every down and up stroke, and you set the speed. Then you play it yourself and the song waits for you. Which songs can I play? 51 songs and classical pieces, from Wonderwall, Hotel California, Let It Be and Perfect to Canon in D and FÃ¼r Elise, each with its key, capo, tempo and strum or picking set up. See them all on the easy guitar songs page, or paste your own from a chord site. Does it work on phones and tablets? Yes. Tap a chord pad and swipe the strings. In portrait, the enlarged neck sits below the strings with four frets per page. In landscape, the neck and strings sit side by side. Tap the frets to play single notes. Solo mode and My guitar need a computer. Can I play guitar with my computer keyboard? Yes. The left side of the keyboard holds 15 chords and the right side strums, picks and mutes. See the table above. How do I slow a song down? Press the tempo button next to Play and drag the speed, from 20% to full speed. The chords, the strum, the pick on screen and the band all slow down together. Can Guitoro teach me to play a real guitar? Yes, as a guide next to your guitar. It shows you what to play and how it should sound: the chord shapes and fingers, which strings each stroke hits, which way to strum, and whole songs at any speed. Watch it slowly, copy it on your guitar, then play along. It can't hear you or check your hand, so listen to yourself and compare with Guitoro. Can I play along on my own guitar? Yes, on a computer. Pick a song and answer "Yes, my guitar", or switch to My guitar at the top of the page. The on-screen keys step aside, the speed goes down to 20%, and Space starts and stops the song. Tune up first with the online tuner . Why can't I hear anything? Browsers only start sound after you touch the page, so tap a chord pad or a string first. Then check the device volume and the tab's sound. Bluetooth headphones can add a delay, and wired headphones or speakers fix it. Where are my songs and recordings saved? In this browser, on this device. Export the takes you want to keep as WAV or a compressed audio file before you clear browser data or switch devices. Play it with your keyboard or by touch, slow any song down and see every chord, string and strum. Free, with no download. Description jsnell opened on Oct 13, 2026 Issue body actions Note Given that this issue has been shared online and is currently getting quite a few visitors, here's some additional context. Rust's type system is intended to prevent memory unsafety. Upholding this promise is something we take very seriously, which is why we've been working on things like the next-generation trait solver , the region constraint rework , and more generally Project Zero . It is a large priority of the Types Team to fix all type system unsoundnesses and to work towards there being a solid foundation to minimize the risk of unknown ones. This bug is a P-high issue and would have been P-critical regardless of whether people encountered it in the wild. The reason that it is "only P-high " is that it's 11 years old. A bug like this which has not been found during the last 11 years cannot actually be that easy to hit. Looking at the bug itself, it is also very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident. While it looks easy to trigger, to exploit this you need an intentionally malicious Drop implementation. ~ @lcnr In the following code: use std :: sync :: Mutex ; static KEPT : Mutex < Vec < Box < dyn std :: any :: Any + Send > > > = Mutex :: new ( Vec :: new ( ) ) ; struct Q < T : ' static + Send > ( Option < T > ) ; impl < T : ' static + Send > Drop for Q < T > { fn drop ( & mut self ) { if let Some ( t ) = self . 0 . take ( ) { KEPT . lock ( ) . unwrap ( ) . push ( Box :: new ( t ) ) ; } } } fn main ( ) { { let l = String :: from ( "hello world, this is long enough" ) ; let mut q = Q ( None ) ; q . 0 = Some ( & l ) ; } let _z = String :: from ( "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX" ) ; let k = KEPT . lock ( ) . unwrap ( ) ; println ! ( "{}" , k [ 0 ] . downcast_ref :: < & ' static String > ( ) . unwrap ( ) ) ; } I expected to see this happen: program is not accepted Instead, this happened: program compiles and prints XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX . body_text: Apple HomeView - Apple Apple Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods Home Entertainment Accessories Support 0 + Apple HomeView Local Nav Menu Local Nav Menu Overview Tech Specs Pre-order Apple HomeView Welcome, Apple HomeView Welcome, Available starting 11.13 November 13 Pre-order Apple HomeView Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) Get the highlights. Watch the Apple HomeView film Apple HomeView Siri AI Multiuser Audio and visuals Ways to connect Smart home dashboard Apple Privacy Apple HomeView keeps the whole home connected, entertained, and in the know. All in one place. Private for all. Siri AI. A personal assistant that helps you find what you need and get more done. 1 Available in English to start. Usage limits may apply. Available in English to start. Usage limits may apply. Recognizes up to six people and delivers a personalized experience for each one. Incredible audio and stunning visuals for your music, videos, FaceTime, and photos. Text back. Make a call. Wave hello. So many ways to connect, even hands-free. The ultimate dashboard for your smart home. The privacy every home and everyone deserves. Take a closer look. View in your space Silver Design Design. The domed aluminum base is fitted with a stainless steel hinge that lets you adjust the display. 2 Available in four colors. Shown in Silver . Apple HomeView Design. Silver Starlight Rose Pink Space Gray Display Display. The 7-inch Liquid Retina display includes True Tone for comfortable viewing in any light. 3 Brightness ranges from 500 nits for sunny rooms to our lowest-ever 0.3 nits for the bedside. Select features respond to your proximity to show more information the closer you get. Camera Camera. The 12MP Center Stage camera is perfect for video calls, keeping everyone centered in the frame even as they move around or when more people join in. Mics and Speakers Mics and Speakers. Four beamforming microphones pick up voices near and far, perfect for Siri requests from across the room and crystal-clear FaceTime calls with reduced background noise. Powerful speakers in the base and display deliver Spatial Audio for rich, room-filling sound. 4 Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted). Available in Space Gray and Silver, the wall-mounted option brings the HomeView experience into places like the entrance or the hallway. 5 Choose from wired and plug-in wall mount options. 6 Shown in Silver. Delights up the house. Apple HomeView is designed to bring more joy and convenience to everyone in your household. Siri AI comes built in for personalized AI assistance that’s truly useful in your everyday life. And with a vibrant display and powerful acoustics, your music, videos, and calls look and sound amazing. Meet the new heart of your home. A perfect face for any space. With a collection of customizable faces, Apple HomeView brings beauty to any room. Relive your favorite memories with the stunning Photos face. Choose playful faces like Snoopy or informative options like Calendar, Weather, and more. Even enjoy interactive artwork with the Flow face, which reacts to your movements with mesmerizing colors and light. Digital picture frame. Whether a single image or a rotating gallery, photos from your collections or shared albums are beautifully framed. Dynamic faces. Select faces change throughout the day. They wake with you in the morning, wind down with you at night, and more. Meet Siri AI. Your AI assistant. More personal. More powerful. Siri AI, powered by Apple Intelligence, comes built into Apple HomeView to help you find what you need and get more done while protecting your privacy. 1 Siri AI adapts to each person and surfaces what matters most to them — all they have to do is ask. Available in English to start. Usage limits may apply. Personal Context World Knowledge Seamless Experience Personal Context Relevant to you. Pull up a party invitation from your calendar, find RSVPs buried in your messages, or play the perfect soundtrack to match the vibe. Siri AI works with your paired iPhone or iPad to find relevant content just for you. 1 World Knowledge Your little brainiac. Ask about virtually any topic, from quick dinner recipes to DIY home repairs to game-night trivia. Siri AI taps into broad world knowledge to give you highly specific, up-to-date answers. Seamless Experience Carries the conversation. Siri AI lets you ask open-ended questions and go back and forth with natural, rich conversations. And your conversations with Siri on HomeView sync to the Siri app on your other Apple devices so you can pick up where you left off. Great powers come with great privacy. Apple Intelligence is designed to protect your privacy at every step. It draws on your personal information without collecting it, and Private Cloud Compute — running on Apple silicon — handles requests without ever storing your data or making it accessible to anyone, including Apple. And because Apple HomeView is made to be shared, everyone’s personal information stays separate and secure. Heaps of help at home. Apple HomeView does the heavy lifting when you’re busy around the house. Check your calendar, set reminders, and stay on top of your to-do list. Pull up a quick crafting tutorial. Ask Siri AI to recommend a new coffee shop. Start and stop multiple timers for your chores, and keep an eye on them with Live Activities when you’re using other apps. Cooking. When you find a recipe in Safari, just tap the Start Cooking button to view a streamlined format that’s easy to follow. Handoff. Start a song, podcast, call, video, or recipe on iPhone, and continue on HomeView without missing a beat. Made to be seen, heard, and enjoyed. Apple HomeView keeps you engaged and entertained with music, podcasts, audiobooks, TV shows, and more. Have an impromptu sing-along. Immerse yourself in a good story. Keep an eye on the game while you do the dishes. With HomeView, there’s never a dull moment. Apple apps. A selection of Apple apps are available on HomeView. Enjoy Music with lyrics and artwork, 7 audio stories on News 8 and Audiobooks, and so much more. Additional apps. HomeView supports compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices. 9 Apple apps. A selection of Apple apps are available on HomeView. Enjoy Music with lyrics and artwork, 7 audio stories on News 8 and Audiobooks, and so much more. Additional apps. HomeView supports compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices. 9 Astounding sound. The mighty yet compact speakers pack a serious punch. Two custom full-range drivers in the display keep everything sounding crisp and clean while delivering room-filling Spatial Audio. 4 Computational audio adjusts consistency and balance in real time to deliver incredible sound every time, from anywhere. And a down-firing woofer and two force-cancelling passive radiators are built into the base — for deep, rich bass. Spatial Audio. Fills the room with rich, textured sound for a high-fidelity listening experience. 4 Multiroom audio. Use AirPlay to connect with HomePod, Apple TV 4K, and compatible speakers — and just like that, you have a fully connected home sound system. 10 Friends and family are just a screen away. Whether you’re calling a friend abroad or calling the kids for dinner, Apple HomeView brings everyone together. Enjoy clear and hands-free FaceTime calls. Use Intercom on HomeView and HomePod speakers to communicate with people throughout the house or on their personal devices like iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch. Send messages and make phone calls using just your voice. And use Find My to help you locate your devices, personal items that have an AirTag, and anybody who chooses to share their location with you. Center Stage keeps everyone in the frame during FaceTime calls, even as they move around or if more people join in. The four-microphone array picks up voices while reducing background noise, for clear calls and Siri requests. Everything connected and under one roof. Apple HomeView is a central hub for your smart home accessories, making it easy to keep things running smoothly. And with the new Apple Home Collection, it’s never been simpler to set up and control a connected home. Integrated with the Home app. Built into HomeView and synced with your other Apple devices, the Home app keeps you on top of your smart home. See who’s at the door, monitor your entryway, access multiple video feeds, adjust the lighting and temperature, and control scenes and automations to fit the routines and rhythms of your household. 11 Learn more about the Home app See it all at a glance. The Home Modular face gives you a clear and concise look at your home accessories, while the Home Camera face lets you stream up to nine videos at the same time. And you can manage it all with just your voice or a tap. Enjoy peace of mind. HomeView can detect the sounds of the smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in your home and alert you on your iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch. Stay caught up. The Home app uses Apple Intelligence to group related notifications together, such as when a family member arrives home, unlocks the door, and disables the alarm. And with descriptions of video footage, you can use HomeView to catch up on key activity in and around the house. Created for a better smart home experience. Designed in collaboration with Apple and select brands, Apple Home Collection accessories — including smart cameras, thermostats, and a door lock — are simple to set up, easy to use, and private with data that’s encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home. And they work seamlessly with your Apple devices. Coming later Shop the Apple Home Collection Your data is private property. Apple HomeView comes with privacy protections built in at every step. Since multiple people can use HomeView, it’s designed to keep everyone’s personal content separate. Multiple users. HomeView can recognize up to six people and seamlessly switch between them. It syncs with each user’s iPhone or iPad and is designed to show their content only when they’re using HomeView. 12 Secure Exclaves. The A18 chip inside HomeView contains Secure Exclaves that process the camera and microphone feeds in a secure compartment that cannot be accessed by the operating system or by Apple. This enables HomeView to recognize the face and voice of each user without exposing the audio and visual data used for recognition to the operating system. Personal content. Users can access their personal content on HomeView when their paired iPhone or iPad is connected to the same Wi-Fi network and has been recently unlocked, and HomeView recognizes the person by face. HomeView is deeply integrated within the Apple ecosystem and features a stunning 7-inch Liquid Retina display and Apple‑engineered audio. Because multiple people can use HomeView, it is designed to keep everyone’s personal information separate. Users can access their personal content like Messages and Calendar on HomeView when their paired iPhone or iPad is connected to the same Wi-Fi network and has been recently unlocked, and HomeView recognizes the person by face. The A18 chip inside HomeView contains Secure Exclaves that process the camera and microphone feeds in a secure compartment that cannot be accessed by the operating system or by Apple. This enables HomeView to recognize the face and voice of each user without exposing the audio and visual data to the operating system. What is the acoustics performance on HomeView? HomeView delivers room-filling sound with support for Spatial Audio, making it a great way to enjoy music and podcasts at home. Its custom-engineered acoustic system combines a down-firing woofer and two full-range drivers to produce deep bass and crisp highs. Powered by the A18 chip and built-in sensors, computational audio continuously optimizes the loudness and bass response at any volume. HomeView (Wall Mounted) brings full, balanced sound with two custom drivers and computational audio tuned specifically for on-wall placement, along with support for Spatial Audio. title: 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692 (With Complete High-Res Scan)
body_text: A 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692: A Complete High-Resolution Digital Scan | Open Culture --> --> --> --> --> --> A 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692: A Complete High-Resolution Digital Scan --> The best free cultural & educational media on the web --> --> --> Online Courses Certificates Degrees & Mini-Degrees --> Audio Books Movies Languages --> Podcasts Textbooks --> K-12 K-12 --> eBooks Languages Donate --> --> Oct 12 --> A 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692: A Complete High-Resolution Digital Scan in Art | October 12th, 2026 Leave a Comment --> --> There’s ahead of its time, then there’s  Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau  — or, in its orig­i­nal Dutch title,  Klaer Ligh­t­ende Spiegel der Ver­fkon­st , a 900-page book of paint col­ors made before any such things were com­mon tools of the artist’s, scientist’s, and indus­tri­al designer’s trade. Author and artist A. Boogert cre­at­ed one, and only one, copy of his extra­or­di­nary man­u­al on col­or mix­ing in 1692 . Appear­ing on the thresh­old of mod­ern col­or the­o­ry, and fea­tur­ing over 700 pages of col­or swatch­es, the book draws on Aristotle’s sys­tem of col­or rather than the new under­stand­ing of the col­or spec­trum, ful­ly elab­o­rat­ed by New­ton in his  Opticks  over a decade lat­er. It would be anoth­er hun­dred years before a flood tide of col­or books began to make the the­o­ry more prac­ti­cal: from Goethe’s 1810  The­o­ry of Col­ors  and Werner’s 1814  Nomen­cla­ture of Colour  to the dream of col­or stan­dard­iza­tion real­ized: the Pan­tone com­pa­ny, launched in 1963. But if A. Boogert had much influ­ence on the the­o­ry or prac­ti­cal appli­ca­tion of col­or in his day, there doesn’t seem to be much evi­dence for it. Of course most of the Dutch mas­ters had died when the book was com­plet­ed, and it seems unlike­ly that those still work­ing in 1692 would have been famil­iar with its sin­gle copy. Instead, the book was meant to edu­cate water­col­orists, hence its French title, which refers to “water-based paint.” (A lit­er­al trans­la­tion of the Dutch runs some­thing like “clear­ly light­ing mir­ror of the paint­ing art.”) Medieval his­to­ri­an Erik Kwakkel found the book in a French data­base, “and it turns out to be quite spe­cial,”  he writes , “because it pro­vides an unusu­al peek into the work­shop of 17th-cen­tu­ry painters and illus­tra­tors. In over 700 pages of hand­writ­ten Dutch, the author, who iden­ti­fies him­self as A. Boogert, describes how to make water­colour paints. He explains how to mix the colours and how to change their tone by adding ‘one, two or three por­tions of water.’… In the 17th Cen­tu­ry, an age known as the Gold­en Age of Dutch Paint­ing, this man­u­al would have hit the right spot.” The book is cur­rent­ly housed at Bib­lio­thèque Méjanes in Aix-en-Provence, where you’ll find  full-page, zoomable, hi-res­o­lu­tion scans . “Beyond being infor­ma­tion­al, the images from the book are stun­ning and addic­tive flip through,” notes  Refinery29 . “They resem­ble page after page of Pan­tone col­or chips, except with­out the house­hold name.” One won­ders if “A. Boogert” would have become a house­hold name had his book been print­ed and dis­trib­uted. But his col­or sys­tem was already pass­ing away in the New­ton­ian age of col­or spec­trums and wheels, until paint chips final­ly came back in style. Vis­it the col­or man­u­al online here . Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019. Relat­ed Con­tent:  Goethe’s Col­or­ful & Abstract Illus­tra­tions for His 1810 Trea­tise, The­o­ry of Col­ors: Scans of the First Edi­tion Werner’s Nomen­cla­ture of Colour, the 19th-Cen­tu­ry “Col­or Dic­tio­nary” Used by Charles Dar­win (1814) The Vibrant Col­or Wheels Designed by Goethe, New­ton & Oth­er The­o­rists of Col­or (1665–1810) Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.  by OC | Permalink | Comments (0) | Sup­port Open Cul­ture We’re hop­ing to rely on our loy­al read­ers rather than errat­ic ads. title: The United Kingdom generates less electricity per person than in the 1970s
body_text: Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak | Our World in Data Our World in Data Browse by topic Data Latest Resources About Subscribe Donate Data Insights Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak October 03, 2026 Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak Hannah Ritchie Download Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century. In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then. You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s. Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to. The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it. Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much. Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too. Explore how electricity generation has changed in your own country Related topic pages: Energy Copy link Our latest Data Insights See all Data Insights Today A long-term perspective on humanity’s battle against malaria Max Roser According to the latest data from the World Health Organization, the global death rate from malaria has almost halved since the year 2000. The chart above puts this recent progress into a larger historical perspective. It combines the latest estimates from the WHO and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation with those for the 20th century published by the late malaria researcher Richard Carter. Since 1900, the global death rate has declined by 96%. If it were still as high as it was then, around 16 million people would die from malaria every year instead of 610,000. Behind this long-run decline is a shift in the distribution of the burden of malaria. In the first half of the 20th century, most malaria victims died in the Asian tropics. It was the substantial progress there — as well as in the Mediterranean and in the Americas — that made this vast improvement in human health possible. Today, more than 9 out of 10 malaria deaths occur in Africa. This means that the recent progress shown in the chart is, above all, Africa’s progress. If you want to be a part of this historic change, read my brief article on how you can contribute to humanity’s battle against malaria October 13 China reduced extreme poverty fast, but Indonesia hasn’t been far behind Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero. Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong : many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart. In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million. Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines . Explore progress against poverty across the world in our data explorer October 10 What share of plastic waste ends up in the ocean? Hannah Ritchie Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean? In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from: A) Less than 1% B) Less than 36% C) Less than 66% Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third. The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean. The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered. From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place. People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way. Read my article, which looks at this question in more detail October 8 The new Living Planet Index reports a 73% average decline in studied wildlife populations Hannah Ritchie The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart. Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it. I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct. But it tells us none of that. It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index. When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable. As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most. Read my explainer on what the Living Planet Index captures, and what’s different in this report from previous ones October 6 Child mortality has declined in all world regions Max Roser In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died. The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined. In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold. Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history. And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day. Explore child mortality data for every country in our interactive data explorer October 1 Europe is older, but Latin America is aging faster Esteban Ortiz-Ospina The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises. That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates. The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42. But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation. Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter. title: Thunderbird for iOS
body_text: Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development - The Thunderbird Blog Product Development Mobile Community Tips & Guides Get Thunderbird Donate Search Product Development Mobile Community Tips & Guides RSS Feed Download Thunderbird Donate Mobile Thunderbird Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development October 1, 2026 Aly Blenkin 30 responses The team has been working hard behind the scenes laying a strong foundation for the Thunderbird iOS app. Rather than leveraging existing code, we are building natively from scratch. This fresh start allows us to take everything we’ve learned from Thunderbird Desktop and Android to ensure a fast, reliable, and modern experience on your iPhone right from the start. Our ultimate goal is seamless cross-device experience. Whether you’re sitting at your desktop computer, checking messages on the go, your workflow should feel effortless and unified.  Right now, we are focused heavily on getting the core foundations right. We are excited about the momentum because having clean architecture today means we can layer on exciting new features much faster in the future. Below we’ve captured some of our work in progress. Nothing is final, but we wanted to share what we are cooking up so far. If you have feedback, keep reading on. At the bottom of the post we have  a link to a user research study where we want to hear from you and what you want to see from Thunderbird for iOS. Hassle-free setup Adding account user flow with options for email services like Google and Microsoft We know people are really busy, often doing more than one thing at a time. We’re making login fast, secure, and fully automatic, so whether you’re signing in with a single click or setting up multiple accounts, you can get to your inbox quickly.  Solid reliable connections Thunderbird inbox An email app is only as good as its connection. Behind the scenes, we’re building a background sync that maintains a steady connection with your provider that keeps your inbox up to date while respecting your battery life. Core daily tools Formatting toolbar (highlighted to show the details) Your daily email routine should feel effortless. We’re polishing the essentials: a clutter-free, easy-to-read inbox layout paired with a clean, modern editor that lets you format messages smoothly without getting in your way. Designed for growth Thunderbird has always belonged to its community. We’re structuring the app with clean code and an experimental feature flag system so it’s easy for community developers to contribute. This means power users will be able to test out new experimental features early, and external contributors can easily help us extend what the app can do. When can you try it? Our goal is to have a first version ready for community testing in the next few months. Building with our community, not just for people, is core to what we are trying to do. To help us decide what to build next after our first release, we’d love your input. If you had to pick the top three things that matter most to your daily email routine, what would they be? ➡️ Survey link Update: the survey has now closed. Thanks to all that responded! A note to the community  Lastly, we know how long many of you have been asking for and waiting for Thunderbird on iOS. Whether you’ve dropped a comment on our forums, tagged us on social media, or simply kept an eye on our progress, thank you for your patience! Bringing Thunderbird to iPhone and iPad isn’t just about building an app; it’s about doing it right so it serves you reliably for years to come. Today, we want to pop open the hood, share where we are, and work with everyone to design the best possible experience. title: OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
body_text: ADVERTISEMENT Skip to main content Open search bar and full menu The San Francisco Standard Sign in Latest News Politics Business Opinion Culture Food & Drink Sports Games Podcasts News Visit $ News The Boom Loop Crisis in the Streets The School Wars Criminal Justice Transportation Investigations Close menu Close menu Sign out Search query Search Latest Obsessions News Politics Business Opinion Culture Food & Drink Sports Mobile App (opens in new tab) Newsletters Podcasts Games Social Links (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) News OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room Federal prosecutors say an employee from Saudi Arabia planted an audio recorder and left another unattended in his bag. An OpenAI engineer concealed a recording device in a conference room used by executives at the company, the Department of Justice claims. | Source: Justin Katigbak/The Standard By George Kelly and Michael McLaughlin Published Oct. 13, 2026 at 1:17pm Updated Oct. 14, 2026 at 7:59am Share Share Copy link to this article Email (opens in new tab) Twitter (opens in new tab) Bluesky (opens in new tab) Facebook (opens in new tab) LinkedIn (opens in new tab) Telegram (opens in new tab) WhatsApp (opens in new tab) Reddit (opens in new tab) Close share menu 2 There are 2 comments on this story Published Oct. 13, 2026 at 1:17pm Updated Oct. 14, 2026 at 7:59am An OpenAI engineer has been arrested on suspicion of hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday and remains in custody. An unattended bag found in the company’s offices contained Alfozan’s wallet and identification, as well as a second recording device, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in San Francisco. ADVERTISEMENT Alfozan has worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors said. He has been a legal permanent resident of the U.S. since Sept. 2020, court documents said. OpenAI personnel found the device Sept. 30. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and had been concealed in toilet paper, the complaint says. The company determined it was installed around Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted. Surveillance footage shows Alfozan near the room on multiple dates before the discovery, though he was not authorized to enter the room or attend meetings there, prosecutors said. Meetings in the room frequently involved confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and government engagements, according to the complaint. Prosecutors say this image shows Alfozan looking behind a television in an OpenAI conference room.​ | Source: Courtesy U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California Before the device was installed, Alfozan used a productivity tool to ask about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities, and calendars, as well as the locations of leadership and outside partner meetings, the complaint alleges. A chatbot account tied to Alfozan’s spouse, which shared identifiers with his own account, submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 about building, installing, obscuring, and remotely accessing a recording device, prosecutors said. Queries included how to “build a continuous audio recorder” and “encrypt the SD card,” prosecutors claimed. On Sept. 27 and 28, the account asked about the specific device that was later found, including its unique MAC address. “For us it is a matter of national security,” U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian said in a statement. On Oct. 5, the complaint says, Alfozan entered the conference room and appeared to look behind the television. That same day, he allegedly left a bag unattended in a printer. Security personnel who opened it found his wallet and ID, along with a second recording device similar to the first. He later reported that he’d misplaced the bag to company officials. OpenAI examined the device in the bag, which had a recording microcontroller and had been customized to obfuscate stored data, “such as potentially intercepted audio communications,” according to an FBI affidavit. When Alfozan retrieved the bag on Oct. 6, it no longer contained the device. He reported that his credit card, approximately $500, two AirPods, headphones, sunglasses and a power bank were stolen, but made no mention of the recording device, the affidavit said. The recording device with encrypted contents. | Source: Courtesy U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California FBI Director Kash Patel said protecting U.S. AI innovation is among the bureau’s highest counterintelligence priorities. Scott Schelble, special agent in charge of the FBI’s San Francisco field office, said the agency is committed to protecting sensitive research and proprietary technology. If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the U.S. attorney’s office for the Northern District of California. OpenAI said on X (opens in new tab) that after discovering the device, employees used the company’s AI models to determine what it was and where it came from, and referred the matter to the FBI. The company thanked the agents and prosecutors who “moved quickly to make an arrest.” According to OpenAI, its technical surveillance countermeasures team found the device during a sweep of a conference room. More about OpenAI Who is the OpenAI engineer accused of hiding a recording device? PODCAST The AI money bomb is about to hit San Francisco That flag-wrapped anti-AI bus in SF? A conservative group drove it here OpenAI described the device as sophisticated and designed to evade detection, saying it had advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data in a way meant to avoid monitoring. The company said investigators used its models to analyze forensic images of the device’s storage and assess changes in the underlying data. Court documents filed by prosecutors identified the recording device as Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage. Amazon sells it for $23.99. The company said it has evidence that Alfozan intended to place other recording devices in sensitive spaces to secretly record meetings. According to OpenAI, Alfozan was a member of the product team. The company said it coordinated the timing of his firing with the FBI to avoid disrupting the investigation, and he was terminated Friday, the day he was arrested. Between Sept. 30 and that date, OpenAI said, it gradually restricted his access to systems and spaces, then suspended his physical and network access, placed him on leave, and secured his company-issued equipment. Listen to The Standard Podcasts Life in Seven Songs Tuesday, Sept. 24 Five things we learned from our bare-all interview with Sam Altman Listen Select Your Platform Close Apple Podcasts (opens in new tab) Spotify (opens in new tab) A YouTube video last month touted him as the only Saudi employee at OpenAI. “Honestly, this one year felt like five years anywhere else,” he said in response to a question about his experience. “The idea of AI is that it handles things one might not want to do, so they can focus on tasks or hobbies they enjoy more or work they take pleasure in and let it do the tedious tasks,” Alfozan said later in the video. A LinkedIn profile that matches Alfozan’s name lists his OpenAI role as engineering lead on the company’s AI agents platform. The resume said he has been a venture partner with Riyadh-based RAED Ventures since 2025. The company did not respond to The Standard’s inquiries. Before joining OpenAI, he was a founding engineer at Nash, an AI infrastructure company for logistics, from 2022 to August 2025, according to the LinkedIn profile. From 2017 to 2022, he was a senior systems engineer at Meta. His earlier experience, according to the profile, includes a stint as a systems engineer at Reach Labs, a wireless power startup in Y Combinator’s summer 2015 batch, and internships at Microsoft, SAP in Berlin and Akamai Technologies. He has a master’s degree in data science from UC Berkeley, the LinkedIn profile says. A man in the passenger seat of a car at Alfozan’s Millbrae home said that the family did not want to speak to reporters. OpenAI said it has no indication that Alfozan improperly accessed or took model weights, source code, or customer data and has not seen activity that compromised the safety of its products or customers’ information. The company said it will continue to support the FBI’s investigation. OpenAI said it treats protecting its technology, data and people “as a matter of national importance” and called the case an example of how AI can counter sophisticated security threats. A detention hearing before U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse is set for Oct. 19.
