title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
body_text: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics - Google Developers Blog Community/Events Learn Blog YouTube Search Community/Events Learn Blog YouTube Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics OCT. 13, 2026 Kanishka Rao Principal Software Engineer Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Mail Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI. You can see this leap in capability on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark , which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model. As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas: Robot control → Mobile manipulation with MuJoCo practice, zero-shot robot control, and closed-loop steering of video world models. Real2Sim → Reconstructing physically calibrated simulation twins from robot camera feeds, egocentric human video, or hand-drawn paper sketches. Physical understanding → Agentic multimodal hindsight labeling including detailed understanding of dexterity, dense value functions and progress estimation. Research and self-improvement → Action improvement via simulation and iterative self-improvement on hardware. Unlocking robot control with Argon 1. Spot mobile manipulation: Putting in the trash bin with MuJoCo practice Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Spot Mobile Manipulation — Real-to-Sim-to-Real foot-pedal trash bin disposal: Spot picking up the soda can, checking its wrist camera, practicing 3-leg tripod balance in MuJoCo, stepping on the foot pedal, verifying hand centering in the open bin, and dropping the can inside. Prompt: There's a Diet Coke can behind you and another on the black table on your left. Use the spot-mobile-manipulation skill to pick them up and trash them in the black foot-pedal bin. Before stepping down on the pedal, verify in the front cameras that your front-right foot target is centered on the pedal, and use a 2-agent verification swarm (foot-verifier and hand-verifier) to verify both the foot-pedal step and the 3D hand-in-bin alignment before releasing. Plain text Copied 2. Zero-shot control Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Left: 3rd-person real robot view; Right: calibrated wrist camera with projected 2 cm world coordinates and jaw-closing reticle. Prompt: [Attached: wrist_cam.png, obs.json] Task: Get the robot arm to reorient the mug upright and put the napkin inside the mug. ## Execution Discipline - Simply output 1 sentence observation followed immediately by your `curl` command (with `# Plan:` on Turn 1 and `# Thought:` on every turn). Everything needed is in `obs.json` and the calibrated reticle/grid drawn on `wrist_cam.png`. ## Visual Coordinate Reference (Annotated on wrist_cam.png) - `+X` (UP in image): Away from robot base | `-X` (DOWN): Towards robot base - `+Y` (LEFT in image): World left | `-Y` (RIGHT): World right - `+Z`: Height above table | `Yellow numbers`: World (X, Y) in centimetres (2 cm grid at `grid_z`) - `Cyan + crosshair`: Current 3D pinch center - `Cyan [ + ] brackets`: Current jaw opening and closing line - `Green line`: Current object long-axis orientation (`yaw_deg`: 0° = vertical along +X, 90° = horizontal along +Y) - `pitch_deg = 90°`: Straight down (-Z) top-down grasp/place; `pitch_deg < 60°`: Tilted coaxial approach along finger axis ## Closed-Loop Turn Workflow 1. Inspect current state & view `wrist_cam.png`: `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/obs` (returns `ee_pos`, `holding`, `status`, `workspace`, `wrist_cam_path`). 2. Select VLM call granularity upfront on Turn 1: - Coarse (2–4 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> `place` -> `done` - Pre-Grasp Hover Verify (4–7 calls): `look_at` -> `goto(z=0.04)` (verify cyan `[ + ]` brackets straddle target) -> `grasp` -> `place_until_contact` -> `done` - Fine Visual Servoing (8–20 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> pre-pose `goto` -> closed-loop `move_by` / `move_until_contact` -> `done` 3. Send motion primitives (`POST /plan`) and verify visually after every turn in the updated `wrist_cam.png`. If `status == "grasp_failed"`, call `robot.look_at(...)` to re-observe and recover closed-loop. ## Code-as-Policies Primitives (`POST http://127.0.0.1:8081/plan`) robot.look_at(x=0.35, y=0.13, z=0.14, grid_z=0.015) x, y = robot.deproject(u=0.52, v=0.48, z_plane=0.015) robot.grasp(x=x, y=y, z=0.015, yaw_deg=-35, pitch_deg=90) robot.place(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.075) robot.place_until_contact(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.015, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002) robot.goto(x=0.28, y=0.05, z=0.04, arc_z=0.14, pitch_deg=25, azimuth_deg=90, roll_deg=0, speed=0.10) robot.move_by(forward=0.025, dz=-0.002, dpitch_deg=-3, droll_deg=5, speed=0.04) robot.move_until_contact(dz=-0.06, speed=0.03, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002) robot.open_gripper() / robot.close_gripper() / robot.home() / robot.done() Plain text Copied 3. Omni control Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles ( G, R, A, N, O ) into a clean row spelling A - R - G - O - N . Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Iterative Video World Model Steering Dexterous Hands: 33-Step Steered Video Rollout Spelling A-R-G-O-N. Prompt: Goal: {task_goal} You are steering a video world model (Gemini Omni) in an iterative visual feedback loop. Inspect the attached frames from the latest rollout and write the next timestamped action prompt for the video world model: - Break complex motions into one simple, single-direction action at a time. - Keep inactive hands retracted and avoid blocking the camera's view of objects in the workspace. - Explicitly state which areas of the workspace become empty after an object moves. - Use [MM:SS.mmm] timestamps for each action beat and wrap your output in <omni_prompt> tags. Example format (sample timestamps only, not the full prompt): <omni_prompt> [00:00.000] Character A's left hand rests at the side while the right hand reaches toward the target object. [00:02.500] Character A's right fingertips push the object smoothly into the center of the table, leaving its starting area empty. [00:05.000] Character A's right hand opens and retracts to the side so all placed objects remain in clear view of the camera. </omni_prompt> Plain text Copied Unlocking Real2Sim with Argon 1. Robot view to simulation Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Left (Real View): synchronized real robot camera feeds; Right (Simulated): 3D MuJoCo scene reconstructed and calibrated by Argon. Prompt: [Attached: robot_rollout_episode] Build a MuJoCo scene of the robot and reconstructed task objects. When each episode is replayed frame by frame, by driving the robot joints toward the logged observation.state with joint-space PD. Iterate using two verification objectives: (1) Visual match: MuJoCo renders from the head_left, left_wrist, and right_wrist cameras line up with, and look like, those real observations. (2) Physical match: the simulated contact force/torque on each Sharpa fingertip, in the sensor frame, matches the logged tactile_force in timing, magnitude and direction. What you can tune happens before simulation starts: (1) Static object assets: realistic geometry, collision shapes, mass, inertia, friction and joints, with appearance close to the real objects, plus the initial object poses at t = 0. (2) Offline-planned robot commands, changed only in frames where the real fingertips are near an object. Each command must stay within 0.55 rad (arm joints) and 0.65 rad (hand joints) of the logged teleop trajectory. Everywhere else, replay the logged trajectory unchanged. No sim cheating: task objects may move only through real MuJoCo contact with the robot hands and the environment (mj_step). Not allowed after t = 0: changing MjModel parameters; applying external forces or torques to objects; welds or equality constraints; feedforward torques beyond joint-space PD; setting or rolling back object qpos/qvel; disabling or excluding collisions; reporting contact forces that don't come from the MuJoCo solver (for example, copying the logged tactile readings). Immediately present the reconstructed scene and rollout results as an interactive HTML session viewer with one page per episode, showing: - At the bottom: A synced timeline (play, scrub, speed control) that drives every panel. - On the left panel: An interactive 3D Blender scene showing the simulated robot and objects, showing contact points and force arrows as replay progresses. - On the right panel: Real vs. sim camera views side by side for all 3 cameras. Real vs. sim finger force visualizations. Plain text Copied 2. Human view to simulation Given an egocentric human video of a manipulation task, Argon identifies the task-relevant objects, replaces crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed meshes for concave containers, and retargets the human hand trajectory onto a 76-DoF bimanual humanoid with 22-DoF five-fingered hands in MuJoCo contact physics. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Human View to Simulation — Egocentric Human Video to Dexterous Humanoid Twin: Left shows the input egocentric human RGB video; Right shows the synchronized 500 Hz MuJoCo + Blender Cycles multi-view simulation rollout. Prompt: [Attached: egocentric_human_video.mp4, candidate_sim_views.png, hand_3d_keypoints.json] You are building a physically solvable 500 Hz MuJoCo manipulation environment (`scene.xml`) and studio Blender render that faithfully reproduces the tabletop task shown in `egocentric_human_video.mp4` on a bimanual humanoid robot with 22-DoF dexterous five-fingered hands: 1. Scene Reconstruction & Camera Calibration: - Identify only the manipulation-relevant objects (the grasped target object and the receiving container or landmark) and triangulate their 3D tabletop coordinates from the egocentric camera intrinsics/extrinsics. - Replace crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed 3D meshes so concave containers (nested bowls, recessed wooden trays, open bins) support physical interior placement. 2. 500 Hz Dexterous Motion-Fitting Stress Test: - Retarget the 3D human wrist and finger keypoints to the humanoid's 7-DoF arm and 22-DoF hand joints, and step the trajectory in MuJoCo at 500 Hz (dt = 0.002s) with zero kinematic weld constraints. - Verify opposing thumb-and-finger force closure, clean object lift (> 2 cm), and stable final placement inside or beside the target landmark. Plain text Copied 3. Sketch to simulation With Argon, a developer can snap a photo of a rough pen-and-paper sketch—showing an Apollo 2 humanoid throwing a ball along a parabolic arc to topple a 3-2-1 stack of boxes on a table—and have Argon automatically construct the GPU-accelerated mujoco_warp scene, synthesize a balanced 76-DoF whole-body and five-finger throw trajectory, verify 6/6 target knockdown in closed-loop physics, and export a Blender 4.5 Cycles render. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Sketch to Simulation — Hand-Drawn Sketch to Dexterous Humanoid Trajectory & Cycles Render. Prompt: [Attached: hand_drawn_throw_sketch.jpg] Translate this hand-drawn sketch into a physically verified humanoid simulation in `mujoco_warp` and a raytraced Blender Cycles video: 1. Scene & Kinematic Setup from Sketch: - Parse the spatial layout from `hand_drawn_throw_sketch.jpg`: place the 76-DoF humanoid (32-DoF body equipped with two 22-DoF five-finger dexterous hands) at the origin facing a table holding a 3-2-1 pyramid of 6 rigid target boxes, with a projectile sphere grasped in the right five-finger hand. 2. Whole-Body Balance & Dexterous Throw Synthesis: - Synthesize a 50 Hz whole-body throwing trajectory (140 steps, 2.80 s) across four phases: (1) stable stance & 5-finger power grasp closure, (2) torso/shoulder wind-up with ankle-hip Center-of-Mass compensation, (3) forward whipping acceleration, and (4) synchronized 22-DoF five-finger opening at peak hand velocity so the ball launches on a ballistic arc into the pyramid's second-tier center of mass. - Verify in `mujoco_warp` contact physics that the humanoid maintains upright balance (< 3 cm pelvis drift) and knocks down all 6 target boxes. Plain text Copied Unlocking physical understanding with Argon 1. Hindsight labeling and data quality Argon has precise physical understanding of dexterous manipulation and can provide detailed segmentation and text labeling from video. Argon is able to identify poor manipulation segments such as pauses, unstable grasps and fumbles. Given an overhead video of a bimanual ALOHA 2 robot folding a square sheet of paper into an origami fox over 136 seconds, Argon produces a time-aligned 4-level hindsight annotation hierarchy: Episode Goal (G1), 6 contiguous Semantic Subtasks (G2), 17 contact-level Atomic Primitives (G3), and automated Quality Control (QC) reweighting that holds task progress flat during fumbles and retries. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon Multi-Granularity Hindsight & Telemetry HUD. Prompt: [Attached: Aloha2_Origami_20250309.mp4] Produce a time-aligned multi-granularity hindsight annotation JSON with four levels: 1. G1_episode_instruction: Concise imperative sentence describing the overall manipulation goal. 2. G2_subtasks: Contiguous semantic subtask phases specifying which arm(s) anchor vs. fold/rotate the object. 3. G3_atomic_primitives: Fine-grained contact-level primitives (3–15s) aligned with grasp closure, crease sweeps, release, or retry attempts. 4. quality_control_and_reweighting: Hold task_progress_pct flat during non-progressing slip/delamination retry loops and downweight them (0.15x–0.25x) for Behavior Cloning. Plain text Copied 2. Find the odd ball To recreate the classic 12-ball balance scale puzzle with robots, Argon builds a bimanual Franka FR3 MuJoCo environment with 12 visually identical pool balls (one secretly heavier or lighter) and an articulated Roberval two-pan balance scale. It then writes a vision-only closed-loop solver that triangulates the balls from stereo RGB cameras, visually reads the scale tilt after each weighing, and isolates the odd ball into the Heavy (Red) or Light (Blue) tray within 3 weighings. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Find the Odd Ball (Vision-Only Closed-Loop Solver): Dual-arm Franka FR3 weighing candidate balls on the Gold/Teal pans, reading stereo scale tilt , and isolating the confirmed Heavy odd ball into the Red tray in 3 weighings. Prompt: # Prompt 1 — Physics-Accurate MuJoCo Environment & Benchmark Generation Make a MuJoCo environment where a dual-arm robot (two 7-DoF Franka FR3 arms with parallel-jaw grippers on a shared tabletop) is tasked to solve the classic 12-ball balance scale weight puzzle from https://www.mathsisfun.com/pool_balls_solution.html. 1. Create 12 visually indistinguishable pool balls in a 2x6 starting rack (11 standard 150 g, 1 odd ball either 270 g or 30 g). 2. Build a functional two-pan Roberval balance scale at the center of the table with parallelogram equality constraints (`mjEQ_JOINT`) so the Left (Gold) and Right (Teal) pans stay horizontal, plus Red (Heavy) and Blue (Light) submission trays. 3. Track distinct settled weighings (`weighing_count`) and reward `1.00` for isolating the true odd ball in the correct Heavy/Light tray within <= 3 weighings. # Prompt 2 — Closed-Loop Vision-Only Solver Implement an independent closed-loop policy relying strictly on stereo RGB camera inputs (`head_camera_left_rgb_image`, `head_camera_right_rgb_image`) and robot proprioception (`add_privileged_task_observations=False`): 1. Segment the 12 balls, Gold/Teal pans, and Red/Blue trays in both stereo views and triangulate their 3D coordinates. 2. Visually read the balance scale tilt after each weighing from stereo vertical pixel disparity (+1 = left heavier, -1 = right heavier, 0 = balanced). 3. Rotate the gripper wrist yaw by 90 degrees when grasping/placing inside the narrow scale pans to clear the raised rims, and isolate the odd ball into the Red or Blue tray within <= 3 weighings. Plain text Copied 3. Value function Argon is a general value function for robotics tasks. Evaluated on a 60-second bimanual ring-sorting episode from a human UMI dataset, Argon iteratively inspects synchronized head, left-gripper, and right-gripper camera feeds around contact transitions to generate dense value function / task progress predictions and decompose the trajectory into 28 segments with positive, neutral, and negative progress slopes. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Value Function: Synchronized 3-camera UMI playback (head, left gripper, right gripper) locked to animated task progress curve and bimanual segment annotations. Prompt: [Attached: umi_head.mp4, umi_left_gripper.mp4, umi_right_gripper.mp4] Look at 3 videos of human wearing a gripper performing activities from head, left, right gripper views. Look at the videos thoroughly and give a detailed plot of progress at the task (with positive, neutral, negative slope), identifying important segments in the video and labeling the activities. Look at individual frames or subsegments of the video if necessary to get a better understanding. Plain text Copied Unlocking research and self-improvement with Argon 1. Action improvement via simulation Argon can generate new data in simulation to improve performance of generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models. Starting from a single RGB photo of the real tabletop, Argon autonomously builds a calibrated MuJoCo simulation twin, defines new tasks, and synthesizes a closed-loop motion generator to collect 4,500+ domain-randomized episodes in simulation—boosting real-world physical robot Success Rate from 56% to 75% and reducing completion time from 35s to 24s . Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Action Improvement via Simulation: improves the real-world evaluation benchmark (56% → 75% Success Rate and 35s → 24s Completion Time). Prompt: [Attached: real_tabletop_photo.jpg] You are given a single overhead RGB camera photo (`real_tabletop_photo.jpg`) of a bimanual robot workspace (two 7-DoF Franka FR3 arms with parallel-jaw grippers and 4 RGB cameras) facing a table arranged with photobooth party props. 1. Reconstruct procedural 3D meshes and compound MuJoCo collision primitives for all 9 party props matching their real-world dimensions, colors, and resting poses, including spring-hinged deformable crown panels for the soft plush cap. 2. Define a 77-task single-arm and bimanual curriculum (pick-and-place, uprighting, directional pushing, mid-air handovers, bimanual scoop-and-push, and pipelined table clearing). 3. Synthesize a closed-loop IK trajectory generator across ±10 cm pose randomization, verify `reward == 1.0` in MuJoCo physics, and export 4,500+ episodes for VLA fine-tuning. Plain text Copied 2. Self-Improvement for visual pick and place On a simple 6-DoF arm, Argon iteratively self-improves both execution speed and placement accuracy on a pick and place task via trial and self-reflection. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video SO-101 Vision-Guided Pick-and-Place — Iterative Hardware Self-Improvement Across Iterations 1 → 2 → 3: Iteration 1 (58.9s), Iteration 2 (22.9s, grazed box rim on drop), and Iteration 3 (17.4s, dead-center drop). Prompt: # Stage 1 — Measure Objects & Dry-Run Plan (No Hardware Motion) Stage 1: measure objects — find the objects and plan the whole motion. The arm does not move in this stage. A. I put a LEGO brick and a box on the table in front of the arm, and the wooden box to one side. Find the brick and the wooden box in the image. And also in the real world. Show this in an annotated image. B. A dry-run plan (no hardware). Write the planner to pick and place the lego block. Print the plan table, draw all poses onto the overhead image, and stop. Do not move the robot. Report with evidence. # Stage 2 — Pre-Pick Hover & Wrist-Camera Verification Stage 2: Put the gripper above the brick without touching it, and verify with the wrist camera that the arm and the vision agree. Please record executions with both cameras (compressed video is OK). # Stage 3 (Autonomous Pick-and-Place → Self-Improvement → Optimization): 1. Execute autonomously: Turn the Stage 1 dry run into a real grasp, lift, and place into the wooden box. Run it yourself subject to safety rules from AGENTS.md. 2. Self-improve: When an attempt fails, diagnose it yourself. Review your own logs and wrist/overhead footage, find the root cause, check the fix in a dry run, and retry. 3. Optimize on feedback: Once it succeeds, make it at least 2× faster within safety limits (rule R5) unless I authorize more, or give feedback. Plain text Copied 3. One-prompt robotics paper reproductions in MuJoCo WebAssembly With a single prompt per paper, Argon reads a robotics control manuscript and any released checkpoints, ports the physics model and closed-loop controller (from 7-network hierarchical locomotion in DeepLoco and 50 Hz PPO actors in HUSKY to Web Worker iLQR in Whole-Body MPC ) into self-contained MuJoCo WebAssembly browser labs, and verifies them in headless Chromium. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Five Landmark Legged & Humanoid Papers Running Live in Browser (MuJoCo WASM): Robotic Soccer OP3 1v1, DeepLoco, Massively Parallel Deep RL ANYmal C, Whole-Body MPC Go2, and HUSKY G1 Skateboarding (from 68 interactive browser sandboxes reproduced by Argon). Prompt: [Attached: paper.pdf, optional author_checkpoints/ or urdf_assets/] Reproduce the paper "<Paper Title & arXiv ID>" from scratch in MuJoCo WebAssembly and deploy a self-contained browser lab + visual essay: 1. Match the paper's exact physics timestep, actuator gains (kp/kv), torque limits, and kinematic constraints in MuJoCo XML, and run real neural inference or Web Worker iLQR in JavaScript at the paper's exact control rates. 2. Build `index.html` (Spatial UI simulator with camera presets, live telemetry plots, and disturbance injection) and `scrollytelling.html` (interactive visual essay). 3. Run a headless Chromium (Playwright) verification loop asserting 0 console errors and non-zero task progress over 300+ frames. Plain text Copied Advancing embodied intelligence with Argon Argon bridges coding, visual perception, physics simulation, and embodied robot control. By reasoning natively over multi-view video, 3D geometry, contact mechanics, and proprioceptive telemetry, Argon understands not just what objects are in a scene, but how they physically interact with agents to accomplish whole-body dexterous tasks. Gemini 4 Argon marks an important milestone accelerating the path toward physical AGI. By building this core intelligence, our goal is to enable robotics that can work alongside humans to solve complex challenges. Getting started You can start building with Gemini 4 Argon today across Google’s developer platforms: Google AI Studio : Available to Google AI Ultra subscribers. Gemini API: Available with the paid tier of the Gemini API in AI Studio. Use gemini-4-argon in the Interactions API with day-one support across the google-genai SDKs. Google Antigravity: Available for Google AI Ultra subscribers. To start building, select Gemini 4 Argon ( gemini-4-argon ) as your active model in Google Antigravity for complex planning, /goal runs, and multi-agent orchestration. posted in: AI Case Studies Announcements Learn Explore Solve Previous Next Related Posts AI Cloud Announcements Problem-Solving Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster OCT. 14, 2026 Gemini AI Cloud Announcements Best Practices Optimizing a 200,000-line Python codebase overnight with Gemini 4 Argon OCT. 13, 2026 AI Cloud Tutorials Case Studies Accelerating Spatio-Temporal Attention for Video Diffusion on TPUs SEPT. 30, 2026 Mobile Web Case Studies Announcements ML Drift: Next-Gen GPU AI/ML Inference at the Edge OCT. 8, 2026 Connect Blog Bluesky Instagram LinkedIn X (Twitter) YouTube Programs Google Developer Program Google Developer Groups Google Developer Experts Accelerators Women Techmakers Google Cloud & NVIDIA Developer consoles Google API Console Google Cloud Platform Console Google Play Console Firebase Console Actions on Google Console Cast SDK Developer Console Chrome Web Store Dashboard Google Home Developer Console Android Chrome Firebase Google Cloud Platform All products Manage cookies Terms Privacy

title: We turned EmbeddingGemma 2 into a speech-to-text model
body_text: Embedding Gemma Transcribe Embedding Gemma Transcribe Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model. We turned it into a speech-to-text model: an hour of audio in about 13 seconds on a base MacBook Air , entirely on device. Download for Mac (free) v1.6 · macOS 14+ · Apple Silicon models download on first launch (715 MB) Can an embedding model transcribe speech? EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model: text, images, audio and video in one shared space. Say a word out loud and its audio lands close to the written word. So we tried reading words straight out of that space. How it works EmbeddingGemma 2's audio encoder stays exactly as it is. A small reader moves each short slice of audio into the model's text space. The closest of ~229,000 English words wins, and the slices become a transcript. A tiny extra model adds punctuation and capitals. Only the reader is trained: under two hours on 8×H100, on openly licensed English speech. The base model was never trained for speech-to-text. How fast? Model Runs on Mac Speed Embedding Gemma Transcribe Neural Engine base M3 MacBook Air, 8 GB 288× 1 hour in 12.6 s IBM Granite Speech 5.0 TurboCTC GPU (MLX) base M3 MacBook Air, 8 GB ~150× 1 hour in 25.7 s NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (FluidAudio) Neural Engine M4 Pro 156× NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (FluidAudio) Neural Engine M5 Pro 335× Phonon-2, a Parakeet v3 fine-tune (FluidAudio) Neural Engine M5 Pro 480× × real time: seconds of audio per second of processing. Rows 1–2: our tests on the same base M3 MacBook Air. Rows 3–5: FluidAudio's published benchmarks on larger, newer Macs and different audio. A rough guide, not a like-for-like ranking. Where it stands Its word error rate is about 5% right now, against 2–3% for leading speech models. We believe a better-trained reader can close that gap; that's the next iteration. Use it Drop in an audio file, or hold Right Option, speak and release to dictate into any app. It runs on the Mac's Neural Engine; your audio never leaves the machine. Download for Mac (free) EmbeddingGemma 2 is made by Google DeepMind and released under Apache 2.0. This is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Google.

I posted to HN, and then my website was flooded with AI BOT traffic For the past few years, I've been working on sprinklz.io , a customizable feed reader that can, among other things, deprioritize certain topics from your news feed. A month ago, I posted it to HN , and it got a hundred or so upvotes, nice! It seems like people are really tired of hearing about LLMs, and they enjoyed being able to deprioritize them from their feed. It was a good demo of why a tool like this is useful. Everything was looking up, and then… My website got slow. Like, really, painfully slow. At first I chalked it up to the extra attention of a suddenly popular post. Like any developer I both celebrated, and vowed to make my website more resiliant in the future. Strangely though, the slowness continued, and even started to get worse several days after my post went live, and the metrics I did log did not make sense. Like, you know, a good handful of genuinely active, logged-in users, and a sever exhibiting exhorbatantly high load. So I took a look at some data. I added top-level logging for every endpoint (how many times was a request made to each url path), and I found that a majority of the requests did not even make an attempt to fetch news articles! For reference, my website is built as a single-page-application, and what this means is that a majority of the requests did not even run the javascript necessary to render the page (!). Digging further, I looked at aggregate NGINX logs to find abusers, and, you're never going to believe this, but it turns out that nearly half of our traffic was coming from one specific user. I won't name names, but I looked them up, and they describe themselves as a service that listens for changes to a website, and then summarizes them into an AI slop news letter. And by 'listens to changes' I mean query our website many many times per-minute. Blocked. Several of the others were your standard known crawlers, and kindly identified themselves as such. Claude bot, OpenAI bot, google's search indexer, and several others. I even picked up a few vulnerability scanners along the way. At least, somebody is trying to access -/wp-content/phpinfo.php (my website is not a wordpress site). I added robots.txt to discourage most of the AI scanners, but allow google-bot and other search-related traffic, and asked claude to query all the vulnerability paths and mimic the scanners to make sure I wasn't leaking anything. I also added reasonable rate limits, etc., etc. The most important lesson though, is that it's time to make my website faster. I want to be the website that can day handle xxx QPS of real traffic, and it should scale better than it did, even under heavy load. Inspired by this encounter, I've made quite a few improvements to the underlying infrastructure over the past few weeks, and these should result in pretty substantial performance gains for all users. P.S. if you'd like to check it out, the website is fully free, and available here The TLDR is that it lets you define your own customizations, in addition to things like the points totals from hacker news. You can use it to filter out topics, like AI or LLMs, but the topics are completely arbitrary and you can program your own customizations. 2. Using LLMs to Make the Emacs Web Browser Great Again When I tell people about the emacs web browser, their first reaction is 'Wait emacs has a web browser?!', followed by, 'yeah… I guess that's kind of a web browser'. The emacs web browser is designed to render webpages in a terminal-based, textonly environment and, well, it goes about exactly the way you'd expect. It works well on HTML-only, small-content websites, but not so good for anything else. The problem is that emacs is primarily a text-only editor, but the modern internet is very much not plain-text based. Simple HTML, designed in the simple style of the 1990s has a clear translation into plain text, but modern UI design, with it's visual styling, heavy javascript, and just, overall chaos, not so much. The emacs web browser would be great, if only we could find a way to go back in time… Ok, so the plan is simple. We take modern webpages, rewrite their source code into old-school simply-styled HTML, and then pipe it through to the emacs web browser. We just need to find a way to do this easily and at scale. So um, you didn't forget about LLMs did you? It's nice to be using them in a way that will hopefully reduce the amount of spam content in the world. Basically, the plan is we write a program that: Opens a webpage in firefox Loads the page and runs all the javascript Asks an LLM to generate a re-usable program that transforms the current-page's contents into simplified text Inject the generated javascript into the firefox browser Grab the new page source and forward it to emacs web browser. Yeah, and so, I've been using it, and it runs very well. Like realistically I can use this on many webpages where eww (emacs web wowser) did not run previously. I have been using it myself and enjoying the experience. The source code lives here: https://github.com/sstraust/simpleweb and is open-source, and free to install, etc., etc. 2. Deft version 0.2.0 Now that deft 0.2.0 is released, I figure it's a good time to talk about what I built, and why I built it. The point of Clojure's everything-is-a-map toolkit is that getters and setters are a waste of time. Clojure was built, in large part, in response to the crappy 2008 Java workflow, where you had to write getters, setters, and builders, and you took on all this bloat that nobody enjoyed. The problem is that if you want to represent your data using the built-in defprotocol and defrecord, and you want to define functions that depend on the presence of a certain field, then the only way to encode that information into the protocol is to add getter and setter metohds to it. icky. You can also use a combination of protocol + malli schema to represent this, but then when you use it, you need to specify 'this function takes as input something that both implements this protocol and implements this Malli schema'. Also icky. What we want is something we can use in the style of defprotocol and defrecord, but gives us all the getters and setters and map-like stuff by default. The key insight is that if a field exists in a record, we get all the other good stuff, so we just need to add support for protocols with required keys. Deft v0.2.0 adds support for namespaced keys in type and protocol definitions. i.e., you can now do: (defp Positioned :required-keys [::pos - ::Point]) and (deft Circle [::location/position radius]) (>Circle ::location/position [1 2] :radius 12) this is useful because you can now define methods that depend on those fields being present i.e.: (defp Gremlin :extends [location/Positioned]) (defmethod game-object/get-hitbox ::Gremlin [self] (js/Matter.Bodies.rectangle (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/x]) (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/y]) 15 15)) Check it out! https://github.com/sstraust/deft 4. How much LLMs is too much LLMs? I finished reading On the Edge last week, and it was bad. Not that I don't respect Nate Silver. I respect him a lot. So when his seminal text on gambling and risk taking was a rambling mess, I was suprised and disappointed. Nevertheless, a completionist at heart, I trudged on, to the very end, where I was greeted with this message: "ChatGPT was a significant help in writing this book, serving as a creative muse when coming up with things like chapter subheadings, metaphors, and analogies, and for refining my understanding of technical topics that are likely to be well represented in its corpus." Technically he wrote the book by hand, and technically he typed the letters onto his keyboard, but you know, did he really? Did he put his whole thought and mind and being into every word on the page? Maybe. I'm reminded of the absolute classic [Simple Made Easy]( https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SxdOUGdseq4 ), a video where so much of the core lecture is built on defining precise language, and saying exactly what you mean. When you offload that work, you don't just skip word choices, you skip that thinking, and you miss out on that organization and mental clarity. In reading Nate's book, there's a real and noticeable difference between the language that feels baked into the organizational fabric of Nate's mentality, and the bits that were added on as an afterthought. The later chapters especially felt like they lacked that sort of mental compactification that cohesifies everything under one vision. I'm sad because this could have been a phenominal work, and it's clear that a lot of effort was made, especially into interviews and data collection, and it feels like it's just lacking that one last missing piece of insight to bring it all the way home. So how much LLMs is too much LLMs? Well, when it comes to human connection, I'd say the answer is near zero. I don't want to read your AI generated e-mails, and I certainly don't want to read your AI generated essays. I'd much rather read your prompt instead, because I care about what you , yes, you personally think about, and I want to understand what you wanted to communicate. Don't get me wrong, I love LLMs for the right purpose. I'd love to use LLMs on doctor's notes to build models that predict whether the flu is spreading. But when it comes to writing, especially this kind of writing, it just feels so unnecessary, because when you write down your thoughts, I already have exactly what I wanted, and it just feels so silly to add an extra stop in between. As a poker player and game theorist, I'm sure Nate would appreciate the phrase "If you couldn't be bothered to write it, then I can't be bothered to read it". And you know, despite a belief that art can live separately from the artist, deep down for me this claim rings true. Not that the same words produced by a person are inherently different than the same words from an LLM, but it throws off my little Bayesian estimator a little. If the smartest person I know spent 10,000 hours writing, editing, polishing, and publishing a 500 page novel, it tells me not just that the smartest person I know had some thoughts on a topic, but it tells me that they decided to spend 10,000 hours of their precious time, and of their precious energy to communicate this idea to me. It feels good that the time it took me to read it is porportional (and usually less than) the time it took you to write it, because it shows me that you care about the time and energy of creating this exchange. And it's not just fully AI generated slop that hits this barrier. When you incorporate LLMs into your writing, even a little bit, you miss out on the ability to process your thoughts and create human connection. 5. Chess is a good trial run for any class and interface system, because it's reasonably small and self-contained (and has some pretty obvious choice for classes), but it also comes with some of the messiness of a real application, in that, you want to write something concise, but you still have to handle edge-cases, like castling and en passant. I hand-drew all of the pieces, and used this little reagent snippet to render the display, [ :h-box ( doall ( for [x (range (count tiles))] ^{ :key x} [ :v-box ( doall ( for [y (reverse (range (count (nth tiles x))))] ^{ :key y} [ :p { :style { :background-color ( cond (= [x y] @currently-selected-location) "yellow" (= (mod (+ x y) 2) 1) "white" :else "black" ) :height "4rem" :width "4rem" } :on-click ( fn [] (move-selected-piece game-board-atom currently-selected-location [x y]))} ( if (not (nil? (get-in tiles [x y]))) [ :img { :src (image-path ( ::piece-type (get-in tiles [x y]))) :style { :height "100%" :width "100%" :filter ( when (= ( ::color (get-in tiles [x y])) ::black ) "invert()" )}}] "" )]))]))] but kind of the interesting bit is how to represent the board state and all of its pieces. I did sort of the obvious thing, and defined types representing a chess piece, and then a board, as a 8x8 grid of pieces (deft ChessPiece [color piece-type]) (deft ChessBoard [tiles - [ :vector [ :vector [ :or :nil ChessPiece]]] curr-move - [ :enum ::white ::black ] move-history - [ :vector ChessMove]]) and then for the piece behavior, I made protocols that define how a piece is displayed, and how it can move. (defp PieceType (image-path [this])) (defp MovablePiece (is-valid-move-for-piece? [this game-board start-location end-location])) here is an example for the knight: (deft Knight [] PieceType (image-path [this] (image-asset "knight_white.png" )) MovablePiece (is-valid-move-for-piece? [this game-board start-location end-location] ( and ( let [direction (map abs (map - end-location start-location))] ( or ( and (= (first direction) 1) (= (second direction) 2)) ( and (= (first direction) 2) (= (second direction) 1)))) (is-valid-end-location? game-board start-location end-location)))) is-valid-move-for-piece? returns a true-false value of "can my piece move to this square". This works great for most pieces, but is insufficient for more complicated moves, like castling, where several pieces move at the same time. To handle this, we use another multimethod (defmulti special-move-for-piece (fn [x & args] (:type x))) that is defined only for special moves, and returns the actual state of the modified gameboard. so for pawns, it would look something like this: ( defmethod special-move-for-piece ::Pawn [this game-board start-location end-location] ( let [curr-piece-color ( ::color (get-in ( ::tiles game-board) start-location)) move-direction (into [] (map - end-location start-location)) prev-move (last ( ::move-history game-board))] ( cond ;; en passant ( and (= (second move-direction) ( if (= curr-piece-color ::white ) 1 -1)) (= (abs (first move-direction)) 1) (= ( :type ( ::piece-type ( ::piece prev-move))) ::Pawn ) (= (apply max (map abs (map - ( ::end-location prev-move) ( ::start-location prev-move)))) 2) (= end-location (into [] (map + (map ( fn [x] (/ x 2 )) (map - ( ::end-location prev-move) ( ::start-location prev-move))) ( ::start-location prev-move))))) ( -> game-board (update ::tiles assoc-in start-location nil ) (update ::tiles assoc-in end-location (get-in ( ::tiles game-board) start-location)) (update ::tiles assoc-in ( ::end-location prev-move) nil )) ( and (is-valid-move-for-piece? this game-board start-location end-location) ( or (= (second end-location) 0) (= (second end-location) 7))) ( -> game-board (update ::tiles assoc-in start-location nil ) (update ::tiles assoc-in end-location (assoc (get-in ( ::tiles game-board) start-location) ::piece-type (>Queen)))) :else nil ))) I'm not going to copy-paste the movesets for every piece in this post, but it was pretty straightforward to define relevant methods for all the different piece types and special-cases, and I'm pretty happy with how the code turned out. When you're reading this code, it really looks like somebody just wrote down all the rules for the game of chess, and that's what makes me feel good, and feel like we've done things in a way that's well organized. But now, sort of the most important question (for me) is: is this library actually helping? did deft make our lives better? I think it did, for the following reasons: deft gives us the features from both protocols/records and multimethods/plain-maps, so we didn't need to decide which tool was right for our use-case. this removes just like a lot of cognitive load, because we can use one tool, and trust that it can do everything pretty well. in particular, it was nice to be able to define :default method dispatch for our protocols, and it was extremely nice to be able to reload protocol method defs from the repl without having to re-instantiate the entire chessboard (and clear the current position) it was really nice to be able to enforce when I wanted method defs to be defined for a particular type, and it was really nice to have an easy way to add Malli schema Overall, I'm pretty happy with how it all turned out, and I'd say the test of our library was a success. Announcing Deft: A class and interface system for Clojure and ClojureScript Today I'm releasing deft! It's a library that replaces clojure's existing class system with plain maps and Malli schema. It took me about 6 months to really think it through all the way, and get the design just right, so it feels good to finally publish it. The library: https://github.com/sstraust/deft Video Tutorial: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlW6YzwUZ-M On Hackernews: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46590958 (plz star the repo!) Synopsis: This library came out of out frustrations with Clojure's existing type ecosystem. Both defrecord/defprotocol, and plain maps+multimethods, the way they are currently used, make Clojure programs fundamentally difficult to organize and refactor. The problem is that: Clojure records use single-colon (unnamespaced) keyword access to lookup record fields Clojure records do not allow you to define abstract classes, or things that rely on complex dispatch behavior. Clojure maps are extremely difficult to nail down and make stable. Even with libraries like Malli, it's hard to declare interfaces that explain "what can I do with this thing?" Unless you are extremely regimented about defining Malli schemas for every single use case, it's easy for things to get disconnected during destructuring, because missed field lookups return nil The goal is to give something that's still enjoyable to work with, but lets you really nail down the behavior when you want to (and still keeps it ergonomic and fun). A secondary goal was to make something that is reliable and stable, and is (hopefully) easy to adopt in existing codebases. check it out! 7. How to Win at Wordle I played my first game of Wordle this week, and I got in 4! Ok, I got a little bit lucky, but it wasn't all luck. While I was playing I had a chance to think through some of the strategies, and saw some pitfalls I think others might have missed. 8.1. Don't guess letters that are already green Unless you're trying to make your final guess to win the game, you shouldn't guess the same letter in the same place. You already tried that, so doing it again doesn't give you new information. Your "guess" is guaranteed to be wrong, but you now rule out (or find!) another possible letter when you go to actually solve the puzzle. Lets see an example: Suppose you have B - A - _ - E - S, all green. You just need to guess the last letter, but there are a lot of remaining options. Among letters you haven't guessed in that slot, D, K, N, R, S all work. You could guess every letter individually, but you most likely won't get it first try, and worst case it will take you five turns. Instead, if you guess D - R - I - N - K, a word that you know is wrong you "guess" every letter at once, so you're guaranteed to get it in 2 (you guess S if there are no yellows). 8.2. When you guess new letters, put them in places they commonly appear Just for a moment, think of worlde a little bit like binary search. Your goal is to learn as much information as possible with every guess. If your guess splits the problem space in half (i.e. you eliminate half of possible words if it shows up green, and half of words if it shows up yellow), you learn (on average) the most possible information with every guess. Now – you only get to guess a letter in one position, so either it's in the one specific position you chose, or it's in any of the other possible four positions. If you want these two outcomes to be roughly equally likely (or as close to equally likely as possible), then that one position you chose had better be really likely to make up for 4 other slots. You learn (on average) way more about the letter 'Y' with a guess like R - A - I - N - Y, than you do with a guess like Y - E - A - R - N. 8.3. Guess common letters first Basically the same logic as above. It's either one of the 5 specific letters you guessed, or it's one of the 21 other letters. You want to guess the 5 that most closely split the problem in half. Going a step further, once you have a few lines guessed, you want to guess the most common/most evenly dividing letters given the letters you already have. Q is a bad first guess, but if you already have a U down, then maybe… 8.4. Think through the list of possible words at every step Remember, your goal is to "divide in half" with every letter. If you have a sense of/random sample of the words in the space, it's easier to pick the letters/positions that divide that list the most precisely. 9. The Power Of Habit (Book Review Pt 1) Charles Duhigg was a reporter for the New York Times, and you can feel it in his writing. This is a modern-science report that's sensational, inspirational, and often highly misleading. This book has it all, self-help transformations from couch potatoes to superstars, the success of Starbucks and the Colts football team, all simply explained by the power of habit. Of course habbit only plays a small role in each of these things. Of course every football game comes down to a little bit of luck (even left up to the wind and the weather). But – someone adopted good habits and later become successful – BOOM – causation – done – problem solved. Beyond the wild conclusions though, there is some real (and recent!) science being done, and our changing understanding of habits is both interesting and powerful. For me the key takeaways are: Habits circumvent our normal process of reasoning (and aren't stored in the same brain-area as planning and short term memory) Habits can be modelled as a sequence of trigger – action – reward. If you're missing one of these pieces, you won't trigger (or learn the habit loop) Habits can live latent for a long time, even as we move on from them. Make no mistake though, this book is meant to be transformative. What can YOU do to change YOUR life, just like Peyton Manning did? Again, the science is mixed here, but it seems like the author's point is: Habits are hard to un-learn, but it's easier if you break them down into the trigger – action – reward lifecycle. If you can swap out the action, but keep the trigger and reward the same, you can hijack your bad habits to learn good behavior. If you want to make a transformative change, it's easiest to focus all your attention on one habit, and then the rest are likely to follow. Habits can be a good thing. Thinking is hard, and deciding what to do takes effort. If something (like choosing what to make for dinner) takes mental effort, your less likely to do it, because that mental effort is as much work as the actual cooking. Try to form habits, and try to think about what you're going to do ahead of time, so that when you get to the moment of truth, it doesn't take effort. 10. Modern Monetary Theory and You Like any political agenda, modern monetary theory isn't perfectly specified, and people often tailor its definition to their own ambitions. As best I can tell it goes like this: If you're a country that controls its own currency, its ok to go into debt, and you can print as much money as you want as long as it doesn't cause inflation. Some people argue that with the power of MMT, we have the money to finance all of our wildest hopes and dreams, if somebody would just have the courage to turn on the money printer. Free college, loan reimbursement, free housing, we could pay for everything with a click of a button, and no negative long-term reprecussions. As long as we don't cause inflation, there really isn't anything to worry about. 10.1. The Big If The thing is, that's a pretty big if. You can "prove" anything you want if you start with a false assumption. If we could print infinite money, and not cause inflation, that'd be pretty awesome, but is such a thing even possible? How did we get here, and why does anybody believe we can do this? In theory, economics is based on supply and demand. If everyone wants apples, but there are no apples available, the price of apples goes up. If nobody wants apples, but every citizen has a stockpile of 100 apples, the price (and the implied value of apples) goes down. In the same way, if everyone in the United States magically had 12 million dollars, they'd all be competing to use that money to buy the same limited supply of things. Many people want 3-bedroom houses, but there aren't magically more of them. It's the same people competing with each other to buy the same house. In order to outbid someone with 12 million dollars for something they really want, you also need to spend millions of dollars. Fundamentally, people want money so that they can use it to buy goods and services. On a global scale, if every government printed more money, but didn't also increase the global amount of available goods and services, you're not increasing everybody's real buying power, because everyone is still competing to buy the same limited number of goods and services. You only increase real wealth if the number of goods and services produced also increases. 10.2. How We Got Here So if America went out tommorrow, and started printing tons of money, and taking on tons of debt, we'd expect the cost of everything to go way up. We'd expect government bonds to be much less valuable, right? Right? Well it turns out that during the 2008 financial crisis, the U.S. did print a lot of money, and did take on a lot of extra debt, and everybody expected inflation to happen, but somehow it just… didn't. Markets are hard to reason about, and nobody really understands why it happened, but people have thrown around some theories: The United States is considered a trustworthy institution, and people need a safe place to put their money. The world financial system is already so invested in the U.S. dollar that the U.S. can do whatever it wants. The stimulus bill spurred so much economic growth that it offset inflation. 10.3. The United States as a Trustworthy Institution Ok, so, we took on a lot of debt before, and it was fine. We printed a truly wild amount of money, and people still trusted us as a stable, reliable institution. Everyone believed that the U.S. government would pay them back, and would pay them back in dollars that held value. Even in a crisis caused by the U.S. economy, the U.S. looked like a safe place to put your money because the U.S. always had been so responsible, and so reliable in the past. So – if we suddenly started being irresponsible, like, racking up huge debts and printing money to pay them back, people will keep lending to us forever, right? Right?? If we don't produce anything, we can just keep printing money forever, and people will just give us stuff, right? There's this idea that because we're borrowing in U.S. dollars, and that U.S. dollars are the de-facto currency of the world, we're never in trouble, because we can just print more money to cover our losses. But do you think people will keep lending to us if, in terms of real physical goods, we're not offering anything meaningful in return? Do you think people will continue to use USD as their default currency if the U.S. government buys all your stuff, but gives you paper, and no items in return? We could technically pay off our debts by printing a shit ton of money, but from an investing perspective, it would be essentially the same as default. We made a promise, and in terms of goods and services, we're not providing any real value to fulfill that promise. Defaulting on a loan is so dangerous because it destroys your credit. If you go bankrupt, it's super hard to get another loan because people don't trust you anymore. In the same way, even if the U.S. doesn't technically default on its debt, if it covers up by printing more money, it's essentially going to have the same effect because people won't trust us anymore. We can "cash in" on our current trust and influence, but once we break that trust we can't rely on it as strongly anymore. 10.4. Take From the Rich and Give to the Poor The argument goes something like this: Wealthy people have money, and poor people don't have money. So, if we print some extra money, and give it to poor people, it lowers the value of the rich people's money, effectively taking buying power from rich people and redistributing it to poor people. It accomplishes a goal people were already after, in a way that's clean and simple. The thing is – rich people don't own wealth in dollars. The very rich know that dollars aren't necessarily stable, and they own houses, stock in businesses, and even precious art. When you inflate the values of dollars, it doesn't really affect a lot of the rich people, but it does hurt others. The people that it does hurt are the ones governed by a fixed $15 (or less) minimum wage. The people it does hurt are the lower-middle class people that don't know much about investing, and just keep all their money in a savings account. It helps people who are in debt, and might have some other positive effects, but for many it's more a destabilizing element than it is helpful. 10.5. Stimulus and Economic Growth Ok so there's a real argument here. The idea is – it's ok to print money because we can generate more goods and services. If we spend it wisely – build bridges, improve broadband, we can create jobs for people who were previously out of work. What's more, that new infrastructure and spending will spur even further economic growth. If for every dollar we spend, it generates $N dollars of economic activity (how is it even possible to reliably calculate these things?), then we're not just printing money, we're printing value. This is one of those arguments that I like because it's logically consistent. If we produce more goods and services, then even though there's more dollars in circulation, there's also more stuff to buy with those dollars. If it really creates that much growth, then it works. The challenge here is it's extremely optimistic. Is your government so smart and well organized that it's going to create 10 trillion dollars worth of value? It might. We've had our shining moments, and I'm hopeful that we'll make it count, but most of the time it doesn't work out that way. 11. The Perfect Camera Every year, sometime around the holidays, I splurge on one really nice thing for myself. Locked inside during quarantine, there hasn't been much to spend on, but I've had a great time doing landscape photography. We still haven't been to bars and restaurants, but we can drive around in a car, and we've been exploring parks in and around New Jersey. This year I set my mind on a new camera. Something a little bit nicer than I already had, maybe that I could use to print pictures and big posters. I bought my first camera in December of 2018. I remember spending ages picking something out, and eventually settling on a Nikon Z6. I really wanted a D850, but along with lenses it was too expensive for consideration. I also looked into the D750, but even though I liked the idea of an optical viewfinder, mirrorless seemed to be the way of the future, and an old DSLR would make me a dinosour. I also looked into some other brands, but Canon didn't have great mirrorless options yet, and I didn't love Sony as a company. Fast forward two years later, and here I was in the same spot, spending ages to pick out a camera. In the mean time, I also had the chance to try out an old school DSLR (the D610), and I absolutely loved it. The image quality was better (SOOC at least). The optical viewfinder was a relief to use. Even more than that, the whole camera was just so well thought out and well constructed. Every button was in exactly the right place and there was always a button when I wanted one. Things like white balance, buried in menus on the Z6 were just one tap here. They even had a well functioning assist light that basically solved all my problems with low light focus. It felt like whenever I needed something, I reached out and the D610 had an answer. This time I had spent so little during the course of the pandemic, I decided it was time to go for a really nice camera. Every brand/style was on the table. I decided that I was going to get the best camera, and then not have to think about upgrading it again, at least not for a really long time. Of course, I quickly found out that it's not so easy. Even if you had all the money in the world, different cameras have different tradeoffs. The ones with the best image quality are big and bulky. Some cameras technically have lower dynamic range, but beautiful and natural image rendering. Mirrorless cameras have face and eye detect, but miss that great optical and mechanical feeling. Really each camera gives you a different experience, and different cameras are "the best" in different situations. If you're taking selfies you want a flippy screen. If you're bringing a camera to dinner, you want something fashionable and lightweight. If you're shooting an event, you need the very best in reliability and focus tracking. I definitely wanted something small that I could take to game night with my friends, but I also wanted something (potentially big and heavy) that could shoot landscapes with the very best image quality. I very quickly realized that I wanted different setups for different situations I was in, and that no camera was going to be perfect for everything for me. Between everything, I kind of narrowed it down to three situations I usually shoot in: Photo walks. I set out specifically to take nice landscape photos. I want an enjoyable shooting experience and the ultimate image quality. Less weight is nice, but I don't really mind heavier cameras or slower autofocus too much. Friends and Family memories. This is the camera that I'm taking to hang out and play minigolf. I don't need the ultimate image quality, but I want something unobtrusive and super reliable. I care that I'm going to get a usable image in any and every situation. If the family photo in front of the Eiffel tower comes out blurry, we're not making another trip, and we're not spending 2 hours readjusting to get the perfect shot. It's also important here that if someone else is taking the picture, it still comes out nice. Portraits/selfies – this is somewhere in between the two above. You have more time to set up your environment/carry the right lenses, but you still want fairly reliable face/eye detect. 4.1 The Contenders 4.1.1 Canon Canon makes professional dslr and mirrorless cameras. It is a 4 year old camera, but it's my favorite, and I think it will remain competitive for a very long time. 12. Camera Lenses: What's in My Bag Camera lenses are expensive. If you own a DSLR, chances are your lenses cost more than the camera body itself. This is because lenses are often the bottleneck for image quality. If you're looking through a blurry window, it doesn't matter how sensitive your sensor is. In addition, camera lenses come in all sorts of shapes and sizes. Physical limitations mean you can't have one lens that just does everything. If your lens has a massive zoom range, then it probably sacrifices some image quality. You want to choose the lens that's right for the situation you're shooting. If you want to find the right glass for you, you should think about the situations you take photographs first, and then choose a lens that is appropriate for that situation. Unless you're in a studio, or have a very patient subject, chances are you don't want to switch lenses on the fly, so you want a lens that encompasses the entirety of that situation. So what's in my bag? 5.1 The portrait lens: Tamron 35-150mm f/2.8-4 Most pro photographers carry two zoom lenses, one 24-70 f/2.8 and one 70-200 f/2.8. But for portraits, neither of these gets you entirely what you want. 85mm is widely considered the "standard" portrait length, but 50mm and even 35mm are also common. The problem is, the range of focal lengths used for portraits is like a normal distribution centered around 70mm. In order to get the right photo, you'd need to constantly swap between the two lenses. I've used a 24-70 for portraits, and I found myself constantly near the long end of the zoom range, often wishing I had just a little more. The Tamron 35-150 is perfect because the center of it's zoom range is also the center of the range I use for portraits. It has a little more zoom (5x vs 3x) than the standard 24-70, but it's not one of these ultra super zooms that sacrifices on image quality. Most of the lab tests rate it similarly to some of the older 70-200 f/2.8 lenses, so you're not losing much over one of the more standard zooms. In addition, it's quite fast. It's variable aperture, so you lose some of that speed at the long end of the zoom range, but 2.8 at 35mm is just as fast as a standard 24-70. This means if you find yourself indoors without a flash, it's still sometimes usable. There isn't quite an everything and the kitchen sink lens, but for me this is as close as it gets. I'll often use it if I'm going on a day trip somewhere unsure of what I'm going to be shooting. The downsides are it's very large (especially with an FTZ adapter), it focuses a little slower and less reliably than some of the native Z lenses, and it's a little less sharp and less fast than a good prime lens. 5.2 In the dark: 50mm f/1.8 G Ok, well, I'm currently looking to upgrade my 50mm to a different lens of the same type, either the 50mm f/1.8 Z or the 50mm f/1.4 Sigma Art. I bought it because it was cheap, and did something none of my other lenses had. It's not even sharper than my zoom lenses at it's only focal length of 50mm, but it does have one thing those zoom lenses do not: a maximum aperature of f/1.8. If it's dark, and you need light, a fast prime is your only option. Once you're already cranking your camera's ISO the extra stop over an f/2.8 makes a huge difference. A fixed length prime is the least flexible, but it's important when you need it. Also, most fixed length lenses are sharper than their zoomy counterparts, but not this one :(. 5.3 Lightweight Travel/Group Photos: 24-70mm f/4 S I'm gonna be honest, the only reason why I own this lens is it was half off when it came with my camera. Don't get me wrong, it's still a good lens, but I probably wouldn't have gone out and purchased it on my own. What I like about this lens is that it's super reliable. It's a native Z mount lens on a Z body camera, and the autofocus just works better than any of the other lenses on the same camera. The image quality is also consistently good at f/4 throughout the zoom range, so much so that I don't have to think about it. If I'm going out for the day with casual people, this is the lens that I take. Most people don't want to wait while you fiddle with your settings, and most group photos don't care about artistic framing. The people care that you got the shot, the one where everyoen was smiling, and it didn't come out weird. If it's blurry that's really bad and you likely don't have that many do-overs. It's also super small on the Z body, and feels nicely balanced. Most travel photos I take are wide-angle anyway, because I want to capture the environment, and you're often in those situations where you have to pull the shot quickly and not mess it up. The lack of light can be inconvenient sometimes, but so far it hasn't been worth it to me to shell out for the much better (and much more expensive) 24-70mm f/2.8 S lens. 13. Why Many Primary Forecasts are Wrong Ok, wrong might be a little bit too severe, but at the very least unfairly biased. I think most models underestimate Warren and Sander's chances of winning the primary because it evaluates the voting in every state as a single event, rather than viewing the primaries as a sequential selection process. In past elections, while the later states still matter, the early voting states have had special significance because they narrow down the pool of candidates by eliminating out candidates which seem unlikely to win. Let's say you're a Democratic moderate. Even if you really really like Tulsi Gabbard, you're probably not going to vote for her, because you know that if you do, your vote won't matter. Since she's not going to run anyway, you might as well vote for Mayor Pete or Joe Biden. When the votes from the early states come in, they tell the people what candidates are unlikely to win. When a candidate does badly in an early state, people become less willing to vote for them and they become even more unlikely to win. While eventually the race usally comes down to two or three, often closely split candidates, it's important to remember that primary elections are an unstable equillibrium, and it can be easy for things to snowball. Right now Biden is by most polling clear favorite to win the election, with roughly double the odds of the next major candidate. But it's important to remember that this is because Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders split the progressive vote, and their policies and supporters are in many ways very similar. If one or the other starts to outpreform in some of the early states, they're going to start picking up all of the progressive votes, and start to become competitive in the states where Biden was heavily favored. While Biden could also gain some ground from early victories, he has less room to grow because the moderate vote is less split, and the other candidates to gain from like Mayor Pete, have some significant ideological differences. 14. The Wonky Math behind the Democratic Primary Oh man, if you thought the electoral college was bad, you're in for a real treat. On paper, it looks like primaries are mostly the same process. Every state gets "electoral college delegates", and the number of delegates for each state is the same as in the presidential election: two plus some extra porportionate to the state's population. The thing is, the number of delegates is porportional to the state's TOTAL population, not the number of people that actually vote in the election. If California has 50 million citizens, but only 5 people actually vote, those 5 people have tremendous influence. In primaries, certain states are dominated by particular parties. That means even though Tennessee has 5 million elligible citizens, it only has 400 thousand voting in the Democratic primary. That means if you're a Democrat in Tenessee, you have much more influence than a Democrat from California. The state is considered large even though the number of Democrats actually voting is small. 7.1 Biden is Winning in States with Low Voter Turnout Ever wonder why Biden seems so unpopular with so many voters, yet forecasts frequently predict him to win the election? Biden's best state's, according to 538: Alabama, Mississippi ,Delaware ,South Carolina, North Carolina, and Louisiana, are ALL low Democratic voter turnout states. Biden isn't actually that popular with the Democratic party overall, but it doesn't matter because he's disporportionately popular among the subsets of people that have the most voting power. By contrast, take a look at the best states for Bernie Sanders: Vermont, Utah, Washington, California, Colorado, New Hampshire, all heavily Democratic states. Because he's appealing to more liberal states, and because his message resonates with certain groups of people, he's being disproportionately hurt by the electoral college relative to his popularity. https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/biden-is-the-front-runner-but-there-is-no-clear-favorite/ 15.
