title: Total Annihilation, rebuilt for modern computers
body_text: Nanolathe: an open-source engine for Total Annihilation Skip to content nanolathe Menu ＋ Get started Features Documentation About GitHub ↗ Play the demo Staged battle in Nanolathe Modern GPU renderer · Silent Play video Total Annihilation, rebuilt for modern computers. Nanolathe is an open-source engine for playing Total Annihilation on Windows, Mac and Linux. It loads the original maps, units and campaigns. You can try it right here with the three-mission browser demo. Play the demo ↗ Install the beta ▶ Watch footage 0:43 The demo needs no game files or installation. Use desktop Chrome, Edge or Safari with a keyboard and mouse. Public beta Campaign, skirmish, Survival and online play are available. Expect bugs and some compatibility gaps. A Jeffy explodes on Greenhaven The Modern renderer lights the Bulldog beside it and adds detail to the grass and trees. Drag the divider to compare with Classic. Classic CPU renderer Modern 2× art · light · glow ‹ › Both captures show the same moment at 2× zoom. Modern adds synthesized terrain and trees, lighting and glow. Captured at 960×640 in a staged scene. Classic Split Modern Capture settings and original files Captured with engine 617540c5 on October 4, 2026. This compares full renderer paths: Modern includes supersampling and its default presentation effects. The tile cache was generated from the installed game’s original 32×32 tiles into 64×64 synthesized tiles. Healthy tree sprites use 2× synthesized feature banks; shadow or missing variants retain the engine’s normal fallback. Authored dead stumps are cleared from this staged display. No screenshot cropping, retouching or resampling was used. WebP exports decode to the exact captured pixels. Open full Classic capture · Open full Modern capture More renderer comparisons Why rebuild TA? I played Total Annihilation as a teenager and got into making mods and 3D models. Years later I wanted to get it running on my MacBook Pro, and that eventually became a project to recreate the engine. Nanolathe loads the original game data directly, including the scripts that turn turrets and open factory doors. First I’m trying to match how TA works. Once that’s reliable, it’s much easier to try changes and see what they actually do. The code is written in Go and available under the MIT license. Daniel Taylor · More about the project Engine source on GitHub ↗ File formats and research Playing the beta The browser demo has three original campaign missions. For the full game, you’ll need your own installed TA folder. You can play skirmish and Survival with friends, including between desktop and browser players. Save compatibility is still being worked on. Online games don’t support saving or reconnecting yet. Installation and game files → Before you play Is this the original Total Annihilation? It’s a new engine that runs the original game’s data. Nanolathe reimplements TA through clean-room research and is an independent project, unaffiliated with the game’s owners. Do I need to own Total Annihilation? You can play the three-mission browser demo without it. For the full game, use the installed files from a copy you own, such as GOG, Steam or the original CDs. Nanolathe’s MIT license covers the engine code; TA’s artwork and other game content have separate terms. How complete is it? Single-player campaign, skirmish and Survival are broadly complete. Bugs and smaller missing features remain, and compatibility varies by mission and content pack. Skirmish and Survival battles are recorded as replays. The gameplay reference lists the systems implemented so far. Which browsers work? The demo supports desktop Chrome, Edge and Safari with a keyboard and mouse. Firefox, phones and tablets haven’t been verified. The demo downloads its game files on first launch and caches them for later visits. For larger battles, install the native beta . How do I play with friends? Choose MULTI on the main menu, create a game and send its code to your friends. Skirmish supports 2 to 10 players; Survival supports 2 or 3. Everyone needs their own game files, so the three-mission demo can’t join online games. The installed game and desktop Chrome or Edge can play together. See the online guide for rules, computer players, alliances and sharing. Nanolathe engine footage × From the announcement reel. Watch on YouTube nanolathe A spare-time project by Daniel Taylor. Play the demo About Brand kit Website source ↗ An independent, MIT-licensed engine project. Total Annihilation belongs to its respective owners. Nanolathe is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
body_text: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Home News US & Canada UK UK Politics England N. Ireland N. Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Theo Leggett International Business Correspondent Stellantis French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market. The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs. As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028. As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors. Farmers’ favourite Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow". The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around. The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs. Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair. The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists. Getty Images Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000. The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor. The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses". By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road. VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success. BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades. Retro-nostalgia But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers. Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well. VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta. Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense. "It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect." Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands. "Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data. Getty Images Back to the future: VW looked to the past when designing its ID-Buzz minivan In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis. "In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says. "The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there." But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller. "A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says. "But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal." title: Making big downloads resumable in Firefox
body_text: Making big downloads resumable in firefox Olivia's silly blog Menu Navigation Blog TIL Notes and random thoughts Some of my projects Things I use Misc gateway Making big downloads resumable in firefox Olivia Published on 2026-10-11 at 17:56:29+02:00 License: CC-by-SA 4.0 (text), MIT (code) firefox For whatever reason, Firefox 28 and newer (i.e. every modern version after like 2014 ) ships with network.http.response.timeout set to 300 seconds. This seems to interfere with resuming big downloads, as well as the general stability of big downloads. Setting network.http.response.timeout to 0 (or something very big) in about:config seems to make big downloads both resumable and at least a little more stable. I don't understand why this works, but experimental testing supports it. Note that this assumes the server supports resumable downloads; if it doesn't, no settings in firefox or any other browser are going to help. However, the problem this fixes is firefox being unable to resume a resumable download on error. I don't entirely know if this is the case, but it experimentally looks like resumable downloads in firefox rely on connection timeouts rather than the .part files they download. Firefox will happily ignore an existing .part without this option, and I do not understand why. Resumable downloads in firefox generally appear to be fairly unstable though. This has been a known problem in some form since as far back as 2005 . I also found that there's a manual .part shuffle to make firefox actually resume downloads , but I'm not doing that shit. As a non-firefox workaround, using wget -c -O "$filename" "$url" also works, and wget overall appears to be fairly stable. I do also suspect firefox does some hidden retries if it can before it considers the download to have failed - from some experimental testing, it does appear that this is at least partly related to network.http.response.timeout , and that exceeding the timeout interferes with this process. I have not attempted to confirm any of this with FF's source code, because I have no clue where to look. title: A look at the math that OpenAI claims computes faster Fourier transforms
body_text: Faster Fourier Transforms - by Ben Recht - arg min arg min Subscribe Sign in Faster Fourier Transforms The OpenAI algorithm for the FFT is less a breakthrough and more a malicious exploit. Ben Recht Oct 12, 2026 220 37 38 Share Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity. The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum. The Fourier transform computes the energy in each frequency band through a simple dot product. 1 Let x denote your input, a length n array of samples, and f a frequency. Then the amount of frequency content in x at f can be computed by the formula: For digital signals, a bit of math shows you only need to compute n of these dot products, one at each multiple of the frequency 2𝜋/n, to understand all of the frequency content. Naively, this requires n multiplications and additions for each frequency. Hence, computing the entire Fourier transform appears to require n 2 arithmetic operations. The fast Fourier transform is a clever recursive procedure devised by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965. 2 The main idea is that a length-n Fourier transform can be computed by shuffling the input vector, computing two Fourier transforms of length n/2 on the shuffled components, and then recombining the outputs using atomic arithmetic operations. The shuffles and recombinations take a linear number of arithmetic operations. Repeating this procedure iteratively, namely, log 2 (n) times, computes the full discrete Fourier transform. With the bookkeeping, the FFT computes a length-n Fourier transform in fewer than 5 n log2 n arithmetic operations. To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application. Since the invention of the FFT, people have looked for even faster Fourier transforms. One question is just how fast you can go. It seems like you probably need at least n operations to compute the FFT, as it takes n steps just to write it down. The FFT is 5*log 2 (n) times slower than that reasonable speed limit, and that 5*log 2 (n) factor can be big. It’s 200 when n is a trillion. Can you do something clever to reduce that prefactor of 200? Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” is I was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT. Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world. Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead, I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language. First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such that That is, the number of steps the algorithm actually takes is upper bounded by a constant times some convenient function F(n) as long as n is large. F(n) is usually something familiar and interpretable, like a polynomial or exponential function. This notation says that we only care about what happens when the size of the computation is large. We care about the asymptotic growth rate of the computation time. All constants are equivalent. Big-O notation is useful for shortcuts in algorithmic accounting, but it also allows for remarkable logical laziness. If we want a practically faster FFT, we want an algorithm that requires fewer than 50n operations for reasonably sized n. But O(n) does not mean 50 n. It could mean 10 80 n. This would be considered a “linear time” algorithm. An algorithm that requires n + 10 80 is also considered a linear time algorithm in the big-O regime. An algorithm that only has linear-time guarantees when n is greater than 10 80 is also considered linear time. 10 80 is approximately equal to the number of atoms in the known universe. That is why Richard Lipton and Ken Regan call algorithms with unfathomably large hidden constants galactic algorithms . The OpenAI FFT algorithm is definitely galactic. The estimated values for C were 10 100 when N=10 12 . So even when n=10 100 , the venerable Cooley-Tukey-Gauss FFT would be 10 99 times faster. So why is this new FFT result interesting? Well, note that in big-O notation, it is technically asymptotically faster than the Cooley-Tukey algorithm because I mean, sure. But given the constants, the algorithm runs faster only when n is impossibly large. Roughly, you need whatever the hell that number means. Lipton and Regan argue galactic algorithms are useful because they spur research. Once you show a running time is asymptotically possible, you can spend your time finding an algorithm that practically achieves this provable running time. Maybe you can send your AI agent swarms after it. You do you. Maybe you can get a practical algorithm out, but I don’t know of any legitimate examples where this happened. I’m particularly doubtful here, because the model of “computation” OpenAI uses bears no resemblance to an actual computer. “The model uses exact complex arithmetic.” That means it assumes you can store and multiply complex numbers at arbitrary precision. Indeed, the algorithm requires you to multiply complex numbers whose magnitudes grow superpolynomially with n. If you stored these numbers as bits, the memory requirement would effectively be exponential in the input length. It assumes you can multiply such arbitrarily large complex numbers together in a single operation. We do not have computers that can do this. So even if this theorem in main.pdf is “true” (no one knows, and I don’t care), it’s not actually solving the problem we set out to solve when looking for a faster FFT. For people familiar with theoretical analyses of the FFT, that you need an absurd model of computation to break the FFT speed limit isn’t surprising. In 1973, Jacques Morgenstern proved that you couldn’t get a Fourier transform faster than ½ n log n if you required that complex coefficients used in the computation had bounded magnitude. That should have been the end of the story! But it wasn’t. People said Morgenstern’s restricted coefficient model was too restrictive. Forty years later, Nir Ailon showed that you couldn’t compute an FFT faster than n log n without severe numerical instabilities . This was also too restrictive for some people, I guess. This new OpenAI result is thus less a mathematical breakthrough and more an oddity of computer scientists being bad at formalizing their design specifications. The “theoretical” definition of a computer is very far removed from the computers we actually build. The “faster” Fourier transform is merely an example where theory gets so unmoored from the original question that an “open problem” becomes nothing more than an academic status puzzle. The solution is like what happens when you set computational bot streams at impossible problems and find them engaging in illegal hacking . Many of the other “big” results in this OpenAI slopository could be critiqued in the same way. For example, one of those results was a galactic algorithm to multiply two matrices in O(n^2.25) operations. The construction used in the paper does not let you even estimate the constant that hides inside big O. 3 It may as well be infinite, computable only with the divine music of the spheres. Still, if written substantially better, these papers would have made it into the most prestigious publication venues for the theory of computer science (i.e., refereed conference proceedings from STOC or FOCS). 4 The matrix multiplication paper would have likely won awards. But neither of these has anything to do with computers! This is because the theory of computer science has a culture that actively discourages running algorithms on a computer. It’s acceptable to write papers in theory conferences that assert an algorithm exists without ever writing it down. The theory of computer science has become a form of mathematics that doesn’t concern itself with computers, and it offers little reward for impact outside those mathematical pursuits. I explained this to a friend who remarked to me that “theory” has the transdisciplinary meaning of “hiding in obscurity of one’s own making.” AI is really good at automating our worst tendencies. It amplifies the unspoken cultural practices no one likes, but no individual can reasonably deviate from. It exploits the mechanized traditions recalcitrant to collective action. In that vein, AI can now write useless theory papers. But perhaps in the absurdity of the distasteful OpenAI trash dump of proofs, we can all look up and realize together that we should consider doing something else. Subscribe 1 Kids these days call it cosine similarity. 2 The wikipedia page says it should be credited to Gauss in 1805! Proper credit assignment is a perennial problem in academia. 3 That one shows that for every epsilon greater than 0, there is a constant C so that T(n) <= n^(2.25 +epsilon + C/log(n)). No matter which queries I try, I can’t get an OpenAI model to give a quantitative estimate of C. Whatever! 4 Another bad tradition is computer science choosing its most prestigious venues as hastily reviewed conference proceedings. 220 37 38 Share Previous Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Kevin Lacker 2d Liked by Ben Recht One nice thing about proving that something is possible epsilon faster than O(f(n)) time is that you can stop looking for a proof that the best you can do is O(f(n)). Reply Share Joe Jordan 2d Liked by Ben Recht Thanks for writing this up. A few weeks ago Anthropic publushed a blog post about "using claude to speed up protein structure prediction." I did a little testing myself and found that basically 100% of the "speedup" was from turning on cuda graphs and all the "optimized kernels" did not add much. Good (in some cosmic sense) to see that the pattern is similar for these math results. Reply Share 1 reply by Ben Recht 35 more comments... Top Latest Discussions No posts Ready for more? title: Muse Wonder
body_text: Muse Wonder: A Frontier Model For Personal & Professional AI Agents Skip to main content AI Research AI Developers Try Muse Loading demo Muse Wonder: A Frontier Model For Personal & Professional AI Agents October 12, 2026 · 6 minute read Play Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Play Show captions for Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Show captions Mute Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Mute Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. playback position 0:00 of 0:00 00:00 / 00:00 A frontier model that leads on personal and professional agents Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together Active Memory and Active Focus to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish. Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code , and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers. Muse Wonder will soon power experiences in Muse , and will roll out first to subscribers. Muse Wonder will also power artifact generation and processes that require more intelligence. And in the future, we’ll be using Muse Wonder to develop specialized models that we can bring to everyone using Muse. Contents Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence Frontier Capabilities Capabilities That Generalize Safety at the Frontier Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence Fourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier. When we introduced Muse Spark , we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products. Frontier Capabilities Model Highlights The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding. The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite. For more details about our evaluations, see our report . The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding. Domain Expertise Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products. Active Memory One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this Active Memory : carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand. Active Focus Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. Active Focus describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects. Frontier Coding Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process. Kitchen Game Wellness Support Insurance Claim Kitchen Game Loading demo Muse Wonder builds a playable 3D kitchen game from customizable image inputs. Capabilities That Generalize Two models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture. To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”). Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training. Saturday Run Planning Personalized Gifts Wedding Seating Chart Saturday Run Planning Play Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration. Play Show captions for Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration. Show captions Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration. playback position 0:00 of 0:00 00:00 / 00:00 Working directly in a browser and across apps, Muse Wonder builds a running plan (Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors) based on personal preferences and circumstances. Muse Wonder designs and orders custom swag based on real photos taken from a personal Instagram profile. Muse Wonder prepares a custom wedding seating chart based on a list of complex matching requirements. Safety at the Frontier Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information. As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework . Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon. We hope that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full give more people the power to pursue their dreams and build the world they want. This is a major technical step toward personal superintelligence for everyone, with much more to come. Play People pursue personal and professional goals as narration introduces Muse Wonder. title: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening
body_text: Andrej Karpathy on X: "Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely co… / X Post Log in Sign up Post Log in Sign up Andrej Karpathy on X: "Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time." For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex , Linux (WSL2) What feature would you like to see? Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false ) for the CLI , or at least ask once before turning it on. Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session: Starts a persistent background daemon ( codex app-server --managed-daemon ). It runs in its own session with no TTY and keeps running after every Codex window is closed (reparented to PID 1) until codex app-server daemon stop or a reboot. Copies the whole platform package (~374 MB: codex , codex-code-mode-host , bundled bwrap / zsh / rg ) into ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/<version>/ — byte-identical to what npm had just installed — and runs the daemon from that copy. From then on the backend's version is decoupled from the CLI version I installed with my package manager. Starts a detached updater ( codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop ) that checks for updates 5 minutes after start and then hourly, downloads new releases and restarts the backend (which can kill active turns, see app-server daemon: auto-update force-kills active turns after a 60s drain budget, and cannot be disabled #40969 ). Pins the environment of whichever session happened to start it. I launch Codex through a wrapper that sets HTTPS_PROXY per invocation; the daemon keeps the first session's proxy variables and its outbound connections go through that proxy, whatever later sessions are launched with. Hooks in --remote mode receive the daemon's cwd, not the session's #42457 and Hooks spawned by the app-server daemon cannot identify the client terminal, breaking terminal-targeting hooks #37537 (daemon cwd / terminal instead of the session's) look like the same root cause. For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when the user explicitly runs codex app-server daemon start / bootstrap . If it stays on by default, please at least: exit an auto-started daemon when its last client disconnects; not copy/self-update when the CLI was installed by a package manager (npm/brew/pacman) — run the installed binary instead ( Support externally managed app-server daemon executables #41188 , npm update leaves app-server on old version, but daemon update/restart refuse recovery #46468 , Codex 0.157.0 no longer starts with the Arch Linux package unless --no-daemon is used #48050 ). Additional information Bug found while turning it off: codex app-server daemon stop stops the app-server but leaves the pid-update-loop updater running (still alive 70 s later, had to kill it manually). Workaround I'm using: codex features disable daemon_auto_start codex app-server daemon stop pkill -f ' app-server daemon pid-update-loop ' # not stopped by `daemon stop` rm -rf ~ /.codex/packages/app-server-daemon With the flag off, a new TUI session no longer spawns a daemon. Related: #40969 , #41188 , #46468 , #48050 , #42457 , #37537 Reactions are currently unavailable Activity github-actions added enhancement New feature or request New feature or request CLI Issues related to the Codex CLI Issues related to the Codex CLI app-server Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces on Sep 25, 2026 megahall commented on Sep 25, 2026 megahall on Sep 25, 2026 More actions @Yihua-Liu-1997 thanks for reporting this, I hit it myself... stuff should not be creating mystery servers and processes all of a sudden on small version number bumps without giving people a heads-up... 👍 React with 👍 21 Reacted by tagor, Flaviu Tamas, Felipe Lopes, Josh Triplett, BigBoyDevBox, Kamil Mielnik, Mikhail, Ayanami Kaine, Mike Elliott, Alexander Williamson and 11 more kr8vka0z commented on Sep 25, 2026 kr8vka0z on Sep 25, 2026 More actions agreed. the CLI is unusable until this is fixed. 👍 React with 👍 27 Reacted by tagor, Steven Dale, Felipe Lopes, krrr, Shaun Pedicini, Christian Hahn, BigBoyDevBox, Mikhail, Ayanami Kaine, Mike Elliott and 17 more tagorr commented on Sep 25, 2026 tagorr on Sep 25, 2026 More actions I can confirm this on Windows 10 LTSC with Codex CLI 0.157.0 Setting daemon_auto_start = false in config.toml resolves the issue Two improvements would help: Automatically fall back to local mode when daemon startup is blocked by elevation, instead of requiring --no-daemon . Make daemon auto-start opt-in rather than the default. This would preserve the security restrictions without disrupting the normal CLI workflow. 👍 React with 👍 4 Reacted by BigBoyDevBox, Leo Razoumov, CodePencil and Lucas Tavares Yihua-Liu-1997 commented on Sep 26, 2026 Yihua-Liu-1997 on Sep 26, 2026 Author More actions @tagorr Indeed — both 1 and 2 would work~ ❤️ React with ❤️ 2 Reacted by tagor and CodePencil breakds added a commit that references this issue on Sep 28, 2026 codex: disable daemon auto-start by default ... b51c036 felipeelopes commented on Sep 29, 2026 felipeelopes on Sep 29, 2026 More actions The Codex CLI is unusable due to this bug on Windows. zdd commented on Sep 30, 2026 zdd on Sep 30, 2026 More actions This is terrible. You should fix this problem as soon as possible and give us 100 banked reset! aetherxeg-source commented on Oct 3, 2026 aetherxeg-source on Oct 3, 2026 – with ChatGPT Codex Connector More actions There is a useful provenance boundary behind this request: installed CLI identity != daemon execution identity Once the CLI copies itself into a managed release directory and a background updater can replace that copy, the process that services a later turn is no longer necessarily the artifact the user explicitly installed or invoked. title: Thinking will become a hobby
body_text: blog dds: 2026-10-08 â Thinking will become a hobby Diomidis Spinellis blog Thinking will become a hobby Search   Search the blog Close These lines are very difficult for me to write because I feel like digging my own grave. AI systems are improving by leaps and bounds. From the early 2022 fumbling release of ChatGPT, which couldnât correctly count the number of aâs in my name (it claimed two), we reached OpenAIâs release of math papers where an internal AI model solved many hundreds of previously open math problems. Aside from philosophical arguments, practical claims regarding the superiority of human thought, on grounds such as hallucinations or bias, increasingly appear to me like rearguard defence. For the bulk of todayâs cognitive work, the writingâs on the wall: AI will take over. The three factors driving AIâs dominance in the modern work environment are better performance, lower cost, and higher availability. The performance of AI models is rising spectacularly on all fronts: perception, knowledge processing and creation, reasoning, judgement, and autonomous action. In parallel, human proficiency in key information-processing skills, low on average among adults , is even declining among students . Consequently, AI systems are performing better than humans in ever-wider range of tasks. AIâs cost is also falling due to huge investments and scientific progress. Successive generations of AI models offer superior performance at lower cost, with older models retained only for backward compatibility. As a result, it is making financial sense to replace or augment human labour with AI systems across an increasingly broad range of activities. Finally, and most obviously, AI systems can operate around the clock, without the need for rest or breaks. They can also help alleviate labour shortages arising from demographic trends or skills gaps. Meanwhile, trillions of dollars in projected data centre investment through 2030 are set to bring vast additional AI processing capacity online. As happened in past technological revolutions, there will undoubtedly be fierce resistance to the replacement of cognitive work with AI. This time it will be fiercer because, unlike previous revolutions, which transformed manual labour, AI challenges knowledge workers, whose specialised expertise, control over information, and decision-making authority afford them greater economic and organisational power. Governments will try to clip AIâs wings through regulation and taxation. Such actions didnât quell past revolutions so thereâs little reason to believe theyâll work now. So whatâs the fate of human thought? My take is that cognitive work will diminish. Thought will increasingly become a leisure pursuit, as hunting did following animal domestication, calligraphy after typography, woodworking after industrialisation, and horse riding after motorisation. Machines transformed much of physical activity from necessity into choice; similarly, AI will decouple human thinking from its economic purpose. Iâll end with my thoughts on how to prepare for and live through this transition. My take is that building this AI-driven world, riding through the bumps along the road, and preparing to live a fulfilling and satisfying life in an environment where AI dominates cognitive work will be hugely demanding, stressful, and intellectually challenging. Such is the nature of revolutions. Consequently, we must keep pace with and capitalise on AIâs advances; be flexible, adaptable, and resilient; and build a purposeful and rewarding life beyond work. My challenge ahead is to move from making a living by thinking, to making thinking part of a life worth living. Comments   Post Toot! title: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?
body_text: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?? | purplesyringa's blog purplesyringa about blog kitchen sink Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?? October 12, 2026 Hacker News Lobsters vfmaddrnd231pd is a unique instruction from the FMA instruction set. Most instructions in that set have mnemonics like vfmadd231pd , but here rnd means something very specific. The Intel Software Development Manual documents it as: VFMADDRND231PD – Fused Multiply-Add of Packed Double-Precision Floating-Point Values with rounding control […] The immediate byte defines several bit fields that control rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression (See Table 5-3). Most x86 floating-point instructions use the global rounding mode and settings, changing which is pretty slow. But vfmaddrnd231pd allows the rounding mode to be controlled on a per-instruction basis, and since FMA can emulate addition, subtraction, and multiplication, this mechanism effectively allows any arithmetic to have controllable rounding without AVX-512 – making some algorithms that rely on rounding incredibly faster. Or so it would , if this instruction actually existed. GNU assembler doesn’t recognize it. The Intel C/C++ Compiler intrinsics _mm_fmaddround_pd and _mm256_fmaddround_pd that SDM mentions are absent not only from Clang, but from ICC as well. Trying to assemble the instructions by hand from the SDM opcode list reveals another issue: VEX.DDS.128.66.0F3A.W1 B8 /r /ib VEX is the VEX prefix, but what is DDS ? This opcode is the only mention of DDS in the SDM, and this SO answer says that DDS is merely used for documentation and was removed from later SDM versions, but the fact that it’s still present here is suspicious. And when you actually run the instruction on a CPU that supports the FMA instruction set, like my Haswell, it raises #UD (“UnDefined instruction”)! I already found it strange that the SDM only lists vfmaddrnd231pd and not other variants like using pd / ps / sd / ss or 132 / 213 / 231 , which other FMA instructions have, but this confirmed my suspicions. It was at that point that I downloaded a more recent version of the SDM and noticed that this instruction is absent in the 2026 edition of the SDM, despite being present in the 2024 version. I must say I’m incredibly confused. This instruction doesn’t look like a typo in the documentation, since the docs contain unique tables and pseudocode that isn’t similar to any other instruction. My best hypothesis is that Intel wanted to add the vfmaddrnd* set, then found an issue with it at the last moment and removed it from the CPU, but didn’t quite adjust the SDM correctly. But I have no way to confirm that. If anyone reading this has a friend at Intel, I’d love to know the answer. Update seastarer and 039234562456 gave me enough pointers to crack this. Back in 2023, Intel failed to add AVX-512 support to consumer CPUs due to hardware limitations, but still wanted to add some goodies from AVX-512. That’s how AVX10 was born – a new extension that looked roughly like AVX-512, but had conditional support for 512-bit vector lengths. AVX-512 uses a strange instruction encoding with the EVEX prefix. For compactness, the bits responsible for the static rounding mode are reused for the operation width (128, 256, or 512 bits), so only scalar and 512-bit operations can customize rounding. This was a problem for AVX10, which didn’t support 512-bit operations: if it interpreted the same instruction as operating on 256-bit values instead of 512-bit ones, different CPUs would behave inconsistently. So AVX10 had to use a different encoding for its own custom rounding modes. My theory is that originally, Intel decided that the easiest way to do this was to add an immediate byte that controls the rounding, which is how vfmaddrnd231pd and similar instructions for other arithmetic operations were born. Notice that it uses a VEX prefix, not the AVX-512-specific EVEX prefix – this would allow CPUs without 512-bit vectors to avoid handling the EVEX prefix at all. Since they added an entire byte, they utilized it in full: 2 bits for the rounding mode, 6 bits for everything else they thought might be useful. It seems like by 2024, Intel decided that this approach won’t work. And I get it: it’s odd that vfmaddrnd231pd was more powerful than AVX-512 instructions, but only supported 256-bit vectors. And if it supported 512-bit vectors, the rounding mode control built into AVX-512 would become obsolete for the most part. So Intel bit the bullet, dedicated the last unused bit in the EVEX prefix to enabling rounding modes for 256-bit vectors, and reused the AVX-512 instruction encoding for AVX10. This also allowed them to reuse the AVX-512 assembly syntax and avoid introducing new mnemonics, at which point the vfmaddrnd231pd mnemonic and others became unnecessary. During this process, someone forgot to remove vfmaddrnd231pd specifically from the SDM draft. By 2025, AVX-512 was considered table stakes due to the popularity of Zen 4, and Intel finally decided to make 512-bit support unconditional in AVX10. This made this entire hack unnecessary, so Intel updated the AVX10 whitepaper : Removed references to 256-bit maximum vector register size, enumeration of vector-length support, and 256-bit instructions supporting embedded rounding . …and submitted patches to GCC removing 256-bit rounding support : In this new whitepaper, all the platforms will support 512 bit vector width (previously, E-core is up to 256 bit, leading to hybrid clients and Atom Server 256 bit only). Also, 256 bit rounding is not that useful because we currently have rounding feature directly on E-core now and no need to use 256-bit rounding as somehow a workaround. HW will remove that support. We can partially confirm this theory by inspecting the patches. One of them is named: Revert “AVX10.2 ymm rounding: Support vfmadd{132, 231, 213}p{s, d, h} intrins” …and removes multiple intrinsics, including _mm256_fmadd_round_pd , which is named very similarly to the documented intrinsic for the ghost instruction, _mm256_fmaddround_pd . At a later point, someone at Intel realized that vfmaddrnd231pd was still mentioned in the SDM and removed it. Summing up: I believe that vfmaddrnd231pd is of AVX10 lineage. I think it was added during the prototyping stage of AVX10, then reworked to use a different instruction encoding, until it finally became unnecessary. Market pressures, timing constraints, and weird tech debt affected the design process enough that things had to be reworked on the fly, and at some point someone slipped up and accidentally documented an instruction that has never existed in released hardware. Made with my own bare hands (why.)
